Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2):

Page 62
(Surat al-Kahf)
One hundred and eleven verses, Meccan.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book and has not made therein any crookedness. [He has made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward, in which they will remain forever.﴾

Surat al-Kahf

Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is Meccan, except for two verses in it which mention ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari. And from Qatadah: it is Meccan. And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who said: "Shall I not direct you to a surah which seventy thousand angels escorted when it was revealed? It is Surat al-Kahf."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book and has not made therein any crookedness. [He has made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward, in which they will remain forever.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: As for the discussion of the realities of our saying "All praise is due to Allah," it has already passed. What I say here is: tasbih (glorification) wherever it occurs comes before tahmid (praise). Do you not see that it is said, "Glory be to Allah and all praise is due to Allah"? Having known this, we say: He, majestic is His majesty, mentioned tasbih when He informed that He took Muhammad (ﷺ) on the Night Journey, saying: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ (al-Isra' 17:1), and mentioned tahmid when He mentioned that He sent down the Book upon Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book﴾. And in this there are benefits:

The first benefit: tasbih is the beginning of the matter, because it is an expression of exalting Allah above what is unfitting, and it is an indication of His being perfect in His essence; tahmid is an expression of His being one who perfects others. There is no doubt that the beginning of the matter is His being perfect in His essence, and the end of the matter is His perfecting others. Therefore the mention began with our saying "Glory be to Allah," then after it He mentioned "All praise is due to Allah," as a reminder that the station of tasbih is a beginning and the station of tahmid is an end. Having known this, we say: at the Night Journey He mentioned the word tasbih, and at the sending down of the Book He mentioned the word tahmid. This is a reminder that the Night Journey with him is the first of the degrees of his perfection, and the sending down of the Book is the ultimate of the degrees of his perfection. And the matter in reality is so, because the Night Journey with him to the Ascension requires the attainment of perfection for him, and the sending down of the Book upon him requires
Page 63
that he be one who perfects human souls and conveys them from the lowest depth of animality to the highest degrees of angelhood. There is no doubt that this second is more complete. And this is a reminder that the highest station of servants is that the servant becomes learned in his own essence and a teacher of others. For this reason it is related in a report that he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever learns and teaches, he is called great in the heavens."

The second benefit: the Night Journey is an expression of raising his essence from below to above, and the sending down of the Book upon him is an expression of sending down the light of revelation upon him from above to below. There is no doubt that this second is more complete.

The third benefit: the benefits of the Night Journey were confined to him, for do you not see that He, exalted is He, said there: ﴿That We might show him of Our signs﴾ (al-Isra' 17:1), whereas the benefits of the sending down of the Book upon him are far-reaching, for do you not see that He said: ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers﴾. And far-reaching benefits are superior to confined ones.

The second issue: The Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) argued from the word "Night Journey" in the previous surah and the word "sending down" in this surah that He, exalted is He, is specific to the direction above. The answer to this is fully mentioned in Surat al-Araf in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ (al-A'raf 7:54).

The third issue: The sending down of the Book is a blessing upon him and a blessing upon us. As for its being a blessing upon him, it is because He, exalted is He, informed him through this noble Book of the secrets of the sciences of tawhid and tanzih, the attributes of majesty and generosity, the secrets of the conditions of the angels and prophets, the matters of qada' and qadar, the connection of the conditions of the lower world with the conditions of the higher world, the connection of the conditions of the afterlife with the world of this life, the manner of the descent of decree from the world of the unseen, the manner in which the corporeal world is connected with the spiritual world, and making the soul like a mirror in which the realm of malakut is manifested and in which the holiness of lahut is revealed. There is no doubt that this is among the greatest blessings. As for this Book being a blessing upon us, it is because it contains obligations, rulings, promise and threat, reward and punishment; in sum, it is a Book complete in the highest degrees, so each one benefits from it according to his capacity and understanding. When this is so, it was incumbent upon the Messenger and upon all his community to praise Allah for it, so Allah, exalted is He, taught them the manner of that praise, saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book﴾. Then He, exalted is He, described the Book with two attributes, saying: ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾, ﴿[He has made it] straight﴾. And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: We have mentioned that a thing must be complete in its essence and then be one who perfects others, and it must be complete in its essence and then be above completeness by bestowing the perfection of others upon others. Having known this, we say: in His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ there is an indication of its being complete in its essence, and His saying ﴿[He has made it] straight﴾ is an indication of its perfecting others, because the qayyim is one who stands over the welfare of others. Its parallel is His saying at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah in describing the Book: ﴿There is no doubt in it; it is guidance for the God-fearing﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:2). So His saying ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ is an indication of its being in itself reaching such soundness and freedom from defect that a sensible person must not doubt it, and His saying ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾ is an indication of its being a means of guiding creation and perfecting their state. Thus His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ stands in place of His saying ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, and His saying ﴿[He has made it] straight﴾ stands in place of His saying ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾. These are subtle secrets.
Page 64

The second discussion: The lexicographers said: crookedness in meanings is like crookedness in physical things. What is meant by it are several aspects:

One of them: the negation of contradiction from its verses, as He said: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:82).

The second: that everything Allah mentioned of tawhid, prophethood, rulings and obligations is true and correct, and there is no defect in any of them whatsoever.

The third: that man appears to have come out from the world of the unseen heading toward the world of the Hereafter and toward the presence of Allah's majesty, and this world is as if it were a caravanserai built on the road of the world of resurrection, so that the traveler, when he alights in it, occupies himself with the matters that must be observed on this journey, then he departs from it heading toward the world of the Hereafter. So everything that calls him in this world to the Hereafter, from corporeal things to spiritual things, from creation to the Truth, from carnal bodily pleasures to being illumined by the eternal lights, is established as being free of crookedness, deviation and falsehood. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾.

The second attribute of the Book is His saying ﴿[He has made it] qayyim (straight)﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means "upright" (mustaqim). This, in my view, is problematic, because there is no meaning to negating crookedness except the attainment of straightness, so explaining qayyim as mustaqim entails repetition, and that is invalid. Rather the truth is what we have mentioned, and that what is meant by His saying "[He has made it] qayyim" is that it is a means of guiding creation, and that it functions like one who is a guardian of children: human souls are like children, and the Qur'an is like the compassionate guardian standing over their welfare.

The third discussion: al-Wahidi said: all the people of language and exegesis have said that this is from inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the meaning is: "He sent down to His servant the Book, qayyim, and did not make therein any crookedness." I say: we have already demonstrated what proves the invalidity of this statement, for we have shown that His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ indicates its being complete in its essence, and His saying ﴿qayyim﴾ indicates its being one who perfects others, and its being complete in its essence is prior by nature to its being one who perfects others. Thus it is established by rational proof that the correct order is the one Allah, exalted is He, mentioned, namely ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾, ﴿[He has made it] qayyim﴾. So it becomes clear that what they mentioned concerning inversion is corrupt, and the intellect refuses to go to it.

The fourth discussion: The grammarians differed concerning the grammatical status of ﴿qayyiman﴾ and mentioned several views:

The first: the author of al-Kashshaf said: it cannot be made a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of al-Kitab, because His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿sent down﴾, so it falls within the scope of the relative clause (ṣilah), and making it a ḥāl of al-Kitab would entail separating the ḥāl from its ṣāḥib by part of the relative clause, and that is not permitted. He said: since this is invalid, it must be governed by an implied verb, and the estimated meaning is: "and has not made therein any crookedness, and made it qayyim."

The second view: al-Isfahani said: what we consider is that His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ is a ḥāl, and His saying ﴿qayyiman﴾ is another ḥāl, and they are two successive circumstantial accusatives, and the estimated meaning is: "He sent down to His servant the Book, not made crooked for him, qayyim."

The third view: al-Sayyid, author of Hall al-ʿAqd, said: it is possible that His saying ﴿qayyiman﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾, because the meaning of "and has not made therein any crookedness" is that He made it straight, so it is as if it were said: "He sent down to His servant the Book, and made it qayyim."

The fourth view: that it is a ḥāl of the pronoun in His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾, i.e., while it is qayyim over the welfare of the servants and the rulings of religion. Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He "sent down to His servant the Book" described with these stated attributes, He followed it with an explanation of the purpose for which He sent it down, saying: ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him﴾. The verb "warn" (andhara) is transitive to two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ (al-Naba' 78:40), except that here He limited it to one of them, and its underlying form is ﴿to warn﴾ [those who disbelieve] ﴿of severe punishment﴾, just as He said of its opposite: ﴿and to give good tidings to the believers﴾. The word ba's (punishment) is derived from His saying: ﴿with a wretched punishment﴾ (al-A'raf 7:165), and "al-adhab bu'isa" (the punishment was wretched) and "ba'is al-rajul" (the man was wretched) with ba's and ba'asah.
Page 65
His saying ﴿from Him (min ladunhu)﴾ means "proceeding from His presence." Al-Zajjaj said: there are several dialects for (ladun): it is said ladun, ladā and ladu, and the meaning is one. He said: it does not take the firm status that ʿinda (at, with) takes, for you say "this statement is correct ʿindī (in my view)," and you do not say "ṣawāb ladunnī"; and you say "ʿindī māl ʿaẓīm (with me is a great wealth)" while the wealth is absent from you, but "ladunnī" is only for what is adjacent to you. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read it with a sukun on the dal together with ishmām of the ḍamm and kasr of the nūn and the hā', and this is the dialect of Banu Kilab. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward﴾. Know that the purpose of sending the messengers is the warning of the sinners and the glad tidings for the obedient. And since averting harm is more important to (people of) intellects than conveying benefit, therefore warning was placed before glad tidings in the wording. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it was also read as (wa-yubashshira) with tashdid and with takhfif. His saying ﴿in which they will remain forever (mākithīna fīhi abadan)﴾ means "abiding eternally," and it is a ḥāl of "the believers," from His saying ﴿that they will have a reward﴾.

Al-Qadi said: the verse indicates the soundness of our position in several issues:

The first: that the Qur'an is created, and its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: that He, exalted is He, described it with sending down and descent, and that is among the attributes of originated things, for the Eternal cannot be subject to change.

The second: describing it as a Book, and kitab means gathering, and it was called a Book because it is gathered from letters and words, and whatever admits of composition and arrangement is originated.

The third: that He, exalted is He, established praise for Himself for sending down the Book, and praise is due only for a blessing, and a blessing is originated and created.

The fourth: He described the Book as not crooked (ghayr mu'wajj) and as upright (mustaqim), and the Eternal cannot be described by that; so it is established that it is created (muhdath makhluq).

The second: the matter of the creation of acts (khalq al-a'mal), for these verses indicate our position on this question in several respects:

The first: the very command to praise. For if the servant had no act, he would not benefit from the Book, since benefit from it occurs only if he is able to do what the Book indicates must be done and to leave what the Book indicates must be left. He does that only if he is self-sufficient in himself. But if he is not self-sufficient, the crookedness of the Book would have no effect on the crookedness of his act, and the Book's being upright (qayyim) would have no effect on the uprightness of his act. But if the servant is able to act and free in it, the crookedness and uprightness of the Book remain effective in his act.

The second: if He, exalted is He, had sent down part of the Book so that it would be a cause for the disbelief of some, and sent down the rest so that the others would believe, then from where would it be known that the Book is upright with no crookedness in it? For if there were crookedness in it, it would not have gone beyond that.

The third: His saying ﴿to warn﴾ (li-yundhira). This indicates that He, exalted is He, intended from him (ﷺ) the warning of all and the glad tidings of all. And on the assumption that the Creator of disbelief and belief is Allah, exalted is He, there would remain no meaning to warning and glad tidings; for when He creates belief in a person, it occurs whether he wills it or not, and when He creates disbelief in him, it occurs whether he wills it or not. Thus warning and glad tidings regarding disbelief and belief would be like warning and glad tidings regarding being tall or short, black or white, things over which he has no power.

The fourth: His describing the believers as those who do righteous deeds (al-salihat). If what occurs is the creation of Allah, exalted is He, then they have no act at all.

The fifth: His making the good reward obligatory for them in return for what they did. If Allah, exalted is He, creates that in them, then there is no obligation and no deserving.

The fourth question: He said: His saying ﴿to warn﴾ indicates that He, exalted is He, does His acts only for sound purposes (li-aghrad sahiha), and that refutes the view of those who say that His act is not caused by a purpose (ghayr mu'allal bil-gharad).

Know that these words have been repeated in this book, so there is no benefit in repeating them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 1–3 (part 1 of 2):

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Kahf

Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is Meccan, except for two verses in it which mention ʿUyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari. And from Qatadah: it is Meccan. And from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who said: "Shall I not direct you to a surah which seventy thousand angels escorted when it was revealed? It is Surat al-Kahf."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book and has not made therein any crookedness. [He has made it] straight, to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a good reward, in which they will remain forever.﴾ In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: As for the discussion of the realities of our saying "All praise is due to Allah," it has already passed. What I say here is: tasbih (glorification) wherever it occurs comes before tahmid (praise). Do you not see that it is said, "Glory be to Allah and all praise is due to Allah"? Having known this, we say: He, majestic is His majesty, mentioned tasbih when He informed that He took Muhammad (ﷺ) on the Night Journey, saying: ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ (al-Isra' 17:1), and mentioned tahmid when He mentioned that He sent down the Book upon Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book﴾. And in this there are benefits:

The first benefit: tasbih is the beginning of the matter, because it is an expression of exalting Allah above what is unfitting, and it is an indication of His being perfect in His essence; tahmid is an expression of His being one who perfects others. There is no doubt that the beginning of the matter is His being perfect in His essence, and the end of the matter is His perfecting others. Therefore the mention began with our saying "Glory be to Allah," then after it He mentioned "All praise is due to Allah," as a reminder that the station of tasbih is a beginning and the station of tahmid is an end. Having known this, we say: at the Night Journey He mentioned the word tasbih, and at the sending down of the Book He mentioned the word tahmid. This is a reminder that the Night Journey with him is the first of the degrees of his perfection, and the sending down of the Book is the ultimate of the degrees of his perfection. And the matter in reality is so, because the Night Journey with him to the Ascension requires the attainment of perfection for him, and the sending down of the Book upon him requires
Page 63
that he be one who perfects human souls and conveys them from the lowest depth of animality to the highest degrees of angelhood. There is no doubt that this second is more complete. And this is a reminder that the highest station of servants is that the servant becomes learned in his own essence and a teacher of others. For this reason it is related in a report that he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever learns and teaches, he is called great in the heavens."

The second benefit: the Night Journey is an expression of raising his essence from below to above, and the sending down of the Book upon him is an expression of sending down the light of revelation upon him from above to below. There is no doubt that this second is more complete.

The third benefit: the benefits of the Night Journey were confined to him, for do you not see that He, exalted is He, said there: ﴿That We might show him of Our signs﴾ (al-Isra' 17:1), whereas the benefits of the sending down of the Book upon him are far-reaching, for do you not see that He said: ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him and to give good tidings to the believers﴾. And far-reaching benefits are superior to confined ones.

The second issue: The Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) argued from the word "Night Journey" in the previous surah and the word "sending down" in this surah that He, exalted is He, is specific to the direction above. The answer to this is fully mentioned in Surat al-Araf in the explanation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ (al-A'raf 7:54).

The third issue: The sending down of the Book is a blessing upon him and a blessing upon us. As for its being a blessing upon him, it is because He, exalted is He, informed him through this noble Book of the secrets of the sciences of tawhid and tanzih, the attributes of majesty and generosity, the secrets of the conditions of the angels and prophets, the matters of qada' and qadar, the connection of the conditions of the lower world with the conditions of the higher world, the connection of the conditions of the afterlife with the world of this life, the manner of the descent of decree from the world of the unseen, the manner in which the corporeal world is connected with the spiritual world, and making the soul like a mirror in which the realm of malakut is manifested and in which the holiness of lahut is revealed. There is no doubt that this is among the greatest blessings. As for this Book being a blessing upon us, it is because it contains obligations, rulings, promise and threat, reward and punishment; in sum, it is a Book complete in the highest degrees, so each one benefits from it according to his capacity and understanding. When this is so, it was incumbent upon the Messenger and upon all his community to praise Allah for it, so Allah, exalted is He, taught them the manner of that praise, saying: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has sent down to His servant the Book﴾. Then He, exalted is He, described the Book with two attributes, saying: ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾, ﴿[He has made it] straight﴾. And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: We have mentioned that a thing must be complete in its essence and then be one who perfects others, and it must be complete in its essence and then be above completeness by bestowing the perfection of others upon others. Having known this, we say: in His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ there is an indication of its being complete in its essence, and His saying ﴿[He has made it] straight﴾ is an indication of its perfecting others, because the qayyim is one who stands over the welfare of others. Its parallel is His saying at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah in describing the Book: ﴿There is no doubt in it; it is guidance for the God-fearing﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:2). So His saying ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ is an indication of its being in itself reaching such soundness and freedom from defect that a sensible person must not doubt it, and His saying ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾ is an indication of its being a means of guiding creation and perfecting their state. Thus His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ stands in place of His saying ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾, and His saying ﴿[He has made it] straight﴾ stands in place of His saying ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾. These are subtle secrets.
Page 64

The second discussion: The lexicographers said: crookedness in meanings is like crookedness in physical things. What is meant by it are several aspects:

One of them: the negation of contradiction from its verses, as He said: ﴿Had it been from other than Allah, they would have found in it much discrepancy﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:82).

The second: that everything Allah mentioned of tawhid, prophethood, rulings and obligations is true and correct, and there is no defect in any of them whatsoever.

The third: that man appears to have come out from the world of the unseen heading toward the world of the Hereafter and toward the presence of Allah's majesty, and this world is as if it were a caravanserai built on the road of the world of resurrection, so that the traveler, when he alights in it, occupies himself with the matters that must be observed on this journey, then he departs from it heading toward the world of the Hereafter. So everything that calls him in this world to the Hereafter, from corporeal things to spiritual things, from creation to the Truth, from carnal bodily pleasures to being illumined by the eternal lights, is established as being free of crookedness, deviation and falsehood. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾.

The second attribute of the Book is His saying ﴿[He has made it] qayyim (straight)﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means "upright" (mustaqim). This, in my view, is problematic, because there is no meaning to negating crookedness except the attainment of straightness, so explaining qayyim as mustaqim entails repetition, and that is invalid. Rather the truth is what we have mentioned, and that what is meant by His saying "[He has made it] qayyim" is that it is a means of guiding creation, and that it functions like one who is a guardian of children: human souls are like children, and the Qur'an is like the compassionate guardian standing over their welfare.

The third discussion: al-Wahidi said: all the people of language and exegesis have said that this is from inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), and the meaning is: "He sent down to His servant the Book, qayyim, and did not make therein any crookedness." I say: we have already demonstrated what proves the invalidity of this statement, for we have shown that His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ indicates its being complete in its essence, and His saying ﴿qayyim﴾ indicates its being one who perfects others, and its being complete in its essence is prior by nature to its being one who perfects others. Thus it is established by rational proof that the correct order is the one Allah, exalted is He, mentioned, namely ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾, ﴿[He has made it] qayyim﴾. So it becomes clear that what they mentioned concerning inversion is corrupt, and the intellect refuses to go to it.

The fourth discussion: The grammarians differed concerning the grammatical status of ﴿qayyiman﴾ and mentioned several views:

The first: the author of al-Kashshaf said: it cannot be made a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) of al-Kitab, because His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿sent down﴾, so it falls within the scope of the relative clause (ṣilah), and making it a ḥāl of al-Kitab would entail separating the ḥāl from its ṣāḥib by part of the relative clause, and that is not permitted. He said: since this is invalid, it must be governed by an implied verb, and the estimated meaning is: "and has not made therein any crookedness, and made it qayyim."

The second view: al-Isfahani said: what we consider is that His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾ is a ḥāl, and His saying ﴿qayyiman﴾ is another ḥāl, and they are two successive circumstantial accusatives, and the estimated meaning is: "He sent down to His servant the Book, not made crooked for him, qayyim."

The third view: al-Sayyid, author of Hall al-ʿAqd, said: it is possible that His saying ﴿qayyiman﴾ is a substitute (badal) for His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾, because the meaning of "and has not made therein any crookedness" is that He made it straight, so it is as if it were said: "He sent down to His servant the Book, and made it qayyim."

The fourth view: that it is a ḥāl of the pronoun in His saying ﴿and has not made therein any crookedness﴾, i.e., while it is qayyim over the welfare of the servants and the rulings of religion. Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He "sent down to His servant the Book" described with these stated attributes, He followed it with an explanation of the purpose for which He sent it down, saying: ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him﴾. The verb "warn" (andhara) is transitive to two objects, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ (al-Naba' 78:40), except that here He limited it to one of them, and its underlying form is ﴿to warn﴾ [those who disbelieve] ﴿of severe punishment﴾, just as He said of its opposite: ﴿and to give good tidings to the believers﴾. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ ﴿They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers. Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but a lie.﴾ ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this discourse, [out of] sorrow.﴾

There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Know that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him﴾. The coordinated element must be different from that to which it is coordinated. The first is general, concerning everyone who deserves punishment, and the second is specific to those who ascribe a son to Allah. It is the custom of the Qur'an that when it mentions a universal matter, it coordinates with it some of its particulars, to draw attention to that particular being the greatest of the particulars of that universal, as in His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 98). So here too the coordination indicates that the most abominable kind of disbelief and disobedience is ascribing a son to Allah, exalted is He.

The second issue: Those who ascribed a son to Allah, exalted is He, are three groups:

The first: the disbelievers of the Arabs, who said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah."

The second: the Christians, who said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah."

The third: the Jews, who said: "'Uzayr is the son of Allah."

The discussion is that ascribing a son to Allah is a great disbelief, and it entails great impossibilities. We have mentioned this in Surat al-An'am in the commentary on His saying: ﴿and they attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge﴾ (Al-An'am: 100), and its completion is mentioned in Surat Maryam. Then He, exalted, denounced those who ascribe a son to Allah, exalted is He, in two respects:

The first: His saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of it, nor did their fathers.﴾ If it is said: taking a son for Allah is impossible in itself, so how is it said, "They have no knowledge of it"? We say: the absence of knowledge of a thing may be due to ignorance of the path that leads to it, and it may be because the thing is impossible in itself, such that knowledge of it cannot be attached to it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 117).

Know that the deniers of qiyas (analogical reasoning) adhered to this verse, saying: This verse indicates that speaking about religion without knowledge is invalid, and speaking by speculative qiyas is speaking about religion without knowledge, so it is invalid. The full statement of this argument is mentioned in His saying: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾ (Al-Isra': 36).

His saying: ﴿nor did their fathers﴾ means: nor did any of their predecessors. This is an exaggeration of the falsehood and corruption of that claim.

The second of what Allah mentioned in refuting it is His saying: ﴿Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths.﴾ In it there are several discussions:

The first discussion: It was read as "kabura kalimatun" (kalimatan) with the accusative as a tamyiz (specification, a noun clarifying the vague subject) and with the nominative as the subject. Al-Wahidi said: The meaning of the tamyiz is that when you say, "the statement became great" or "the word became great," it could be imagined that it became great in lying, ignorance, or fabrication. When you said "a word," you specified it from its possible meanings, so it was put in the accusative as a tamyiz. The implied sense is: "The word became great as a word," so there is an implicit element in it. As for the one who reads it in the nominative, he implies nothing, as you say: "So-and-so became great." Therefore the grammarians said: the accusative is stronger and more emphatic, and it carries the sense of amazement, as if it were said: "How great is it as a word!"

The second discussion: His saying: ﴿Grave is a word﴾ means: the word became great. The intended word is what Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿They said, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ So it is implied in "became great," and it is called a word just as they call a poem a word.

The third discussion: Al-Nazzam argued from this verse that speech is a body (jism). He said: He, exalted, described the word as coming out of their mouths, and "coming out" is an expression for motion, and motion is valid only of bodies. The answer: Letters arise only through the exit of breath from the throat. When the exit of breath was the cause of the word's arising, the word "coming out" was applied to the word.

[Page 67]

The fourth discussion: His saying: ﴿comes out of their mouths﴾ indicates that this speech is extremely repugnant to reason, as if He is saying: What they say is not judged by their intellect and thought at all, because it is in utter corruption and falsehood. It is as if it is something their tongues run through by way of imitation, for even though it is their saying, their intellects and thoughts reject it and recoil from it.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿they say nothing but a lie﴾, and its meaning is clear.

Know that people have differed about the reality of lying. According to us, it is a report that does not correspond to what it reports, whether the reporter believes it corresponds or not. Some people said: The condition for it being a lie is that it does not correspond to what it reports while its speaker knows that it does not correspond. This condition is invalid according to us, and the evidence for this is this verse, for He, exalted, described their saying of ascribing a son to Allah as a lie, although many of them say it without knowing it to be false. So we know that every report that does not correspond to what it reports is a lie, whether the speaker knows it corresponds or does not know.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this discourse, [out of] sorrow.﴾ In it there are discussions:

The first discussion: The purpose is to say to the Messenger: Do not let your sorrow and grief over their disbelief be great, for We sent you only as a warner and a bringer of glad tidings. As for producing faith in their hearts, you have no power over it. The aim is to console the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning this.

The second discussion: Al-Layth said: A man "bakha'a" himself when he kills himself out of extreme grief over something. Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: The origin of bakh' is exertion. It is said: "Bakhtu laka nafsi," meaning I exerted myself for you. In a hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, she mentioned Umar and said: "Bakha'a al-ard," meaning he exhausted it, until he took what was in it of the wealth of kings. Al-Kisa'i said: "Bakhtu al-ard bil-zira'a" when you make the land weak by constant plowing, and "bakha'a al-rajulu nafsahu" when he wears himself out. Accordingly, the meaning of ﴿bakhi'un nafsaka﴾ is: wearing yourself out and exerting yourself until you destroy yourself. But all the exegetes said: killing yourself and destroying yourself. The origin is what we have mentioned. Thus said al-Wahidi.

The third discussion: His saying: ﴿over their traces﴾ means: after them. It is said: "So-and-so died upon the trace of so-and-so," meaning after him. The origin of this is that when a person dies, his marks and traces remain for a period after his death, and then they fade and are completely erased. So if his death is close to the death of the first, his death occurs while the traces of the first still remain, and it is correct to say: "So-and-so died upon the trace of so-and-so."

There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Know that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And to warn those who say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying ﴿to warn of severe punishment from Him﴾. The coordinated element must be different from that to which it is coordinated. The first is general, concerning everyone who deserves punishment, and the second is specific to those who ascribe a son to Allah. So here too the coordination indicates that the most abominable kind of disbelief and disobedience is ascribing a son to Allah, exalted is He.

The second: the Christians, who said: "The Messiah is the son of Allah."

The third: the Jews, who said: "'Uzayr is the son of Allah."

The discussion is that ascribing a son to Allah is a great disbelief, and it entails great impossibilities. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah, for which he has no proof﴾ (Al-Mu'minun: 117).

**Allah the Exalted says:** ﴿Indeed, We have made what is upon the earth an adornment for it, so that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed.﴾ ﴿And indeed, We will surely reduce what is upon it to barren dust.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**First issue:** The judge (al-Qadi, ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: The sequence of the verses is as if Allah the Exalted says: "O Muhammad, I created the earth, adorned it, and brought forth from it various kinds of benefits and goods. The purpose of creating it with these benefits is to test creation through these obligations. Then, despite this, they disbelieve and rebel, yet I do not cut off the sources of these blessings from them. So you too, O Muhammad, should not go so far in grief over their disbelief that you abandon occupying yourself with calling them to the true religion."

**Second issue:** They differed concerning the interpretation of this adornment. Some said: it is plants and trees. Others added to this gold, silver, and minerals. Others added all the animals. Some said: rather, what is meant is people, for they are the adornment of the earth. In sum, there is nothing on the earth except the three kinds of generated beings: minerals, plants, and animals. The noblest kind of animal is the human being. The judge said: It is preferable that the accountable person (al-mukallaf) not be included in this adornment, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is upon the earth an adornment for it, so that We may test them﴾. Whoever is tested must not be included in this. As for the rest of the plants and animals, they are included in it just as all that is benefited from is included. His saying ﴿an adornment for it﴾ means for the earth. There is no impediment to what beautifies the earth being an adornment for the earth, just as Allah made the heaven adorned with the adornment of the stars.

As for His saying ﴿so that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾, there are issues concerning it:

**First issue:** Hisham ibn al-Hakam held that Allah the Exalted does not know events except at the moment they come into existence. Accordingly, testing and examination are permissible for Allah. He argued for this by saying: If Allah were knowing of particulars before their occurrence, then everything He knew would occur would be necessary to occur, and everything He knew would not occur would be impossible to occur; otherwise, His knowledge would turn into ignorance, and that is impossible. And whatever leads to an impossibility is impossible. If that (occurrence) were necessary, then the one whose occurrence He knows must be the agent of it and has no power to abstain, and the one whose non-occurrence He knows is impossible to occur and has no power to do it. On this basis, it would follow that Allah has no power over anything at all, but would be an agent by essence (mūjib bi-l-dhāt). Furthermore, it would follow that the servant has no power either to act or to abstain, because what Allah knows will occur is impossible for the servant to abstain from, and what Allah knows will not occur is impossible for him to do. Therefore, the claim that He is knowing of things before they occur undermines both lordship and servanthood, and that is false. Thus it is established that Allah knows things only when they occur. On this assumption, testing, examination, and trial are permissible for Him. At this point he said: the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿so that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾ remains on its apparent meaning.

As for the majority of the scholars of Islam, they regarded this view as far-fetched, and said: Allah, from pre-eternity to post-eternity, knows all particulars. Therefore testing and examination are impossible for Him. Wherever these expressions occur, what is meant is that He treats them in a manner which, if it proceeded from another, would be by way of testing and examination. We have discussed this issue many times.

**Second issue:** The judge said: The meaning of His saying ﴿so that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾ is that He tests them in order to see which of them is more obedient to Allah and more persistent in serving Him, for the one with this condition is the one who wins Paradise. Thus Allah the Exalted made clear that He imposed obligations for this reason and not in order that they be disobeyed. This indicates the invalidity of the view of those who say: He created some of them for the Fire.

**Third issue:** The particle *lām* in His saying ﴿so that We may test them﴾ apparently indicates that the acts of Allah are causally grounded in purposes (taʿlīl bi-l-aghrāḍ), according to the Muʿtazila. Our companions (the Ashʿarīs) said: This is impossible, because causation by purpose is valid only regarding one who cannot achieve that purpose except through that intermediary, and this implies incapacity, which is impossible for Allah.

[p. 69]

**Fourth issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: *Ayyuhum* (أيُّهم) is in the nominative case by being the subject of an inchoative (mubtadaʾ), but its form is that of an interrogative, and the meaning is: "that We may test and examine which of these is best in deed, this one or that one." Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And indeed, We will surely reduce what is upon it to barren dust.﴾ The meaning is that Allah the Exalted made clear that He adorned the earth only for the sake of examination and testing, and not so that a person would remain in it enjoying comfort forever, for this makes one renounce it through His saying ﴿And indeed, We will surely reduce what is upon it﴾, etc. A parallel to this is His saying ﴿Everything upon it will perish﴾ (al-Raḥmān: 26), and His saying ﴿and He will leave it as a level plain﴾ (Ṭāhā: 106), etc., and His saying ﴿and when the earth is stretched out﴾ (al-Inshiqāq: 3), etc. The meaning is that there must be recompense after the perishing of what is upon the earth. The restriction of annihilation and destruction to what is upon the earth may give the impression that the earth itself remains; however, other verses indicate that the earth too does not remain, namely His saying ﴿On the day the earth will be changed into other than the earth﴾ (Ibrāhīm: 48).

Abū ʿUbayda said: *al-ṣaʿīd* is the level part of the earth. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the path in which there is no vegetation. We have already mentioned the explanation of *al-ṣaʿīd* in the verse of tayammum (the ritual dry ablution, tayammum, using clean earth). As for *al-juruz* (جُرُزًا), al-Farrāʾ said: *al-juruz* is the earth on which there is no vegetation. It is said: "The earth became *jaraza*, so it is *majrūza*," and "locusts, sheep, and camels *jarazahā* when they eat what is upon it." A woman who is *jarūz* is one who eats much, and a sword that is *jirāz* is one that cuts off completely. A parallel to this is His saying the Exalted: ﴿We drive the water to the barren land﴾ (al-Sajda: 27).

Therefore testing and examination are impossible for Him. Wherever these expressions occur, what is meant is that He treats them in a manner which, if it proceeded from another, would be by way of testing and examination. We have discussed this issue many times.

**Second issue:** The judge said: The meaning of His saying ﴿so that We may test them as to which of them is best in deed﴾ is that He tests them in order to see which of them is more obedient to Allah and more persistent in serving Him, for the one with this condition is the one who wins Paradise. Thus Allah the Exalted made clear that He imposed obligations for this reason and not in order that they be disobeyed. This indicates the invalidity of the view of those who say: He created some of them for the Fire.

**Third issue:** The particle *lām* in His saying ﴿so that We may test them﴾ apparently indicates that the acts of Allah are causally grounded in purposes (taʿlīl bi-l-aghrāḍ), according to the Muʿtazila. Our companions (the Ashʿarīs) said: This is impossible, because causation by purpose is valid only regarding one who cannot achieve that purpose except through that intermediary, and this implies incapacity, which is impossible for Allah.

[p. 69]

As for *al-juruz* (جُرُزًا), al-Farrāʾ said: *al-juruz* is the earth on which there is no vegetation. It is said: "The earth became *jaraza*, so it is *majrūza*," and "locusts, sheep, and camels *jarazahā* when they eat what is upon it." **The third issue:** *al-Kahf* (the cave) is a wide cavity in a mountain; when it is smaller, it is called *al-ghār*. As for *al-Raqīm*, there are several views:

The first: 'Ikrima reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "I know all of the Qur'an except four words: *ghisslīn*, *ḥanān*, *al-awwāh*, and *al-raqīm*."

The second: 'Ikrima reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about *al-Raqīm*, and he said: "Ka'b claims that it is the town from which they went out." This is also the view of al-Suddi.

The third: Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: *al-Raqīm* is a tablet of stone. It was also said that it is a tablet of lead on which their names and their story were written, and that tablet was fixed over the entrance of the cave. This is the view of all the people of the meanings (*al-ma'ānī*) and of Arabic grammar. They said: *al-Raqīm* means the book, and its origin is *al-marqūm* (the inscribed), which was then transferred to the pattern *fa'īl*. *Al-raqm* means writing, and from it is God's words: *A written book* (83:9), that is, a written one. Al-Farra' said: *al-Raqīm* is a tablet on which their names and attributes were written. We suppose that it was called *raqīm* because their names were inscribed on it. It was also said: the people inscribed their account by engraving it in the side of the mountain.

As for His words: *that they were a wonder among Our signs*, the meaning is: Do you suppose that their event was a marvel among the creatures We have made? Do not suppose that. That event is not a marvel in comparison with Our creatures. The word *'ajab* here is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) used in place of the passive participle (*ism al-maf'ūl*). The implied meaning is: they were "one who is marveled at" (*ma'jūban minhum*). Thus they were called by the verbal noun, and what is formed from this is used in the form of the verbal noun.

Then He said: *When the youths took refuge in the cave.* It is not permissible for *idh* here to be connected to what precedes it, with the sense "Did you suppose, when the youths took refuge?", because there was a long period between the Prophet and them, so the supposing was not attached to that time when they took refuge in the cave. Rather it is connected to an omitted element, and the sense is: "Remember when they took refuge." The meaning of *awā al-fityatu fi al-kahf* ("the youths took refuge in the cave") is that they went to it and made it their abode.

He said: *They said: "Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself"*, that is, mercy from the treasuries of Your mercy, the great bounties of Your grace and Your kindness, and this is guidance through knowledge, patience, provision, and security from enemies. Regarding the interpretation of the word there are two views:

The first: the sense is "prepare for us an affair that has rightness, so that through it we may become rightly guided." 

The second: "make our whole affair rightness," as when you say: "I saw rightness from you."

Then He said: *So We struck upon their ears* (*fa-ḍarabnā 'alā ādhānihim*). The commentators said: its meaning is that We made them sleep. The sense of the phrase is that God struck over their ears a veil that prevents the waking sounds from reaching their hearing. The implied meaning is: "We struck over them a veil," but He omitted the object, which is the veil, as one says *banā 'alā imra'atihi* ("he consummated the marriage with his wife"), meaning "he erected a dome over her." Then He said: *Then We raised them up* (*thumma ba'athnāhum*), meaning: after their sleep, that is, We woke them after their sleep.
