Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 22 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 89]
His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus did We cause them to be found, so that they might know that the promise of Allah is true, and that the Hour, there is no doubt about it. When they disputed among themselves about their affair, and said: "Build over them a structure; their Lord knows best about them." Those who prevailed over their affair said: "We will surely take over them a place of worship."﴾ ﴿They will say: "They were three, the fourth of them their dog"; and they will say: "They were five, the sixth of them their dog," guessing at the unseen; and they will say: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog." Say: "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few. So do not argue about them except with an apparent argument, and do not consult any of them concerning them."﴾

Know that the meaning is as we have stated: We increased them in guidance, bound upon their hearts, put them to sleep, turned them over and raised them up, for the manifest wisdoms therein. So "thus did We cause them to be found" means: We made others acquainted with their circumstances. It is said: "I came upon (ʿathartu ʿalā) such-and-such," meaning "I came to know it." They said: the origin of this is that whoever was heedless of something and stumbled upon it looked at it and recognized it; thus stumbling became a cause for the attainment of knowledge and clarity, and so the name of the cause was applied to the effect. They differed concerning the cause by which people came to know the event of the People of the Cave, in two respects:

The first: their hair and nails grew to an extraordinary length, contrary to custom, and wondrous marks appeared on the skin of their faces indicating that their period had lasted an extraordinary length beyond custom.

The second: when that man entered the market to buy food and took out the silver coins for the price of the food, the owner of the food said: "These coins are not current on this day; they were current long ago, in a long time and an ancient age. Perhaps you have found a treasure." People differed about it, and they brought that man to the king of the city. The king said: "From where did you get these coins?" He said: "I sold some dates with them yesterday, and we fled from the king Daqyanus." The king then knew that he had not found a treasure, and that Allah had raised him after his death. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿so that they might know that the promise of Allah is true﴾, meaning: We only made the people acquainted with their circumstances so that the people might know that the promise of Allah is true, concerning the resurrection, the gathering and the raising.

It is narrated that the king of that time was among those who denied resurrection, but he, despite his disbelief, was just; so Allah made the matter of the youths a proof for the king. It was also said: rather, the community differed in that era; some of them said: the body and the spirit are both raised, and others said: only the spirit is raised, while the body is consumed by the earth. Then that king would supplicate Allah to show him a sign by which he could establish what is true in this question. So Allah made him acquainted with the matter of the People of the Cave, and the king took their event as evidence for the validity of the resurrection of bodies, since their waking after that long sleep resembles one who dies and is then raised.

His saying: ﴿when they disputed among themselves﴾ is connected to "We caused them to be found": that is, We caused them to be found upon them when they were disputing among themselves. They differed about what this dispute was. It was said: they disputed about the validity of the resurrection; those who affirmed it used this event as evidence for its validity, saying: just as Allah was able to preserve their bodies for three hundred and nine years, so He is able to gather bodies after they die. It was also said: when the king and his people saw the People of the Cave and learned of their circumstances, the people returned to their cave, and Allah caused them to die.

At this point people differed:
Some said: they are asleep, as in the first state.
Others said: rather, they have now died.

The third view: some said: the better course is to block the door of the cave so that no one enters upon them and no person comes to know their circumstances. Others said: rather, the better course is to build a mosque over the door of the cave. This view indicates that those peoples were acquainted with Allah and acknowledged worship and prayer.

The fourth view: the disbelievers said: "They were upon our religion, so we will build a structure over them," and the Muslims said: "They were upon our religion, so we will take a place of worship over them."

The fifth view: they disputed about the length of their stay.

The sixth: they disputed about their number and their names. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿their Lord knows best about them﴾, and in this there are two possibilities:

One of them: it is part of the speech of the disputants, as if, when they discussed their affair and passed around talk about their names, their circumstances and the length of their stay, and did not arrive at the truth of that, they said: "Their Lord knows best about them."

The second: that this is the speech of Allah, exalted is His remembrance, refuting those who engaged in discussion of their story from among
[p. 90]
those disputants. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who prevailed over their affair said﴾. It was said the meant ones are the Muslim king; it was said: the guardians of the People of the Cave; and it was said: the leaders of the city: ﴿"We will surely take over them a place of worship"﴾, we worship Allah in it and preserve the traces of the People of the Cave by means of that mosque. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will say: "They were three, the fourth of them their dog"﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿They will say﴾ refers to the disputants.

It is narrated that al-Sayyid and al-Aqib and their companions from the people of Najran were with the Prophet ﷺ, and the story of the People of the Cave came up. Al-Sayyid, who was a Jacobite, said: "They were three, the fourth of them their dog." Al-Aqib, who was a Nestorian, said: "They were five, the sixth of them their dog." The Muslims said: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog." Most of the exegetes said: this last is the truth, and the following points indicate it:

First: the waw in His saying ﴿and the eighth of them﴾ is the waw that enters upon a clause that is a qualifier of an indefinite noun, just as it enters upon one that is a circumstantial clause of a definite noun, as in your saying: "A man came to me with another with him," and "I passed by Zayd and in his hand is a sword," and from it His saying: ﴿And We never destroyed a town but it had a known decree﴾ (al-Hijr: 4). Its benefit is to affirm the stability of the qualifier for the qualified, and to indicate that his being characterized by it is a fixed and established matter. So this waw indicates the truthfulness of those who said: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog," and that they spoke a statement that was established, certain, from firmness, knowledge and tranquility of soul.

The second point: they said: He, exalted is He, specified this place with this additional particle, the waw, so it must be that a further benefit is achieved by it, to preserve the wording from being idle; and whoever affirmed this additional benefit said: its purpose is to specify this statement for affirmation and correctness.

The third point: He, exalted is He, followed the first two statements with His saying ﴿conjecturing about the unseen﴾, and specifying a thing by a description indicates that the case in the rest is otherwise. So the one specified by baseless guessing must be the first two statements, and the third statement must be different from them in that they are guesses.

The fourth point: when He, exalted is He, related their saying ﴿and they will say: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog"﴾, He said after it: ﴿Say: "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few."﴾ So following the first two statements with their being guesses about the unseen, and following this third statement with His saying ﴿Say: "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few"﴾, indicates that this statement is distinguished from the first two by greater strength and correctness.

The fifth point: He, exalted is He, said: ﴿none knows them except a few﴾, and this implies that knowledge of their number was attained by that few; and everyone among the Muslims who spoke on this matter said: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog," so it must be that the few meant are those who said this statement. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "They were seven, and their names were these: Yamlīkhā, Maksalmīnā, Mislīnā; these three were the companions of the king's right side, and on his left were Marnūs, Darnūs and Sādanūs; and the king used to consult these six in his affairs."

And the seventh: he was the shepherd who joined them when they fled from their king. The name of their dog was Qiṭmīr. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, used to say: "I am of that few number," and he used to say: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog."

The sixth point: when He, exalted is He, said ﴿And they will say: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog." Say: "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few"﴾, the apparent meaning is that when He related the statements, He related every statement made, true and false; for it is unlikely that He mentioned the false statements without mentioning what is true. Thus it is established that the totality of true and false statements is nothing but these three, and then He specified
[p. 91]
the first two as being guesses about the unseen, so the truth must be this third one.

The seventh point: He, exalted is He, said to His Messenger: ﴿So do not argue about them except with an apparent argument, and do not consult any of them concerning them﴾. Allah forbade him from disputing with them and from seeking their opinion on this matter, and this would only be the case if He had taught him the ruling on this event. Also, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿none knows them except a few﴾, and it is unlikely that this knowledge is attained by someone other than the Prophet while it is not attained by the Prophet himself. So we know that knowledge of this event was attained by the Prophet, peace be upon him. And the apparent meaning is that this knowledge was attained only through this revelation, because the原 default regarding anything else is non-existence, and the matter being thus, the truth was His saying: ﴿and they will say: "They were seven, and the eighth of them their dog"﴾. Know that although some of these points are weaker than others, when some of them are strengthened by others, a completeness and perfection is achieved in it. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Remaining in the verse are some discussions:

The first discussion: there is an ellipsis in the verse; the estimated reading is: "They will say, they are three," so the subject was omitted because the context indicates it.

The second discussion: the first statement was specified with the future particle sa- in His saying "sayaqūlūna" (they will say), and the reason for this is that the conjunctive particle makes the other two statements included in it.

The third discussion: rajm is throwing, and al-ghayb is what is hidden from a person. So His saying ﴿conjecturing about the unseen﴾ means that one sees what is hidden from him and does not know it in reality; it is said: "So-and-so throws words (yarmī bi-l-kalām) with a throw," meaning he speaks without reflection.

The fourth discussion: they mentioned, concerning the benefit of the waw in His saying ﴿and the eighth of them their dog﴾, several points:

The first point: what we mentioned, that it indicates this statement is preferable to all other statements.

And the second point: among the Arabs, seven is the basic unit for expressing exaggeration in number. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Even if you seek forgiveness for them seventy times﴾ (al-Tawbah: 80). Since this is so, when they reached eight they used a word that signals a new start, so they said: "wa-thamaniyah" (and eight). This statement follows this pattern. They said: its parallel in three verses supports this, namely His saying: ﴿and those who forbid evil﴾ (al-Tawbah: 112), because this is the eighth of the numbers mentioned before it; His saying: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates have been opened﴾ (al-Zumar: 73), because the gates of Paradise are eight and the gates of Hell are seven; and His saying: ﴿[wives] previously married and virgins﴾ (al-Tahrim: 5), which is the eighth of what preceded it. People call this waw the "waw of eight" (wāw al-thamāniyah), and its meaning is what we have mentioned.

Al-Qaffal said: "This is worthless. The proof against it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He is Allah, other than whom there is no deity, the King, the Pure, the Source of Peace, the Granter of Security, the Guardian, the Mighty, the Compeller, the Superior﴾ (al-Hashr: 23). He did not mention the waw before the eighth attribute." Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few﴾. This is the truth, because knowledge of the detailed realities of the world and of the events that occurred in the past and will occur in the future is attained only by Allah, the Exalted, and by those whom Allah informs of them. Ibn Abbas said: "I am one of those few." Al-Qadi said: "If he knew it through the explanation of the Messenger, then it is sound; but if he relied on the letter waw in it, then it is weak. It may be said that the seven aspects mentioned, although they do not produce certainty, do produce probable opinion."

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, mentioned this story, He followed it by forbidding His Messenger from two things:

Disputation and seeking rulings. As for the prohibition of disputation, it is His saying: ﴿So do not argue concerning them except with an apparent argument﴾. The meaning of "apparent argument" is that he should not deny them the specification of that number, but should say: "This specification has no proof, so it is necessary to withhold judgment and not to assert with certainty." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a manner that is best﴾ (al-'Ankabut: 46). As for the prohibition of seeking rulings, it is His saying: ﴿and do not inquire about them from any of them﴾. That is because, since it was established that they had no knowledge in this matter, it became obligatory to forbid seeking their opinion.

Know that the rejectors of analogical reasoning (qiyas) relied on this verse, saying: because His saying ﴿guessing about the unseen﴾ places "rajm" (conjecture) where "zann" (supposition) should be. It is as though it had been said: "supposition about the unseen," because they very often said "rajm bil-zann" (conjecture by supposition) in place of their saying "zann" (supposition), until there was no difference left for them between the two expressions. Do you not see the verse:

*And he is not, concerning it, with the speech that is conjectured*

That is, the speech that is supposed. This is what the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said. This indicates that speaking by supposition is blameworthy before Allah. Then, when He, Exalted is He, blamed this method, He made the seeking of rulings from these supposers a consequence of it. This shows that giving a ruling based on conjecture is not permissible before Allah. The reply of those who affirm qiyas to this has been mentioned by us many times.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 23:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿unless [you add], "If Allah wills." And remember your Lord when you forget and say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer to right conduct than this."﴾ ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and exceeded by nine.﴾ ﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and hears. They have not besides Him any protector, and He does not share His command with anyone."﴾

Know that there are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: The exegetes said: When the people asked the Prophet ﷺ about the three questions, he said, "I will answer you about them tomorrow," and he did not say, "If Allah wills." So the revelation was withheld for fifteen days, and in another report forty days. Then this verse was revealed. The judge (al-Qadi) raised two objections to this statement:

The first: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew that if he reported that he would do such-and-such an act tomorrow, he might die before tomorrow, or some other obstacle might prevent him from doing that act tomorrow. Since all these possibilities are conceivable, if he had not said, "If Allah wills," his speech might have contradicted what actually exists, and that would bring aversion to him and to his words, peace be upon him. But if he said, "If Allah wills," he would have guarded against this danger. Given that, it would be far-fetched for him to promise something without saying "If Allah wills" about it.

The second: This verse contains many benefits and numerous rulings, so it is unlikely to be restricted to this one cause.

The first objection may be answered: There is no dispute that the better course is to say, "If Allah wills." However, it may happen that he forgot this statement for some reason, and so this was a case of leaving what is preferable and better.

The second objection may be answered: That this verse contains many benefits does not prevent one of them from being the cause of its revelation.

Page 93

The second issue: His saying, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾, does not specify what Allah wills, and there are two opinions on this:

The first: The sense is: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ that He permit you to say that statement. The meaning is that it is not for you to report about yourself that you will do such-and-such an act, except when Allah permits you to make that report.

The second opinion: The sense is: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ unless you say, "If Allah wills." The reason why it is necessary to mention this statement is that when a person says, "I will do such-and-such an act tomorrow," it is not unlikely that he will die before tomorrow comes, and it is also not unlikely, even if he remains alive, that some obstacle will prevent him from that act. So if he does not say, "If Allah wills," he becomes a liar in that promise, and lying is abhorrent, and that is not fitting for the prophets, peace be upon them. For this reason, it became obligatory for him to say, "If Allah wills," so that even if it becomes impossible for him to fulfill that promise, he does not become a liar, and thus aversion is not produced.

The third issue: Know that the position of the Mu'tazilah is that Allah, exalted is He, wills faith and obedience from the servant, while the servant wills disbelief and disobedience for himself. Thus the servant's will takes effect and Allah's will does not take effect; the servant's will is dominant and Allah's will is overcome. But according to us, whatever Allah, exalted is He, wills certainly occurs. So He wills disbelief from the disbeliever and wills faith from the believer. On this formulation, Allah's will is dominant and the servant's will is overcome. Having understood this, we say: When the servant says, "I will certainly do such-and-such tomorrow, unless Allah wills," Allah only averts lying from him if Allah's will prevails over the servant's will. On this view, the sense is: the servant said, "I will do such-and-such act, unless Allah's will is otherwise." Then, on this formulation, I will not act, because Allah's will prevails over mine; when a dominant impediment arises, I am no longer able to act. But if Allah's will were overcome, it would not serve as an excuse in this matter, because the overcome does not prevent the dominant.

Given that this is established, we say: The community has agreed that if a man says, "By Allah, I will certainly do such-and-such," and then says, "If Allah wills," as a means of averting the breach of oath, then it averts the breach only if Allah's will is dominant. Since averting the breach was achieved by consensus, it becomes certain that Allah's will is dominant, and that nothing comes into existence except what Allah has willed. Our companions have emphasized this point in a specific case: if a man is owed a debt by another person, and that debtor is able to pay the debt, and the creditor says, "By Allah, I will certainly collect this debt tomorrow," and then says, "If Allah wills," and when tomorrow comes the debtor has not paid the debt, the creditor does not break his oath. According to the Mu'tazilah, Allah wills from him the payment of the debt, and on this view his saying "If Allah wills" would be a conditioning of that ruling upon a condition that has occurred, so he ought to break his oath. Since they all agreed that he does not break it, we know that this is because Allah did not will that act, even though Allah commanded that act, encouraged it, and warned against neglecting it. It is established that He, exalted is He, sometimes forbids a thing and wills it, and sometimes commands a thing and does not will it, and this is the point being sought. If it is objected: Granting that the command is as you have stated, many jurists have said: If a man says to his wife, "You are divorced, if Allah wills," the divorce does not take effect. What is the reason for this?

We say: The reason is that when he made the taking effect of the divorce contingent upon the will of Allah, it did not take effect, unless we know that the divorce has taken effect; and we do not know that the divorce has taken effect unless we first know that this will has occurred. But the will of Allah, exalted is He, is unseen, so there is no way to know that it has occurred unless we know that the object of the will has taken place and been realized, namely the divorce. On this path, we do not know the occurrence of the will unless we know the occurrence of the divorce, and we do not know the occurrence of the divorce unless we know the occurrence of the will. So knowledge of each of them depends on knowledge of the other, and this is a circular argument (dawr), and circularity is invalid. For this reason they said: the divorce has not taken effect.

The fourth issue: Those who hold that the nonexistent is a thing argued from His saying: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿unless Allah wills﴾. They said: The thing that the doer will do tomorrow, Allah, exalted is He, has called, at present, a "thing," by His saying: 

Page 94

﴿And never say of anything﴾. And it is known that the thing the doer will do tomorrow is nonexistent at present, so it is necessary to name the nonexistent a "thing."

The answer: This argument establishes only that the nonexistent is named "a thing." According to us, the reason for this is that what will become a thing may be called a thing at present, just as He said: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ (an-Nahl: 1), while what is meant is "the command of Allah will come." As for His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾, there are two views concerning it:

The first: It is a statement connected to what precedes it, and the sense is: if he forgets to say, "If Allah wills," then let him mention it when he recalls it. On this point they differed. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: If the recollection occurs only after a long period, then saying "If Allah wills" at that time suffices to avert the breach of oath. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that it may be after a year, a month, a week, or a day. From Tawus: he may make the exception within his sitting. From 'Ata': he may make the exception for as long as it takes to milk a heavy-milking she-camel. The general body of jurists hold that it has no effect on rulings unless it is connected. Ibn 'Abbas argued from His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾, because the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ is the one previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿unless Allah wills﴾. And His saying ﴿And remember your Lord﴾ is not restricted to a specific time, but encompasses all times. Therefore this remembrance becomes obligatory for him at whatever time the recollection occurs. And everyone who said that this remembrance is obligatory said that it is obligatory only to avert the breach of oath, and that conveys the intended point.

Know that Ibn 'Abbas's argument, may Allah be pleased with them both, is clearly to the effect that the exception need not be connected. As for the jurists, they said: If we permitted that, it would follow that no contract or oath would ever be settled. It is related that news reached al-Mansur that Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, disagreed with Ibn 'Abbas concerning the detached exception, so he summoned him in order to rebuke him. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This turns back on you, for you take the pledge of allegiance by oaths. Do you suppose that they will leave your presence and make an exception, and then go out against you? Al-Mansur admired his reply and was satisfied with it.

Know that the upshot of this discussion returns to restricting the text by analogy, and there is much to be said about that. Also, if someone says "If Allah wills" in a hidden way, with his tongue, such that no one hears it, it is valid and averts the breach by consensus, even though the danger you mentioned is present in it. Thus it is established that what they relied upon is not strong. The better argument for requiring that the exception be connected is that many verses indicate the obligation to fulfill contracts and covenants. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Fulfill the contracts﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 1), and He said: ﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾ (al-Isra': 34). So whoever makes a covenant is obliged to fulfill its terms by virtue of these verses. We have departed from this evidence in the case where the exception is connected, because the exception together with what it excepts from is like a single utterance, as shown by the fact that the word of exception alone conveys nothing. It is like half of a single word, so the whole statement is like one meaningful word. On this view, when the exception is mentioned, we know that nothing has been obligated, unlike when the exception is connected: then a complete commitment has been made by the utterance, and so it is obligatory to fulfill that commitment.

The second view: His saying ﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾ has no connection to what precedes it, but is a new, independent statement. On this view there are several meanings:

One of them: Remember your Lord with glorification and seeking forgiveness when you forget the word of exception; the purpose is to encourage attention to mentioning this word.

Another: Remember your Lord when forgetfulness overtakes you, so that He may remind you of what you have forgotten.

A third: Some have understood it as referring to performing a forgotten prayer when one remembers it. This view, with its three possibilities, is far-fetched, because connecting this statement to what precedes it serves to complete the discussion of this matter, whereas making it an independent statement would cause the speech to begin anew and be cut off, and that is not permissible.

ثُمَّ قالَ

Then He said, Exalted is He: "And say, 'Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right guidance.'" Concerning this there are several aspects:

The first: that abandoning his saying "if Allah wills" is not good, and mentioning it is better than abandoning it. His saying "to what is nearer than this to right guidance" means the intent of mentioning this phrase.

The second: if he promised them something and said with it "if Allah wills," then he says, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something better and more complete than what I promised you."

The third: that His saying "to what is nearer than this to right guidance" is a reference to the account of the People of the Cave, and its meaning is: perhaps Allah will give me, from the clear proofs and evidences of the correctness of my being a Prophet from Allah, truthful in claiming prophethood, what is greater in indication and nearer to right guidance than the account of the People of the Cave.

Allah has indeed done that, when He gave him, from the stories of the Prophets and reports of the unseen, what is greater than that. As for His saying, Exalted is He: "And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine." "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How seeing is He and how hearing! They have not besides Him any protector, and He does not share His command with anyone." Know that this verse is the last of the verses mentioned in the story of the People of the Cave. Regarding His saying "And they remained in their cave" there are two views:

The first: that this is a quotation of the speech of the people, and the evidence for it is that He, Exalted, said: "They will say, 'They were three, the fourth of them their dog,'" and so on until He said: "And they remained in their cave," meaning that those groups said that. This is confirmed by His saying after it: "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained," which resembles a rebuttal of the statement mentioned before it. It is also confirmed by what is reported in the codex of Abdullah: "And they said, and they remained in their cave."

The second view: that His saying "And they remained in their cave" is the speech of Allah, Exalted, for He informed about the quantity of that period. As for His saying "They will say, 'They were three, the fourth of them their dog,'" it is a statement that came earlier, and between it and this verse has intervened what requires the separation of one from the other, namely His saying "So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument," and His saying "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth," which does not necessitate that what precedes it is a quotation. This is because He, Exalted, intended: "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth," meaning: refer to the report of Allah rather than what the People of the Book say.

The second issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "thalatha mi'at sinin" without tanwin, and the rest read it with tanwin. That is because His saying "sinin" (years) is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to His saying "thalatha mi'a" (three hundred). Since He said "And they remained in their cave," it was not known whether these were days, months, or years; when He said "sinin," this became an explanation of "thalatha mi'a," so it is an explanatory apposition to it. It was also said that it is by inversion of order, meaning they remained "sinin thalathamia" (years, three hundred). As for the reading of Hamzah, its basis is that the obligatory form in the construct phrase would be "thalathu mi'atin sanatan," but it is permissible to place the plural in the position of the singular in the specification, as in His saying: "Say, 'Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds?'" (al-Kahf: 103).

The third issue: His saying "And they added nine" means: they added nine years. If they say: Why did He not say "three hundred and nine years"? And what is the benefit of His saying "and they added nine"? We say: some of them said: the period was three hundred years by the solar calendar and three hundred and nine years by the lunar calendar. This is problematic, because this view is not valid by calculation. It may be said: perhaps when they completed three hundred years, their condition drew close to the Prophets, then something happened that caused them to remain asleep for nine years after that. Then He said: "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained," meaning: He, Exalted, knows best the measure of this period among the people who disagreed about it. He is more fitting to know it because He is the originator of the heavens and the earth and the governor of the world, and when this is so, He knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth,

Page 96

and so He necessarily knows this event. Then He, Exalted, said: "How seeing is He and how hearing!" This is an expression used in exclamation, and the meaning is: how seeing He is and how hearing He is. We have elaborated on the exclamatory expression in Surat al-Baqarah in explaining His saying, Exalted: "How patient they are over the Fire" (al-Baqarah: 175). Then He, Exalted, said: "They have not besides Him any protector," and regarding this there are several aspects:

The first: the People of the Cave have no protector besides Allah, for He is the One who takes charge of their preservation during that long sleep.

The second: these people who differ concerning the duration of the People of the Cave's stay have no protector besides Allah who takes charge of their affairs and establishes for them the management of their own selves. If they need Allah's management and protection, how could they know this event without His informing them?

The third: that some of the people, when they stated in this matter views contrary to the word of Allah, they deserved punishment, so Allah made clear that they have no protector besides Him who could prevent Allah from sending punishment upon them. Then He said: "and He does not share His command with anyone." The meaning: since He, Exalted, has decreed that their stay is this measure, no one may say a statement contrary to it. The principle is that when two are partners, objection from each of them against the other increases, and this prevents each of them from carrying out the matter according to what he wants. Its ultimate conclusion returns to His saying, Exalted: "Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined" (al-Anbiya': 22). So Allah, Exalted, negated that of Himself by His saying: "and He does not share His command with anyone." Ibn ʿAmir read "wa lā tushrik" with the ta' and jazm, as a prohibition and address, coordinated with His saying "and do not say of anything" or with His saying "and remember your Lord when you forget." The meaning: do not ask anyone about what Allah has informed you of regarding the number of the People of the Cave; confine yourself to His judgment and explanation, and do not make anyone a partner in seeking knowledge of that event. The rest read it with the ya' and raf', as a report, and the meaning: He, Exalted, does not do that.

* * *

The fourth issue: People differed about the time of the People of the Cave and their place. As for the time in which they lived, it was said: they were before Moses, peace be upon him, and Moses mentioned them in the Torah, and for this reason the Jews asked about them. It was said: they entered the cave before the Messiah, and the Messiah informed of their story, then they were raised in the period between ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: they entered the cave after the Messiah. Al-Qaffal related this view from Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

Some people said: they have not died and will not die until the Day of Resurrection. As for the place of this cave, al-Qaffal related from Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi the astrologer that al-Wathiq sent him to learn the condition of the People of the Cave, to the Romans. He said: the king of the Romans sent with me people to the place where they are said to be. He said: the man appointed over that place frightened me from entering upon them. He said: I entered and saw the hair on their chests. He said: I realized that it was a deception and a trick, and that people had treated those bodies with drying medicines for the bodies of the dead to preserve them from decay, such as smearing with aloe and other things. Then al-Qaffal said: what we know is that it is not known whether that place is the place of the People of the Cave or another place, and what Allah has reported about it must be held with certainty, and the word of the people of Rome that this place is the place of the People of the Cave is of no weight. It is mentioned in al-Kashshaf from Muʿawiyah that he invaded the Romans and passed by the cave and said: "If it were uncovered for us about these, so that we could look at them." Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "That is not for you; Allah has prevented one better than you." He said: "If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight and been filled with terror from them." He said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "I will not stop until I know their condition." So he sent people and said to them: "Go and look." When they entered the cave, Allah sent a wind upon them and it burned them. I say: knowledge of that time and that place has no room for the intellect, and it is only obtained from a text, and that is absent, so it is established that there is no way to it.

The fifth issue: Know that the basis of the argument for affirming resurrection and the Last Day rests on three principles:
One of them: that He, Exalted, is capable of all possibilities.

The second: that He, Exalted, knows all knowables, universal and particular.

The third: that whatever is possible to occur at some times is possible to occur at all times. When these three principles are established, the argument for the possibility of resurrection and the Last Day is established. Likewise here: it has been established that He, Exalted, is knowing and capable of all things, and it has been established that a person's remaining alive in sleep for a day is possible, so likewise his remaining for three hundred years must be possible, in the sense that the God of the world preserves him and guards him from harm.

As for the philosophers, they also say: it is not far-fetched that strange celestial configurations occur that cause, in the matter of the world of generation and corruption, the occurrence of strange, rare conditions. I say: these three consecutive surahs each contain the occurrence of a wondrous, rare condition in this world. Surat Bani Isra'il contains the Night Journey of the body of Muhammad (ﷺ) from Mecca to Syria, which is a wondrous condition. This surah contains the people's remaining in sleep for three hundred years and more, which is also a wondrous condition. Surat Maryam contains the occurrence of a child without a father, which is also a wondrous condition. The reliance in demonstrating the possibility of all these wonders and strange things mentioned in these three consecutive surahs is the method we have mentioned.

What shows that this meaning is among the possibilities is that Abu ʿAli Ibn Sina mentioned, in the chapter on time in his book al-Shifa', that Aristotle the Sage mentioned that a condition resembling the condition of the People of the Cave befell a group of the divine-minded. Then Abu ʿAli said: history also indicates that they were before the People of the Cave.

ثُمَّ قالَ

Then He said, Exalted is He: "And say, 'Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this to right guidance.'" Concerning this there are several aspects:

The first: that abandoning his saying "if Allah wills" is not good, and mentioning it is better than abandoning it. His saying "to what is nearer than this to right guidance" means the intent of mentioning this phrase.

The second: if he promised them something and said with it "if Allah wills," then he says, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to something better and more complete than what I promised you."

The third: that His saying "to what is nearer than this to right guidance" is a reference to the account of the People of the Cave, and its meaning is: perhaps Allah will give me, from the clear proofs and evidences of the correctness of my being a Prophet from Allah, truthful in claiming prophethood, what is greater in indication and nearer to right guidance than the account of the People of the Cave.

Allah has indeed done that, when He gave him, from the stories of the Prophets and reports of the unseen, what is greater than that. As for His saying, Exalted is He: "And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine." "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth. How seeing is He and how hearing! They have not besides Him any protector, and He does not share His command with anyone." Know that this verse is the last of the verses mentioned in the story of the People of the Cave. Regarding His saying "And they remained in their cave" there are two views:

The first: that this is a quotation of the speech of the people, and the evidence for it is that He, Exalted, said: "They will say, 'They were three, the fourth of them their dog,'" and so on until He said: "And they remained in their cave," meaning that those groups said that. This is confirmed by His saying after it: "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained," which resembles a rebuttal of the statement mentioned before it. It is also confirmed by what is reported in the codex of Abdullah: "And they said, and they remained in their cave."

The second view: that His saying "And they remained in their cave" is the speech of Allah, Exalted, for He informed about the quantity of that period. As for His saying "They will say, 'They were three, the fourth of them their dog,'" it is a statement that came earlier, and between it and this verse has intervened what requires the separation of one from the other, namely His saying "So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument," and His saying "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth," which does not necessitate that what precedes it is a quotation. This is because He, Exalted, intended: "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth," meaning: refer to the report of Allah rather than what the People of the Book say.

The second issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "thalatha mi'at sinin" without tanwin, and the rest read it with tanwin. That is because His saying "sinin" (years) is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to His saying "thalatha mi'a" (three hundred). Since He said "And they remained in their cave," it was not known whether these were days, months, or years; when He said "sinin," this became an explanation of "thalatha mi'a," so it is an explanatory apposition to it. It was also said that it is by inversion of order, meaning they remained "sinin thalathamia" (years, three hundred). As for the reading of Hamzah, its basis is that the obligatory form in the construct phrase would be "thalathu mi'atin sanatan," but it is permissible to place the plural in the position of the singular in the specification, as in His saying: "Say, 'Shall we inform you of the greatest losers in deeds?'" (al-Kahf: 103).

The third issue: His saying "And they added nine" means: they added nine years. If they say: Why did He not say "three hundred and nine years"? And what is the benefit of His saying "and they added nine"? We say: some of them said: the period was three hundred years by the solar calendar and three hundred and nine years by the lunar calendar. This is problematic, because this view is not valid by calculation. It may be said: perhaps when they completed three hundred years, their condition drew close to the Prophets, then something happened that caused them to remain asleep for nine years after that. Then He said: "Say: Allah knows best how long they remained," meaning: He, Exalted, knows best the measure of this period among the people who disagreed about it. He is more fitting to know it because He is the originator of the heavens and the earth and the governor of the world, and when this is so, He knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth,

and so He necessarily knows this event. Then He, Exalted, said: "How seeing is He and how hearing!" This is an expression used in exclamation, and the meaning is: how seeing He is and how hearing He is. We have elaborated on the exclamatory expression in Surat al-Baqarah in explaining His saying, Exalted: "How patient they are over the Fire" (al-Baqarah: 175). Then He, Exalted, said: "They have not besides Him any protector," and regarding this there are several aspects:

The first: the People of the Cave have no protector besides Allah, for He is the One who takes charge of their preservation during that long sleep.

The second: these people who differ concerning the duration of the People of the Cave's stay have no protector besides Allah who takes charge of their affairs and establishes for them the management of their own selves. If they need Allah's management and protection, how could they know this event without His informing them?

The third: that some of the people, when they stated in this matter views contrary to the word of Allah, they deserved punishment, so Allah made clear that they have no protector besides Him who could prevent Allah from sending punishment upon them. Then He said: "and He does not share His command with anyone." The meaning: since He, Exalted, has decreed that their stay is this measure, no one may say a statement contrary to it. The principle is that when two are partners, objection from each of them against the other increases, and this prevents each of them from carrying out the matter according to what he wants. Its ultimate conclusion returns to His saying, Exalted: "Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined" (al-Anbiya': 22). So Allah, Exalted, negated that of Himself by His saying: "and He does not share His command with anyone." Ibn ʿAmir read "wa lā tushrik" with the ta' and jazm, as a prohibition and address, coordinated with His saying "and do not say of anything" or with His saying "and remember your Lord when you forget." The meaning: do not ask anyone about what Allah has informed you of regarding the number of the People of the Cave; confine yourself to His judgment and explanation, and do not make anyone a partner in seeking knowledge of that event. The rest read it with the ya' and raf', as a report, and the meaning: He, Exalted, does not do that.

The fourth issue: People differed about the time of the People of the Cave and their place. As for the time in which they lived, it was said: they were before Moses, peace be upon him, and Moses mentioned them in the Torah, and for this reason the Jews asked about them. It was said: they entered the cave before the Messiah, and the Messiah informed of their story, then they were raised in the period between ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and Muhammad (ﷺ). It was said: they entered the cave after the Messiah. Al-Qaffal related this view from Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

Some people said: they have not died and will not die until the Day of Resurrection. As for the place of this cave, al-Qaffal related from Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi the astrologer that al-Wathiq sent him to learn the condition of the People of the Cave, to the Romans. He said: the king of the Romans sent with me people to the place where they are said to be. He said: the man appointed over that place frightened me from entering upon them. He said: I entered and saw the hair on their chests. He said: I realized that it was a deception and a trick, and that people had treated those bodies with drying medicines for the bodies of the dead to preserve them from decay, such as smearing with aloe and other things. Then al-Qaffal said: what we know is that it is not known whether that place is the place of the People of the Cave or another place, and what Allah has reported about it must be held with certainty, and the word of the people of Rome that this place is the place of the People of the Cave is of no weight. It is mentioned in al-Kashshaf from Muʿawiyah that he invaded the Romans and passed by the cave and said: "If it were uncovered for us about these, so that we could look at them." Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "That is not for you; Allah has prevented one better than you." He said: "If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight and been filled with terror from them." He said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "I will not stop until I know their condition." So he sent people and said to them: "Go and look." When they entered the cave, Allah sent a wind upon them and it burned them. I say: knowledge of that time and that place has no room for the intellect, and it is only obtained from a text, and that is absent, so it is established that there is no way to it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 27–28 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted said: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can alter His words, and you will not find any refuge other than Him.﴾

Know that from this verse up to the story of Musa and al-Khidr is one continuous statement about one single story. The reason is that the leading disbelievers of Quraysh argued and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If you want us to believe in you, then drive away from your presence these poor people who have believed in you." Allah, exalted is He, forbade him from doing so and prevented him from it. In this group of verses He elaborated on showing that what they proposed and demanded was a corrupt request and a false suggestion. Then He, exalted is He, made the principle in this matter one single thing: that he should persevere in reciting the Book that Allah revealed to him, and in acting upon it, and that he should not turn to the proposals of those who make proposals or the obstinacy of the obstinate. So He said: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord.﴾

In the verse there is an issue, which is this:

The word "recite" (اتْلُ, ut-lu) covers both reading (القِراءَة, al-qira'a) and following (الِاتِّباع, al-ittiba'), so the meaning is: "Keep to reading the Book that was revealed to you, and keep to acting upon it." Then He said: ﴿None can alter His words﴾, meaning that the possibility of change and substitution entering it is impossible. This verse can be used to establish that the specification of a textual ruling (تَخْصِيص النَّصِّ, takhsis al-nass) by analogy (القِياس, qiyas) is not permissible. This is because His saying ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord⦆ means: "Keep to acting in accordance with the requirement of this Book," and that requires the obligation to act in accordance with its apparent meaning.

If it is said: then abrogation (النَّسْخ, naskh) should not enter it. We reply: this is the position of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, so it is not far-fetched. Moreover, abrogation in reality is not a substitution, because the abrogated ruling remains valid in its time until the time when the abrogating ruling arrives. So the abrogating ruling is like an end-point; how then could it be a substitution?

As for His saying ﴿and you will not find any refuge other than Him﴾: they agreed that al-multahad (المُلْتَحَد) means the place of refuge (المَلْجَأ). The lexicographers said: it derives from lahada and alhada, meaning "to incline." From this is His saying: ﴿the tongue of the one they refer to⦆ (al-Nahl: 103). The one who inclines away from religion is al-mulhid (المُلْحِد). The meaning is: "You will not find any refuge other than Him in clarity and guidance."

﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face; and do not let your eyes turn past them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life; and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair is neglected.﴾

Know that the leaders of Quraysh gathered and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If you want us to believe in you, then drive these poor people away from your presence. When we attend, they should not attend, and you should appoint for them a time at which they gather with you." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord⦆ (al-An'am: 52), up to the end of the verse. In it He made clear that it is not permissible to drive them away; rather, you should sit with them, agree with them, and honour their status, and not turn to the statements of those disbelievers, nor give them any weight in your view, whether they are absent or present. This story is separate from what came before it, and is an independent, self-contained statement. A parallel to this verse has already occurred in Surat al-An'am, namely His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening⦆ (al-An'am: 52). In that verse the Messenger (ﷺ) was forbidden from driving them away, and in this verse he was commanded to sit with them and to be steadfast with them.

As for His saying ﴿keep yourself patient﴾ (wa-isbir nafsaka): the basic meaning of sabr (الصَّبْر, patience) is restraint (الحَبْس). From this, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade al-masbura (المَصْبُورَة), which is an animal that is restrained and then shot at.

As for His saying ﴿with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening⦆, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: Ibn Amir read bi-al-ghudwa with a dammah on the ghayn (غُدْوَة), while the rest read bi-al-ghada (الغَداة). Both are dialectal forms of the language.

The second issue: regarding His saying ﴿morning and evening⦆, there are several interpretations:

The first: what is meant is that they are constant in this practice at all times, like the saying of someone: "So-and-so has no activity morning and evening except insulting people."

The second: what is meant is the prayer of dawn and the afternoon prayer.

The third: what is meant is that al-ghada (the morning) is the time in which a person passes from sleep to wakefulness, and this transition resembles the transition from death to life. Al-'ashiy (the evening) is the time in which a person passes from wakefulness to sleep, and from life to death. A rational person, during these two times, is greatly mindful of Allah and deeply grateful for the blessings and favours of Allah.

Then He said: ﴿and do not let your eyes pass beyond them⦆. One says: "'adaahu" when he went beyond it, and from this comes the saying: "'ada tawrahu" (he exceeded his limit), and "jaa'a al-qawmu 'ada Zaydan" (the people came, excluding Zayd). It is only transitive with the particle "'an" because it conveys distance, so it is as if He forbade that distancing. It was also read: "wa la tu'addi 'aynayka" (ولا تُعَدِّ عَيْنَيْكَ), from a'daahu and 'addaahu, a causative form with a hamza and an intensified middle radical. From this is the line of poetry:

"So turn away from what you see, for there is no return for it."

The purpose of the verse is that He forbade the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from looking down on the poor believers and from his eyes turning away from them, out of his desire to sit with the rich and their fine appearance. His saying ﴿desiring the adornment of the worldly life⦆ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (حال, hal), meaning: "If you do that, your undertaking of it would be only out of your desire for the adornment of the worldly life."

* * *

When He had emphasised in the matter of sitting with the poor among the Muslims, He emphasised the prohibition against turning to the statements of the rich and the arrogant. So He said: ﴿and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair is neglected.⦆ In this are several issues:

[Page 99]

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) used this verse to argue that He, exalted is He, is the one who creates ignorance and heedlessness in the hearts of the ignorant, because His saying ﴿We have made heedless (aghfalna)⦆ indicates this meaning. The Mu'tazilites said: what is meant by His saying ﴿whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance⦆ is that We found his heart heedless; it does not mean that We created heedlessness in it. The evidence for this is what is reported from Amr ibn Ma'dikarib al-Zubaydi, who said to Banu Sulaym: "We fought you and did not answer you (i.e., we did not fail); we asked you and did not make you stingy; we satirised you and did not render you speechless." That is, we did not find you cowardly, nor stingy, nor unable to speak.

Then we say: taking the wording in this sense is preferable, and several points indicate this:

The first: if it were so, they would not deserve blame.

The second: He, exalted is He, said after this verse: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve⦆ (al-Kahf: 29). If He had created heedlessness in his heart, this would not be valid.

The third: if the meaning were that He made his heart heedless, it would have been necessary to say: "and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, so he followed his desire," because on this assumption it would be one of the verbs of result (أفعال المُطاوَعَة, af'al al-mutawa'a), and such verbs are joined with fa' (the particle of consequence), not with waw. One says: "I broke it, so it broke (fa-nkasara)," and "I pushed it, so it was pushed (fa-ndafa'a)," and one does not say "wa-nkasara" or "wa-ndafa'a."

The fourth: His saying ﴿and who follows his desire⦆. If He had in reality made his heart heedless, it would not be permissible to attribute that to his following of his desire.

The answer: his saying, "The meaning of 'aghfalna' is: we found him heedless, and what is meant is not the causing of heedlessness in him."

We reply to this answer in two ways:

The first: the homonymy (الاشْتِراك, al-ishtirak) is contrary to the original principle, so it is necessary to hold that the pattern of these verbs is literal in one of the two senses and metaphorical in the other. Taking it literally in the sense of causing (التَّكْوِين, takwin) and metaphorically in the sense of finding (الوِجْدان, wijdan) is preferable to the reverse. This is shown in several ways:

One: the use of this verbal pattern in the sense of causing is more frequent than its use in the sense of finding, and frequency is evidence of preponderance.

Two: the understanding that comes first from this pattern is toward causing more than toward finding, and immediate understanding is evidence of preponderance.

Three: if we take it as literal in the sense of causing, it is possible to take it as metaphorical in the sense of finding, because knowledge of a thing follows the existence of the known. So making the word literal for the thing that is followed and metaphorical for what follows is consistent with reason. But if we took it as literal in finding and metaphorical in causing, it would follow that it is literal for what follows and metaphorical for what is followed, which is the reverse of what reason requires. Thus it is established that the original use of this pattern is literal for causing, not for finding.

The second way of answering the objection: we grant that the word is homonymous between causing and finding. Nevertheless we say that His saying ﴿aghfalna⦆ must be understood as the causing of heedlessness. This is because rational proof shows that it is impossible for a servant to be the one who causes heedlessness in himself. The proof: if he attempts to cause heedlessness, then either he attempts to cause heedlessness in general, or he attempts to cause heedlessness of a specific thing. The first is false, for otherwise it would not be more fitting for him to be heedless of this thing than of another thing, because the common nature shared among many kinds has an equal relation to all those kinds. The second is also false, because heedlessness of such-and-such is a heedlessness that is not distinguished from the other kinds of heedlessness except by being related to that specific thing. Therefore, he cannot intend to cause heedlessness of such-and-such unless he conceives that this heedlessness is heedlessness of such-and-such, and he cannot conceive that this heedlessness is heedlessness of such-and-such unless he conceives of such-and-such; because knowledge of one thing's relation to another is conditioned on conceiving each of the two related things. Thus it is established that he cannot intend to cause heedlessness of such-and-such except while being aware of such-and-such. But heedlessness of such-and-such is the opposite of awareness of such-and-such. So it is established that the servant cannot cause this heedlessness except when two opposites come together, and that is impossible; and what depends on the impossible is impossible. Hence it is established that the servant is unable to cause heedlessness, and therefore the creator of heedlessness and its originator in the servants must be Allah. This is a decisive point in establishing this claim.

[Page 100]

At this point it becomes clear that what is meant by His saying ﴿and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless⦆ is the causing of heedlessness, not the finding of it. As for the argument about praise and blame, we have countered it many times and in many ways with knowledge and motive. As for His saying after this verse ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve⦆ (al-Kahf: 29), the discussion of it will come later, if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

As for His saying ﴿and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless⦆: if what is meant were the causing of heedlessness, it would have been necessary to mention the fa' and not the waw. We say: this would only be necessary if the creation of heedlessness in the heart entailed the occurrence of following desire, just as breaking entails the occurrence of being broken. But this is not the case, because heedlessness of Allah does not necessarily entail following desire, since it is possible that he becomes heedless of the remembrance of Allah while nevertheless not following his desire, but remaining in suspension, which is compatible with a state of bewilderment, astonishment, and fear of the whole. Thus this objection falls away.

Al-Qaffal mentioned several other interpretations of the verse according to the Mu'tazilite position:

The first of them: when He poured the worldly life upon them in abundance, and this led to the firm establishment of heedlessness in their hearts, it is valid under this interpretation that He caused heedlessness in their hearts, as in His saying: ﴿But my call only increased them in flight⦆ (Nuh: 6).

The second interpretation: the meaning of "aghfalna" is "We left him heedless, and did not mark him with the mark of the people of purity and piety." It is from their saying: "a camel that is ghufl" (بَعِيرٌ غُفْل), meaning one that has no mark on it.

The third: what is meant by "We made his heart heedless" is that We left it with Satan, and did not prevent Satan from it.

It is said regarding the first interpretation: whether the opening of the door of worldly pleasures to him has an effect in causing heedlessness in his heart or has no effect. If it has an effect, then the effect of delivering pleasures to him becomes a cause for the occurrence of heedlessness in his heart, and this is exactly the claim that He did what necessitates heedlessness in his heart. If it has no effect in causing this heedlessness, then its attribution to Him is invalidated.

Al-Razi, Mafatih al-Ghayb (Commentary on Surah 18, verses 27–28, part 2 of 2):

It may be said regarding the second aspect: His saying, "We have made his heart heedless of Our remembrance," is equivalent to His saying, "We have blackened his heart and whitened his face," and it conveys nothing other than what we have mentioned.

It may be said regarding the third aspect: If that abandonment (al-takhliyah) had an effect in bringing about that heedlessness, then our statement is established; otherwise, the attribution of that heedlessness to Allah Most High is invalidated.

Second issue: His saying, ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his own desire﴾, indicates that the worst state of a human being is for his heart to be empty of the remembrance of the Truth and filled with desire that calls him to occupy himself with creation. The explanation is this: the remembrance of Allah is light, and the remembrance of other than Him is darkness. For existence is the nature of light, and non-existence is the source of darkness. The Truth, Exalted is He, is necessarily existent in His own essence, so the true light is Allah, and whatever is other than Allah is contingent in its existence in its own essence. Contingency is a privative nature, so it is the source of darkness. Thus when the remembrance of Allah shines in the heart, light, radiance and illumination have come into it; and when the heart turns toward creation, injustice and darkness, indeed darkness upon darkness, have come into it. For this reason, when the heart turns away from the Truth and turns toward creation, it is pure and complete darkness. Turning away from the Truth is what is meant by His saying, ﴿We have made his heart heedless of Our remembrance﴾, and turning toward creation is what is meant by His saying, ﴿and who follows his own desire﴾.

Third issue: It has been said that ﴿furutan﴾ means "exceeding the limit," from the expression "a horse that is furut," meaning one that is ahead of the horses. Al-Layth said: al-furut is a matter in which one is excessive. It is said: "Everything of so-and-so is furut." He recited a line of poetry:
"He burdened me with excess and a hopeless matter, furut."
That is, wasted (muday‘a). So His saying, "and his affair has been furut," means: the affair which requires him to preserve it and be concerned with it, namely the affair of his religion, becomes specifically one in which neglect and shortcoming occur. This condition is the description of one who does not look to his religion, and whose only concern is his worldly life. Thus Allah Most High explained that the state of those heedless of the remembrance of Allah who follow their desires is that they are negligent in their important matters and turn away from what was obligatory upon them of reflection on the verses (page 101) and of safeguarding the affairs of this world and the Hereafter. The summary is this: Allah Most High described those poor believers as persistently remembering Allah and turning away from other than the remembrance of Allah, saying, ﴿Keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance﴾. And He described these rich ones as turning away from the remembrance of Allah Most High and turning toward other than Allah, which is His saying, ﴿whose heart We have made heedless﴾ and ﴿and who follows his desire﴾. Then He commanded His Messenger to sit with those and to keep away from these.

Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated: "I was sitting in a group of weak emigrants, some of whom were covering others from nakedness, and there was a reciter reciting the Qur'an. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came and said: 'What were you doing?' We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, one of us was reciting from the Book of Allah while we were listening.' He, peace be upon him, said: 'Praise be to Allah who has placed among my community those whom I was commanded to keep myself patient with.' Then he sat down in the midst of us and said: 'Rejoice, O poor emigrants, for the complete light on the Day of Resurrection: you will enter Paradise before the rich by a period of five hundred years.'"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 27–28 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted said: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord; none can alter His words, and you will not find any refuge other than Him.﴾

Know that from this verse up to the story of Musa and al-Khidr is one continuous statement about one single story. The reason is that the leading disbelievers of Quraysh argued and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If you want us to believe in you, then drive away from your presence these poor people who have believed in you." Allah, exalted is He, forbade him from doing so and prevented him from it. In this group of verses He elaborated on showing that what they proposed and demanded was a corrupt request and a false suggestion. Then He, exalted is He, made the principle in this matter one single thing: that he should persevere in reciting the Book that Allah revealed to him, and in acting upon it, and that he should not turn to the proposals of those who make proposals or the obstinacy of the obstinate. So He said: ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord.﴾

In the verse there is an issue, which is this:

The word "recite" (اتْلُ, ut-lu) covers both reading (القِراءَة, al-qira'a) and following (الِاتِّباع, al-ittiba'), so the meaning is: "Keep to reading the Book that was revealed to you, and keep to acting upon it." Then He said: ﴿None can alter His words﴾, meaning that the possibility of change and substitution entering it is impossible. This verse can be used to establish that the specification of a textual ruling (تَخْصِيص النَّصِّ, takhsis al-nass) by analogy (القِياس, qiyas) is not permissible. This is because His saying ﴿And recite what has been revealed to you of the Book of your Lord⦆ means: "Keep to acting in accordance with the requirement of this Book," and that requires the obligation to act in accordance with its apparent meaning.

If it is said: then abrogation (النَّسْخ, naskh) should not enter it. We reply: this is the position of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, so it is not far-fetched. Moreover, abrogation in reality is not a substitution, because the abrogated ruling remains valid in its time until the time when the abrogating ruling arrives. So the abrogating ruling is like an end-point; how then could it be a substitution?

As for His saying ﴿and you will not find any refuge other than Him﴾: they agreed that al-multahad (المُلْتَحَد) means the place of refuge (المَلْجَأ). The lexicographers said: it derives from lahada and alhada, meaning "to incline." From this is His saying: ﴿the tongue of the one they refer to⦆ (al-Nahl: 103). The one who inclines away from religion is al-mulhid (المُلْحِد). The meaning is: "You will not find any refuge other than Him in clarity and guidance."

﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His face; and do not let your eyes turn past them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life; and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire and whose affair is neglected.﴾

Know that the leaders of Quraysh gathered and said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If you want us to believe in you, then drive these poor people away from your presence. When we attend, they should not attend, and you should appoint for them a time at which they gather with you." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord⦆ (al-An'am: 52), up to the end of the verse. In it He made clear that it is not permissible to drive them away; rather, you should sit with them, agree with them, and honour their status, and not turn to the statements of those disbelievers, nor give them any weight in your view, whether they are absent or present. This story is separate from what came before it, and is an independent, self-contained statement. A parallel to this verse has already occurred in Surat al-An'am, namely His saying: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening⦆ (al-An'am: 52). In that verse the Messenger (ﷺ) was forbidden from driving them away, and in this verse he was commanded to sit with them and to be steadfast with them.

As for His saying ﴿keep yourself patient﴾ (wa-isbir nafsaka): the basic meaning of sabr (الصَّبْر, patience) is restraint (الحَبْس). From this, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade al-masbura (المَصْبُورَة), which is an animal that is restrained and then shot at.

As for His saying ﴿with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening⦆, there are two issues in it:

The first issue: Ibn Amir read bi-al-ghudwa with a dammah on the ghayn (غُدْوَة), while the rest read bi-al-ghada (الغَداة). Both are dialectal forms of the language.

The second issue: regarding His saying ﴿morning and evening⦆, there are several interpretations:

The first: what is meant is that they are constant in this practice at all times, like the saying of someone: "So-and-so has no activity morning and evening except insulting people."

The second: what is meant is the prayer of dawn and the afternoon prayer.

The third: what is meant is that al-ghada (the morning) is the time in which a person passes from sleep to wakefulness, and this transition resembles the transition from death to life. Al-'ashiy (the evening) is the time in which a person passes from wakefulness to sleep, and from life to death. A rational person, during these two times, is greatly mindful of Allah and deeply grateful for the blessings and favours of Allah.

Then He said: ﴿and do not let your eyes pass beyond them⦆. One says: "'adaahu" when he went beyond it, and from this comes the saying: "'ada tawrahu" (he exceeded his limit), and "jaa'a al-qawmu 'ada Zaydan" (the people came, excluding Zayd). It is only transitive with the particle "'an" because it conveys distance, so it is as if He forbade that distancing. It was also read: "wa la tu'addi 'aynayka" (ولا تُعَدِّ عَيْنَيْكَ), from a'daahu and 'addaahu, a causative form with a hamza and an intensified middle radical. From this is the line of poetry:

"So turn away from what you see, for there is no return for it."

The purpose of the verse is that He forbade the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from looking down on the poor believers and from his eyes turning away from them, out of his desire to sit with the rich and their fine appearance. His saying ﴿desiring the adornment of the worldly life⦆ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (حال, hal), meaning: "If you do that, your undertaking of it would be only out of your desire for the adornment of the worldly life."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.
