Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place."﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: regarding the arrangement of the discourse (taqrir al-nazm), there are several aspects.

The first: when He, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger not to turn toward those wealthy people who said, "If you drive away the poor, we will believe in you," He then said after it: ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord"﴾, meaning: say to these people, "This true religion has come only from Allah. If you accept it, the benefit returns to you, and if you do not accept it, the harm returns to you. There is no connection of this to poverty and wealth, ugliness and beauty, obscurity and fame."

The second aspect of the arrangement: it is possible that the meaning is that the truth is what has come from Allah, and the truth that has come to me from Him is that I should restrain myself with these poor people and not drive them away, and not turn toward the leaders and the people of this world.

The third aspect of the arrangement: that the meaning is that the truth which has come from Allah is that whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve; and that Allah, exalted is He, did not permit driving away those who believe and do righteous deeds, in order that a group of disbelievers might enter into faith. If it is said: does not reason require preferring the more important over the less important? Driving away those poor people entails only the loss of their dignity, and this is a minor harm; whereas not driving them away entails the continuation of the disbelievers in disbelief, and this is a great harm. We reply: as for the claim that not driving them away entails the continuation of the disbelievers in disbelief, this is granted; but whoever abandons faith out of fear of sitting with the poor, his faith is not faith, but rather vile hypocrisy. Therefore it is obligatory for the intelligent person not to give heed to the faith of one whose state and description are like this.

The second issue: The Mu'tazilah said: His saying, ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾, is explicit that the matter of faith and disbelief, obedience and disobedience, is entrusted to the servant and his choice. Whoever denies this has contradicted the explicit Qur'an. Some people asked me about this verse, and I said: this verse is among the strongest proofs for the soundness of our position, because the verse is explicit that the occurrence of faith and the occurrence of disbelief are contingent upon the occurrence of the will to faith and the occurrence of the will to disbelief. Sound reason also indicates this, for voluntary action cannot occur without intention toward it and without choice of it. Knowing this, we say: if the occurrence of that intention and choice is by another intention preceding it and another choice preceding it, it would follow that every intention and choice is preceded by another intention, ad infinitum, and this is impossible. Therefore those intentions and choices must terminate in an intention and choice which Allah, exalted is He, creates in the servant by necessity at the occurrence of that necessary intention, and the necessary choice necessitates the act. So the human, whether he wills or does not will: if that decisive will free of opposition does not arise in his heart, the act does not follow; and when that decisive will arises, whether he wills or does not will, the act must follow from it. Thus the occurrence of the will is not contingent upon the occurrence of the act, nor is the occurrence of the act contingent upon the will; the human is compelled in the form of one who chooses. Shaykh Abu Hamid al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, established this meaning in the chapter on trust in God (tawakkul) in his book Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din, saying: If you say: "I find in myself an immediate awareness that if I will the act, I am able to do the act, and if I will the omission, I am able to omit it; so the act and the omission are by me, not by another," he answered it, saying: Suppose you find this meaning in yourself; but do you find in yourself that if you will the willing of the act, that willing occurs, and if you do not will that willing, it does not occur? Rather, reason testifies that you will the act without a prior will preceding that will; and when you will the act, the act must occur without any power or choice in this situation. Thus the occurrence of the will in the heart is a necessary matter, and the act's following upon the occurrence of the will is also a necessary matter, and this indicates that all of it is from Allah, exalted is He.

The third issue: His saying, ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾, contains several benefits.

The first benefit: the verse indicates that the proceeding of an act from an agent without intention and motive is impossible.

The second benefit: the imperative form not used for the sense of demand is numerous in the Book of Allah. It is then reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: this form is a threat and a warning, and not an option.

The third benefit: it indicates that He, exalted is He, does not benefit from the faith of believers nor is harmed by the disbelief of disbelievers; rather the benefit of faith returns to them, and the harm of disbelief returns to them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, it is for them﴾ (al-Isra': 7). Know that when He, exalted is He, described disbelief and faith, and falsehood and truth, He followed it with mention of the threat against disbelief and deeds of falsehood, and mention of the promise for faith and righteous deeds. As for the threat, it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire﴾, meaning: We have prepared for whoever wronged himself and placed worship in other than its proper place, and pride in other than its proper locus. When he found it pleasing according to his desire and disdained accepting the truth because those who accepted it were poor and needy, all of this is wrongdoing and placing a thing in other than its place. So He, exalted is He, informed that He has prepared for these people a Fire, which is the Blazing Hell. Then He, exalted is He, described that Fire with two attributes:

The first attribute: His saying: ﴿whose enclosure will surround them﴾. The suradiq (enclosure) is the chamber that surrounds the tent (fustat); so He affirmed for the Fire something similar to that which surrounds them from all directions. The meaning is that there is no escape for them from it, and no opening through which they may look out at what lies beyond the Fire; rather it encompasses them on all sides. Some have said: the intended meaning of this suradiq is the smoke that Allah described in His saying: ﴿Proceed to a shade of three branches﴾ (al-Mursalat: 30). They said: this encompassing of them occurs before they enter the Fire, so this smoke overspreads them and surrounds them like the enclosure around the tent.

The second attribute of this Fire is His saying: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like molten brass﴾. It was said in a hadith traced to the Prophet: it is the dregs of oil. And it is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he entered the treasury of wealth, took out a residue that was in it, and kindled a fire upon it until it glittered, then said: this is the muhl. Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said: everything you melt of gold, copper or silver is muhl. It was also said: it is pus and matter; and it was said: it is a kind of tar. Then it is possible that this "relief" is because when they ask for water to drink, they are given this muhl. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Burning in a scorching fire﴾, ﴿Given to drink from a boiling spring﴾ (al-Ghashiyah: 4-5). And it is possible that they seek relief from the heat of Hell, so they ask for water to pour over themselves for cooling, and they are given this water. He, exalted is He, said, relating about them: ﴿Pour upon us some of the water﴾ (al-A'raf: 50). And in another verse He said: ﴿Their garments of tar, and the Fire covers their faces﴾ (Ibrahim: 50). So when they seek relief from the heat of Hell, tar is poured upon them, which covers all their bodies like a shirt. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they will be relieved with water like molten brass﴾ is stated in the manner of mockery, like the saying of the poet:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Wretched is the drink﴾, meaning: the water which is like molten brass is a wretched drink, because the purpose of drinking is to quench heat, and this reaches the burning of bodies to a tremendous degree. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and evil is the resting place﴾. Some said: the Fire is an evil dwelling and gathering place for companionship, because the people of the Fire gather as companions just as the people of Paradise do. He, exalted is He, said describing the people of Paradise: ﴿And excellent are those as companions﴾ (al-Nisa': 69). As for the companions of the Fire, they are the disbelievers and the devils, and the meaning is: evil are these as companions, and evil is the place of companionship, the Fire, just as excellent are the companions, the people of Paradise, and excellent is the place of companionship, Paradise. Others said: murtafaqan means reclining; and the elbow (mirfaq) was named so because one leans upon it, and reclining is only for rest, and the murtafaq is the place of rest. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 30–31:

God, exalted is He, pronounced the verses: "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not waste the reward of one who does good work. Those, for them are Gardens of Eden (jannat 'adn), beneath them rivers flow. They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold, and they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade, reclining therein on couches. Excellent is the reward, and good is the resting place."

Know that when God, exalted is He, mentioned the threat against the falsifiers, He followed it with the promise to the true believers. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: His saying, "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds," indicates that righteous deeds are distinct from faith, because the conjunction (al-'atf) requires distinction.

The second issue: His saying, "Indeed We do not waste the reward of one who does good work," its apparent meaning requires that the believer, by the goodness of his deed, merits a reward from God. According to our companions (the Ash'ari scholars), this merit arises by virtue of the promise. According to the Mu'tazila, it arises from the act itself. This is false, because God's blessings are many, and they necessitate gratitude and worship. Therefore, gratitude and worship do not become grounds that necessitate another reward, because the performance of an obligation does not necessitate anything else.

The third issue: Similar to His saying, "Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds," etc., is the saying of the poet:

Indeed the caliph, indeed God has clothed him
with the garment of kingship, by which the endings (of affairs) are hoped for.

He repeated "indeed" (inna) for emphasis regarding the deeds and the recompense for them.

The fourth issue: "Those" (ulā'ika) is the predicate of "indeed" (inna). The clause "indeed We do not waste" is a parenthetical interjection. You may make "indeed We do not waste" and "those" two predicates together. You may also make "those" an independent statement explaining the undefined reward. Know that when God, exalted is He, established the undefined reward, He followed it with detail in several aspects:

The first of these is the description of their place, which is His saying, "Those, for them are Gardens of Eden, beneath them rivers flow." The word 'adn in the language denotes residence (iqama). So it is possible that the meaning is: "Those, for them are gardens of residence," as one says, "This is a house of residence." It is also possible that 'adn is the name of a specific place within Paradise, namely its middle and the most noble of its places, and we have examined this extensively earlier. His saying "gardens" (jannat) is a plural form. It is possible that what is meant is what God, exalted is He, said: "And for one who fears the standing before his Lord are two gardens" (al-Rahman 46). It is also possible that what is meant is that the share of each of the accountable persons is a separate garden. It has been mentioned that among the attributes of those gardens is that rivers flow beneath them, because the best dwellings in this world are gardens through which rivers flow.

The second: The clothing of the people of this world is either clothing of adornment or clothing of covering. As for the clothing of adornment, God, exalted is He, described it: "They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold." The meaning is that God, exalted is He, adorns them with that, or the angels adorn them. Some have said that each of them has three bracelets: a bracelet of gold, due to this verse; a bracelet of silver, due to His saying, "And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver" (al-Insan 21); and a bracelet of pearls, due to His saying, "And pearls, and their clothing therein is silk" (al-Hajj 23). As for the clothing of covering, it is His saying: "And they will wear green garments of fine silk and brocade." What is meant by the sundus of the Hereafter and the istabraq of the Hereafter: the first is thin brocade, which is khazz, and the second is thick brocade. It has been said that its origin is Persian, arabized as istabrah, meaning thick.

If it is asked: What is the reason that God, exalted is He, said concerning the adornments, "They will be adorned" (yuhallawna) in the passive form, while concerning the sundus and istabraq He said, "and they will wear" (wa yalbasuna), attributing the wearing to them? We say: It is possible that the wearing is an indication of what they merited by their deeds, and that the adornment is an indication of what God graciously bestowed upon them initially from the surplus of His generosity.

The third: The manner of their sitting. He said in describing it: "reclining therein on couches" (ala al-ara'ik). They said: al-ara'ik is the plural of arika, which is a couch within a canopy (hajla). As for a couch alone, it is not called arika. When God, exalted is He, described these categories, He said: "Excellent is the reward, and good is the resting place (murtafaqan)." The intent is that this should be in contrast to what was mentioned earlier in His saying: "And evil is the resting place (murtafaqan)."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men: for one of them We made two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them with date palms, and between them We placed fields of crops.﴾ ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fall short of it in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth between them.﴾ ﴿And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while he was conversing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾ ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself, and said, "I do not think that this will ever perish.﴾ ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a return."﴾ ﴿His companion said to him while he was conversing with him, "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you as a man?"﴾ ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I associate none with my Lord.﴾ ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills [will be]; there is no power except in Allah"? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children,﴾ ﴿it may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden and send upon it a calamity from the heaven, so it becomes a barren slippery ground,﴾ ﴿or its water becomes sunken so you will not be able to seek it."﴾ ﴿And his fruit was encompassed [by ruin], and he began to turn his palms over [in regret] for what he had spent upon it while it was fallen upon its trellises, and he said, "I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ ﴿And he had no company to support him other than Allah, nor was he [able to] defend himself.﴾ ﴿There, protection belongs to Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾

The purpose of this is that the disbelievers boasted of their wealth and their supporters against the poor among the Muslims. So Allah, exalted is He, explained that this is not something that necessitates boasting, since the poor man may become rich and the rich man poor. As for that by which boasting is due, it is obedience to Allah and His worship, and this is available to the poor among the believers. He explained this by presenting this parable mentioned in the verse, so He said: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men﴾, meaning: the situation of the disbelievers and the believers is likened to the situation of two men who were brothers among the Children of Israel, one of them a disbeliever named Barātūs and the other a believer named Yahūdhā. It was also said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A speaker among them said, "Indeed, I had a companion"﴾ (al-Saffat: 51). They inherited from their father eight thousand dinars, and each of them took half. The disbeliever bought land, and the believer said, "O Allah, I buy from You land in Paradise for a thousand," and gave it in charity. Then his brother built a house for a thousand, and the believer said, "O Allah, I buy from You a house in Paradise for a thousand," and gave it in charity. Then his brother married a woman for a thousand, and the believer said, "O Allah, I have made a thousand a dowry for the large-eyed maidens (ḥūr ʿīn)." Then his brother bought servants and estates for a thousand, and the believer said, "O Allah, I have bought from You the young boys for a thousand, so accept it as charity." Then he was afflicted with need, so he sat on his brother's path, and when his brother passed by him with his retinue, he approached him, but he drove him away and rebuked him for giving away his wealth in charity.

As for His saying: ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾, know that Allah, exalted is He, described that garden with attributes:

The first attribute: that it is a garden (jannah). A plantation was called a garden because what is hidden within it is concealed by the shade of the trees, and the root of the word is from concealment and covering.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿And We surrounded them with date palms﴾, meaning, We made the palms encircle the two gardens. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne (ḥāffīn min ḥawl al-ʿarsh)﴾ (al-Zumar: 75), meaning standing around the Throne encircling it. Al-ḥifāf is the side of a thing, and al-aḥiffah is its plural. So the meaning of the saying of one who says, "The people surrounded him (ḥaffa bihi al-qawm)," is that they became at its sides, which are its edges. The poet said:

He has glances at the two sides of his couch, when he turns them there is punishment and bounty.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "They surrounded him (ḥaffūhu) when they went around him, and I surrounded him with them (ḥaffaftuhu bihim), meaning I made them surrounding him." It is transitive to one object, so the preposition bāʾ makes it take a second object, like His saying: "I covered him (ghashītuhu)" and "I covered him with it (ghashītuhu bihi)." He said: "This attribute is one that the landowners (ad-dahāqīn) prefer in their vineyards, which is that they make them surrounded by fruit-bearing trees, and this is also beautiful in appearance."

The third attribute: ﴿And We placed between them fields of crops﴾, and what is intended by it are several matters:

One: that this land should combine staple foods and fruits.

Second: that this land should be wide in its extents and far-spread in its sides, and yet nothing intervenes in it that would cut off part of it from part.

Third: that such land brings a different benefit at every time, another fruit, so its benefits were continuous and uninterrupted.

The fourth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fall short of it in anything﴾. Kilā is a singular definite noun used to emphasize two masculine definite nouns, and kiltā is a singular noun used to emphasize two feminine definite nouns. When they are in construction with an apparent noun, both take the alif in all three cases, as in your saying: "The two brothers of yours (kilā akhawayka) came to me," "I saw both your brothers," and "I passed by both your brothers." Likewise: "Both your sisters (kiltā ukhtayka) came to me," "I saw both your sisters," and "I passed by both your sisters." When they are in construction with a pronoun, they take the alif in the nominative case, and in the genitive and accusative they take the yāʾ. Some say: with a pronoun they take the alif in all three cases as well. His saying: ﴿brought forth its produce (ātat ukulahā)﴾ is taken according to the wording, because kiltā's form is that of a singular, and if it were said "ātatā" according to the meaning, it would be permissible. His saying: ﴿and did not fall short of it in anything (lam tazlim minhu shay'an)﴾, meaning it did not diminish. Ẓulm means diminution; a man says, "He wronged me of my right (ẓalamanī ḥaqqī)," meaning he diminished me of it.

The fifth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾, meaning the river flowed within those two gardens. In the reading of Yaʿqūb it is "wa-fajara" with a light form, and in the reading of the rest it is "wa-fajjarnā" with a doubled form. The light form is the original, since it is one river, and the doubled form is for emphasis, since the river extends and thus becomes like rivers. And khilālahumā means between them and among them. From it is His saying: ﴿And they would have hurried between you (la-awḍaʿū khilālakum)﴾ (al-Tawbah: 47). From it is said: "I wedged between the people (khallaltu al-qawm)," meaning I entered among the people.

The sixth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he had fruit﴾. ʿĀṣim read with a fatḥa on the thāʾ and the mīm in both places, and it is the plural of thimār or thamarah. Abū ʿAmr read with a ḍamma on the thāʾ and a sukūn on the mīm in both words, and the rest read with a ḍamma on the thāʾ and the mīm in both words. The people of lexicography mentioned that with the ḍamma it means kinds of wealth such as gold, silver and other things, and with the fatḥa it means the fruit of trees. Quṭrub said: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ used to say: "al-thumur is wealth and children." He recited for al-Ḥārith ibn Kildah:

Indeed I have seen people who have multiplied (athmarū) wealth and children.

And al-Nābighah said:

Patience; all the people are a ransom for you, for whatever they have multiplied, whether of wealth or of children.

And His saying: ﴿And he had fruit﴾ means kinds of wealth, from "thamara māluhu" when his wealth increased. From Mujāhid: gold and silver, meaning that along with the two gardens there were things of currency.

When Allah mentioned these attributes, He said after it: ﴿so he said to his companion while he was conversing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾ The meaning is that the Muslim was conversing with him by admonition and calling to faith in Allah and in the Resurrection. Al-muḥāwarah is the back-and-forth of speech, from their saying "ḥāra" when he returned, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, he thought that he would never return.﴾ ﴿Yes...﴾ (al-Inshiqaq: 14–15). So He, exalted is He, mentioned that at this conversation the disbeliever said: ﴿I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men.﴾ Al-nafar is a man's clan and companions who defend him and rally with him. The sum of the matter is that the disbeliever exalted himself over the believer by his status and wealth. Then he wanted to show that Muslim his abundance of wealth, so Allah, exalted is He, informed about this condition, and said: ﴿And he entered his garden﴾, and showed it to him in a state that brings delight and joy, and informed him of the kinds of wealth he possessed. If it is asked: why did He make the garden singular after the dual? We say: the meaning is that he had no garden and no share in the garden promised to the pious believers; this which he possessed in the world is his garden only, and he did not intend the two gardens nor either one of them. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾, and this is a parenthetical interjection that occurred in the midst of the speech, and the purpose is to alert that when he took pride in those blessings and used them as a means to disbelief and denial of his power over resurrection, he was placing those blessings in other than their proper place. Then Allah, exalted is He, related of the disbeliever that he said: ﴿I do not think that this will ever perish.﴾ ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, so he combined these two. The first he asserted with certainty that those things would not perish or come to an end ever, although they are changing and transforming. If it is said: suppose he doubted the Resurrection, how did he say: ﴿I do not think that this will ever perish﴾, when intuition indicates that the conditions of this world in their entirety are passing, vain, and not lasting? We say: the meaning is that they would not perish for the duration of his life and existence. Then he said: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a return.﴾ Meaning a place of return and outcome, and its accusative is as a specification (tamyīz). Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed for me with Him is the best [reward]﴾ (Fussilat: 50), and His saying: ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾ (Maryam: 77). The cause of this doubt is that when Allah gave him wealth in the world, he thought that He gave him that only because he deserved it, and that deserving remains after death, so it was necessary that the gift be obtained. The first premise is false, for opening the door of the world to a person is, in most cases, for gradual deception and respite. Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read: ﴿khayran minhumā﴾, and the intended reference is back to the two gardens; the rest read: ﴿minhā﴾, and the intended reference is back to the garden which he entered.

* * *

Then He mentioned the reply of the believer, so He, majestic is His majesty, said: ﴿His companion said to him while he was conversing with him, "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you as a man?"﴾ And in this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The first man said: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, and this second one declared him a disbeliever when he said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust﴾. This indicates that one who doubts the occurrence of resurrection is a disbeliever.

The second discussion: This argument admits of two aspects:

The first: it returns to the method mentioned in the Qur'an, which is that when He is able to originate creation, it is necessary that He be able to repeat it. So His saying: ﴿created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you as a man﴾ is an allusion to the creation of man at the beginning.

The second aspect: that since He created you thus, He did not create you in vain, but created you for worship. And if He created you for this purpose, it is necessary that the obedient obtain reward and the sinner obtain punishment. Its exposition is what we mentioned in Surat Yasin. This aspect is indicated by His saying: ﴿then proportioned you as a man﴾, meaning He fashioned you in a form that understands and is fit for responsibility. Is it then permissible by reason, with this condition, that He neglect your affair?

Then the believer said: ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord﴾, and in this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The people of lexicography said: "lākinnā" originally is "lākin anā", so the hamza was dropped and its vowel was placed on the nūn of lākin, the two nūns came together, and the nūn of lākin was assimilated into the nūn following it. A similar example is the poet's:

You shun me, but I do not shun you (la-kinna iyyāka lā aqlī).

That is, "lākin anā lā aqlīki." In His saying: ﴿Huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾, the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the saying ﴿Allāhu rabbī﴾ is a nominal sentence occurring in the position of the predicate of "huwa." If it is asked: the "lākinnā" is a contrast (istidrāk) with respect to what? We say: with respect to His saying ﴿Do you disbelieve﴾; as if he said to his brother: "You disbelieve in Allah, but I am a believer, a monotheist," just as you say: "Zayd is absent, but ʿAmr is present."

The second discussion: Ibn ʿĀmir, Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī, and Nāfiʿ in one narration read: ﴿lākinnā huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾ with an alif in continuous recitation, and in the reading of the rest: ﴿lākinna huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾ without an alif, and the meaning is one. Then the believer said: ﴿and I associate none with my Lord, anyone.﴾ Al-Qaffāl mentioned several aspects regarding it:

[p. 109]

First: I see poverty and wealth only as coming from Him. So I praise Him when He gives, I am patient when He tests, I am not arrogant when He bestows favour upon me, and I do not regard the abundance of wealth and helpers as coming from myself. This is because the disbeliever, when he took pride in his abundance of wealth and status, was as though he had ascribed a partner to Allah in the giving of honour and wealth.

Second: Perhaps that disbeliever, while denying the Resurrection, was also a worshipper of an idol, and so this believer exposed the corruption of his claim by affirming partners [to Allah].

Third: Since this disbeliever attributed to Allah an inability to resurrect and gather [the dead], he made Him equal to creation in this inability. And whoever affirms equality has affirmed a partner. Then the believer said to the disbeliever: ﴿Why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "As Allah wills. There is no power except through Allah"?﴾ So he commanded him to say these two statements:

The first is his saying: ﴿As Allah wills.﴾ Concerning it there are two possibilities:

The first: that *mā* (ما) is conditional, and the apodosis (jazā') is omitted, the meaning being: "Whatever thing Allah wills, it comes to be."

The second: that *mā* is a relative pronoun in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, and the implied meaning is: "The matter is what Allah wills." Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) used this as evidence that whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. This indicates that He did not will belief from the disbeliever, and it is explicit in refuting the view of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that holds that human acts are created by humans and that Allah's will is limited accordingly).

Al-Ka'bi (a Mu'tazili scholar) answered this by saying that their saying "what He wills" should be interpreted as referring to what He undertakes to do Himself, not to what is the act of His servants. Likewise, they say: "No one can avert the command of Allah," meaning He did not will what He commanded the servants [to do]. Then he said: "It is not impossible that there occurs in His dominion what He does not will, just as there occurs in it what He has forbidden." Know that what al-Ka'bi mentioned is not an answer to the argument; rather, it is a commitment to contradicting the apparent meaning of the text. Analogizing will to command is invalid, because this text indicates that nothing exists except what Allah wills, whereas the texts contain nothing indicating that nothing enters existence except what He commands. Thus the difference is clear.

Al-Qaffal (a commentator) answered it by saying: "Why, when you entered your orchard, did you not say: 'As Allah wills,' like a person's saying concerning the things present in this orchard: 'As Allah wills.'" Similar to this is His saying: ﴿They will say: "[They were] three, the fourth of them their dog."﴾ [18:22] and they were three. And His saying: ﴿And say: "Ḥiṭṭah."﴾ [7:161], meaning: say "this is ḥiṭṭah." If that is so, then what is meant by this thing present in the orchard is a thing whose existence Allah willed. On this interpretation it does not follow that everything Allah wills occurs, because this ruling is not general to all things but is specific to the things witnessed in the orchard. This interpretation of al-Qaffal's is far better than what al-Jubba'i and al-Ka'bi mentioned. 

I say: even on his answer, the problem for the Mu'tazila is not resolved, because the cultivation of that orchard may have been achieved through usurpation and severe injustice. Thus it is also not valid, according to the Mu'tazila, to say: "This has occurred by the will of Allah." Unless we say that what is meant is that these fruits came about by the will of Allah, but this is a restriction of the apparent text without evidence.

The second statement which the believer commanded the disbeliever to say is his saying: ﴿There is no power except through Allah.﴾ That is: no one has power over any matter except by the help and empowerment of Allah.

The intended meaning is that the believer said to the disbeliever: "Why did you not say, upon entering your garden: 'The matter is what Allah wills, and what exists is what Allah has decreed,' acknowledging that it and all good in it are by the will and grace of Allah, for its affair is in His hand: if He wills, He leaves it; if He wills, He ruins it? And why did you not say: 'There is no power except through Allah,' affirming that whatever strength you were given for its cultivation and the management of its affairs is by the aid and support of Allah? No one has strength in his body or in what his hand possesses except through Allah."

Then, when the believer had taught the disbeliever faith, he answered him concerning his boasting of wealth and kinsmen, saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children.﴾ Whoever reads *aqalla* (أقل) in the accusative has made *anā* (أنا) a separating pronoun (fasl) and *aqalla* the second object. Whoever reads it in the nominative has made *anā* the subject (mubtada'), *aqallu* the predicate (khabar), and the whole clause the second object of *tarani* (ترني).

Know that the mention of children here indicates that what is meant by "kinsmen" (nafar) in His saying ﴿and more powerful in kinsmen﴾ [18:34] is helpers and children. It is as if he says to him: "If you see me as less in wealth, children, and helpers in this fleeting world, then ﴿perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾ either in this world or in the Hereafter, ﴿and send upon your garden a reckoning from the heaven﴾, that is, a punishment and destruction. *Ḥusbān* is a verbal noun like *ghufrān* and *buṭlān*, meaning "reckoning": that is, a measure which Allah has determined and computed, namely the decree of its destruction. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and commentator) said: "a punishment of reckoning, and that reckoning is the reckoning of what your hands have earned." It was also said: *ḥusbānan* means "missiles," the singular of which is *ḥusbānah*, namely thunderbolts. ﴿So that it becomes smooth earth (ṣa'īdan zalaqan)﴾, that is, your garden becomes a smooth ground with no vegetation in it. *Ṣa'īd* is the surface of the earth; *zalaqan* means it becomes such that a foot slips upon it. Then He said: ﴿Or its water sinks away (ghawran)﴾, that is, it sinks and descends into the earth. ﴿Then you will not be able to seek it.﴾ That is, it will become such that you cannot restore it to its place.

The lexicographers said concerning His saying ﴿its water (ghawran)﴾: that is, *ghā'iran* (sunken). It is an adjective in the form of a verbal noun, as one says: "So-and-so is a *zawr* and a *ṣawm*," applying to the singular, the plural, the masculine and the feminine. And one says: "*nisā'un nawḥ*" meaning *nawā'iḥ* (women mourners).

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that He fulfilled what this believer had decreed, and said: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (ahīṭa bi-thamarihi)﴾. This is an expression for its total destruction. Its origin is from an enemy's encirclement, since when one is encircled, he is owned and dominated. It was then used for every destruction. From it is His saying: ﴿unless you are encompassed [by them]﴾ [12:66], and similar to it the saying: "*atā 'alayhi*" meaning he destroyed him, from "the enemy came upon them" when he came to them overpowering them.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he began to turn his palms (yuqallibu kaffayhi)﴾. This is a metaphor for regret and grief, for whoever's grief is great claps one hand upon the other, or sometimes rubs one of them upon the other. He does this only out of remorse for what he spent on the garden in which his brother had admonished and rebuked him. ﴿And it was fallen upon its trellises (khāwiyatun 'alā 'urūshihā)﴾, that is, collapsed upon its trellises. It is possible that the meaning of "trellises" is the trellises of the vines: these trellises fell, then the walls fell upon them. It is also possible that "trellises" means the roofs, which fell upon the walls. The summary of the matter: this expression is a metaphor for its nullification and ruin.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And he said: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ The meaning is that when the believer said: ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾, this disbeliever recalled his words and said: ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord.﴾

If it is said: this statement suggests that his garden was destroyed only because of the ill omen of his polytheism, and this is not the case, because most kinds of affliction befall believers. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And were it not that the people would be one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways upon which they climb﴾ [43:33]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Affliction is reserved for the prophets, then the saints, then the most excellent, and then the next most excellent." Furthermore, when he said: ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord,﴾ he regretted polytheism and desired monotheism, so it was necessary that he become a believer. Why then did He say after it: ﴿And he had no group to help him against Allah, nor was he [able to be] victorious﴾?

The answer to the first question is that his grief was great because he had spent his life in pursuit of this world and had turned away throughout his life from seeking religion. When this world was utterly lost, deprivation of both this world and religion remained upon him. For this reason his grief was great.

The answer to the second question is that he regretted polytheism only because he believed that if he had been a monotheist and not a polytheist, his garden would have remained for him. Thus he desired monotheism and turned away from polytheism only for the sake of seeking [worldly gain]<br>

[p. 110]

the world, and for this reason his monotheism was not accepted by Allah.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And he had no group to help him against Allah.﴾ In this verse there are two discussions.

The first discussion: Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿and there was not (lam yakun) for him a group﴾ with the *yā'* (masculine), because *fi'ah* (group) is a collective noun, and when it precedes the pronoun it is permissible to use the masculine; and also because it respects the sense. The others read it with the *tā'* (feminine), dotted with two dots above, because the pronoun refers to the word *fi'ah*.

The second discussion: What is meant by His saying ﴿who would help him against Allah﴾ is that no group came into existence for him that could help him against Allah. That is, Allah alone, exalted is He, is able to help him, and no one other than Him can help him. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾

First matter: The reciters differed in three places in this verse.

The first: concerning the word *walāyah* (guardianship). In the reading of Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī it is with a *kasrah* on the *wāw*, and in the reading of the rest it is with a *fatḥah*. It is reported from Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā' that he said: "Kasrah on the *wāw* is a solecism (laḥn)." The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: *al-walāyah* with a *fatḥah* means support and alliance, and with a *kasrah* means authority and dominion.

The second: Abū 'Amr and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿al-ḥaqq﴾ with a *ḍammah* (nominative), the sense being "There, the guardianship is the Truth, belonging to Allah." The rest read it with a *kasrah* (genitive) as an adjective of Allah.

The third: Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr, Nāfi', al-Kisā'ī and Ibn 'Āmir read *'uquban* with a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. 'Āṣim and Ḥamzah read *'uqbā* with the *qāf* sukun.

Second matter: ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah﴾ has several interpretations:

The first: When He mentioned the story of the two men that He mentioned, we knew that victory and the praiseworthy outcome belonged to the believer over the disbeliever. We understood that this is how it is with regard to every believer and every disbeliever. So He said: ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah, the Truth,﴾ that is, in such a time and such a situation, guardianship belongs to Allah: He gives support to His friends, so He makes them prevail over their enemies, and He entrusts the affair of the disbelievers to them. Thus His saying *hunālika* ("there") is an indication of the place and the time in which Allah wills to manifest the honour of His friends and the humiliation of His enemies in them.

The second interpretation: the meaning is that in such a severe state, every needy and distressed person turns to Allah and seeks refuge in Him. That is, His saying ﴿And he said: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ is a word to which that disbeliever was compelled, and he said it out of distress at what his polytheism had brought upon him. Had it not been for that, he would not have said it.

The third interpretation: the meaning: there, guardianship belongs to Allah, by which He gives victory to His believing friends over the disbelievers, avenges them, and heals their hearts from their enemies. That is, He, exalted is He, gave victory to the believing brother by what He did to the disbeliever, and confirmed his words in His saying ﴿It may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden and send upon it a reckoning from the sky﴾. This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome,﴾ that is, for His friends.

The fourth interpretation: His saying *hunālika* refers to the Hereafter; that is, in that Hereafter guardianship belongs to Allah, like His saying: ﴿"To whom belongs the dominion today? To Allah"﴾ [40:16]. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He is best in reward﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, for whoever believes in Him and turns to Him; ﴿and best in outcome﴾, that is, He is best in consequence for whoever hopes in Him and acts for His sake. We have already mentioned that it was read as *'uqbā* with a *ḍammah* and sukun on the *qāf*, and *'uqbā* on the pattern *fu'lā*; all of them mean "outcome."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men: for one of them We made two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them with date palms, and between them We placed fields of crops.﴾ ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fall short of it in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth between them.﴾ ﴿And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while he was conversing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾ ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself, and said, "I do not think that this will ever perish.﴾ ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a return."﴾ ﴿His companion said to him while he was conversing with him, "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you as a man?"﴾ ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I associate none with my Lord.﴾ ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills [will be]; there is no power except in Allah"? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children,﴾ ﴿it may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden and send upon it a calamity from the heaven, so it becomes a barren slippery ground,﴾ ﴿or its water becomes sunken so you will not be able to seek it."﴾ ﴿And his fruit was encompassed [by ruin], and he began to turn his palms over [in regret] for what he had spent upon it while it was fallen upon its trellises, and he said, "I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ ﴿And he had no company to support him other than Allah, nor was he [able to] defend himself.﴾ ﴿There, protection belongs to Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾

The purpose of this is that the disbelievers boasted of their wealth and their supporters against the poor among the Muslims. So Allah, exalted is He, explained that this is not something that necessitates boasting, since the poor man may become rich and the rich man poor. As for that by which boasting is due, it is obedience to Allah and His worship, and this is available to the poor among the believers. He explained this by presenting this parable mentioned in the verse, so He said: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men﴾, meaning: the situation of the disbelievers and the believers is likened to the situation of two men who were brothers among the Children of Israel, one of them a disbeliever named Barātūs and the other a believer named Yahūdhā. It was also said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A speaker among them said, "Indeed, I had a companion"﴾ (al-Saffat: 51). They inherited from their father eight thousand dinars, and each of them took half. The disbeliever bought land, and the believer said, "O Allah, I buy from You land in Paradise for a thousand," and gave it in charity. Then his brother built a house for a thousand, and the believer said, "O Allah, I buy from You a house in Paradise for a thousand," and gave it in charity. Then his brother married a woman for a thousand, and the believer said, "O Allah, I have made a thousand a dowry for the large-eyed maidens (ḥūr ʿīn)." Then his brother bought servants and estates for a thousand, and the believer said, "O Allah, I have bought from You the young boys for a thousand, so accept it as charity." Then he was afflicted with need, so he sat on his brother's path, and when his brother passed by him with his retinue, he approached him, but he drove him away and rebuked him for giving away his wealth in charity.

As for His saying: ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾, know that Allah, exalted is He, described that garden with attributes:

The first attribute: that it is a garden (jannah). A plantation was called a garden because what is hidden within it is concealed by the shade of the trees, and the root of the word is from concealment and covering.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿And We surrounded them with date palms﴾, meaning, We made the palms encircle the two gardens. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne (ḥāffīn min ḥawl al-ʿarsh)﴾ (al-Zumar: 75), meaning standing around the Throne encircling it. Al-ḥifāf is the side of a thing, and al-aḥiffah is its plural. So the meaning of the saying of one who says, "The people surrounded him (ḥaffa bihi al-qawm)," is that they became at its sides, which are its edges. The poet said:

He has glances at the two sides of his couch, when he turns them there is punishment and bounty.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "They surrounded him (ḥaffūhu) when they went around him, and I surrounded him with them (ḥaffaftuhu bihim), meaning I made them surrounding him." It is transitive to one object, so the preposition bāʾ makes it take a second object, like His saying: "I covered him (ghashītuhu)" and "I covered him with it (ghashītuhu bihi)." He said: "This attribute is one that the landowners (ad-dahāqīn) prefer in their vineyards, which is that they make them surrounded by fruit-bearing trees, and this is also beautiful in appearance."

The third attribute: ﴿And We placed between them fields of crops﴾, and what is intended by it are several matters:

One: that this land should combine staple foods and fruits.

Second: that this land should be wide in its extents and far-spread in its sides, and yet nothing intervenes in it that would cut off part of it from part.

Third: that such land brings a different benefit at every time, another fruit, so its benefits were continuous and uninterrupted.

The fourth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fall short of it in anything﴾. Kilā is a singular definite noun used to emphasize two masculine definite nouns, and kiltā is a singular noun used to emphasize two feminine definite nouns. When they are in construction with an apparent noun, both take the alif in all three cases, as in your saying: "The two brothers of yours (kilā akhawayka) came to me," "I saw both your brothers," and "I passed by both your brothers." Likewise: "Both your sisters (kiltā ukhtayka) came to me," "I saw both your sisters," and "I passed by both your sisters." When they are in construction with a pronoun, they take the alif in the nominative case, and in the genitive and accusative they take the yāʾ. Some say: with a pronoun they take the alif in all three cases as well. His saying: ﴿brought forth its produce (ātat ukulahā)﴾ is taken according to the wording, because kiltā's form is that of a singular, and if it were said "ātatā" according to the meaning, it would be permissible. His saying: ﴿and did not fall short of it in anything (lam tazlim minhu shay'an)﴾, meaning it did not diminish. Ẓulm means diminution; a man says, "He wronged me of my right (ẓalamanī ḥaqqī)," meaning he diminished me of it.

The fifth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾, meaning the river flowed within those two gardens. In the reading of Yaʿqūb it is "wa-fajara" with a light form, and in the reading of the rest it is "wa-fajjarnā" with a doubled form. The light form is the original, since it is one river, and the doubled form is for emphasis, since the river extends and thus becomes like rivers. And khilālahumā means between them and among them. From it is His saying: ﴿And they would have hurried between you (la-awḍaʿū khilālakum)﴾ (al-Tawbah: 47). From it is said: "I wedged between the people (khallaltu al-qawm)," meaning I entered among the people.

The sixth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he had fruit﴾. ʿĀṣim read with a fatḥa on the thāʾ and the mīm in both places, and it is the plural of thimār or thamarah. Abū ʿAmr read with a ḍamma on the thāʾ and a sukūn on the mīm in both words, and the rest read with a ḍamma on the thāʾ and the mīm in both words. The people of lexicography mentioned that with the ḍamma it means kinds of wealth such as gold, silver and other things, and with the fatḥa it means the fruit of trees. Quṭrub said: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ used to say: "al-thumur is wealth and children." He recited for al-Ḥārith ibn Kildah:

Indeed I have seen people who have multiplied (athmarū) wealth and children.

And al-Nābighah said:

Patience; all the people are a ransom for you, for whatever they have multiplied, whether of wealth or of children.

And His saying: ﴿And he had fruit﴾ means kinds of wealth, from "thamara māluhu" when his wealth increased. From Mujāhid: gold and silver, meaning that along with the two gardens there were things of currency.

When Allah mentioned these attributes, He said after it: ﴿so he said to his companion while he was conversing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾ The meaning is that the Muslim was conversing with him by admonition and calling to faith in Allah and in the Resurrection. Al-muḥāwarah is the back-and-forth of speech, from their saying "ḥāra" when he returned, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, he thought that he would never return.﴾ ﴿Yes...﴾ (al-Inshiqaq: 14–15). So He, exalted is He, mentioned that at this conversation the disbeliever said: ﴿I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men.﴾ Al-nafar is a man's clan and companions who defend him and rally with him. The sum of the matter is that the disbeliever exalted himself over the believer by his status and wealth. Then he wanted to show that Muslim his abundance of wealth, so Allah, exalted is He, informed about this condition, and said: ﴿And he entered his garden﴾, and showed it to him in a state that brings delight and joy, and informed him of the kinds of wealth he possessed. If it is asked: why did He make the garden singular after the dual? We say: the meaning is that he had no garden and no share in the garden promised to the pious believers; this which he possessed in the world is his garden only, and he did not intend the two gardens nor either one of them. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿while he was wronging himself﴾, and this is a parenthetical interjection that occurred in the midst of the speech, and the purpose is to alert that when he took pride in those blessings and used them as a means to disbelief and denial of his power over resurrection, he was placing those blessings in other than their proper place. Then Allah, exalted is He, related of the disbeliever that he said: ﴿I do not think that this will ever perish.﴾ ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, so he combined these two. The first he asserted with certainty that those things would not perish or come to an end ever, although they are changing and transforming. If it is said: suppose he doubted the Resurrection, how did he say: ﴿I do not think that this will ever perish﴾, when intuition indicates that the conditions of this world in their entirety are passing, vain, and not lasting? We say: the meaning is that they would not perish for the duration of his life and existence. Then he said: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a return.﴾ Meaning a place of return and outcome, and its accusative is as a specification (tamyīz). Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, indeed for me with Him is the best [reward]﴾ (Fussilat: 50), and His saying: ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾ (Maryam: 77). The cause of this doubt is that when Allah gave him wealth in the world, he thought that He gave him that only because he deserved it, and that deserving remains after death, so it was necessary that the gift be obtained. The first premise is false, for opening the door of the world to a person is, in most cases, for gradual deception and respite. Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read: ﴿khayran minhumā﴾, and the intended reference is back to the two gardens; the rest read: ﴿minhā﴾, and the intended reference is back to the garden which he entered.

* * *

Then He mentioned the reply of the believer, so He, majestic is His majesty, said: ﴿His companion said to him while he was conversing with him, "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you as a man?"﴾ And in this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The first man said: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established﴾, and this second one declared him a disbeliever when he said: ﴿Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust﴾. This indicates that one who doubts the occurrence of resurrection is a disbeliever.

The second discussion: This argument admits of two aspects:

The first: it returns to the method mentioned in the Qur'an, which is that when He is able to originate creation, it is necessary that He be able to repeat it. So His saying: ﴿created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you as a man﴾ is an allusion to the creation of man at the beginning.

The second aspect: that since He created you thus, He did not create you in vain, but created you for worship. And if He created you for this purpose, it is necessary that the obedient obtain reward and the sinner obtain punishment. Its exposition is what we mentioned in Surat Yasin. This aspect is indicated by His saying: ﴿then proportioned you as a man﴾, meaning He fashioned you in a form that understands and is fit for responsibility. Is it then permissible by reason, with this condition, that He neglect your affair?

Then the believer said: ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord﴾, and in this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The people of lexicography said: "lākinnā" originally is "lākin anā", so the hamza was dropped and its vowel was placed on the nūn of lākin, the two nūns came together, and the nūn of lākin was assimilated into the nūn following it. A similar example is the poet's:

You shun me, but I do not shun you (la-kinna iyyāka lā aqlī).

That is, "lākin anā lā aqlīki." In His saying: ﴿Huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾, the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the saying ﴿Allāhu rabbī﴾ is a nominal sentence occurring in the position of the predicate of "huwa." If it is asked: the "lākinnā" is a contrast (istidrāk) with respect to what? We say: with respect to His saying ﴿Do you disbelieve﴾; as if he said to his brother: "You disbelieve in Allah, but I am a believer, a monotheist," just as you say: "Zayd is absent, but ʿAmr is present."

The second discussion: Ibn ʿĀmir, Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī, and Nāfiʿ in one narration read: ﴿lākinnā huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾ with an alif in continuous recitation, and in the reading of the rest: ﴿lākinna huwa Allāhu rabbī﴾ without an alif, and the meaning is one. Then the believer said: ﴿and I associate none with my Lord, anyone.﴾ Al-Qaffāl mentioned several aspects regarding it:

[p. 109]

First: I see poverty and wealth only as coming from Him. So I praise Him when He gives, I am patient when He tests, I am not arrogant when He bestows favour upon me, and I do not regard the abundance of wealth and helpers as coming from myself. This is because the disbeliever, when he took pride in his abundance of wealth and status, was as though he had ascribed a partner to Allah in the giving of honour and wealth.

Second: Perhaps that disbeliever, while denying the Resurrection, was also a worshipper of an idol, and so this believer exposed the corruption of his claim by affirming partners [to Allah].

Third: Since this disbeliever attributed to Allah an inability to resurrect and gather [the dead], he made Him equal to creation in this inability. And whoever affirms equality has affirmed a partner. Then the believer said to the disbeliever: ﴿Why, when you entered your garden, did you not say: "As Allah wills. There is no power except through Allah"?﴾ So he commanded him to say these two statements:

The first is his saying: ﴿As Allah wills.﴾ Concerning it there are two possibilities:

The first: that *mā* (ما) is conditional, and the apodosis (jazā') is omitted, the meaning being: "Whatever thing Allah wills, it comes to be."

The second: that *mā* is a relative pronoun in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, and the implied meaning is: "The matter is what Allah wills." Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) used this as evidence that whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur. This indicates that He did not will belief from the disbeliever, and it is explicit in refuting the view of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that holds that human acts are created by humans and that Allah's will is limited accordingly).

Al-Ka'bi (a Mu'tazili scholar) answered this by saying that their saying "what He wills" should be interpreted as referring to what He undertakes to do Himself, not to what is the act of His servants. Likewise, they say: "No one can avert the command of Allah," meaning He did not will what He commanded the servants [to do]. Then he said: "It is not impossible that there occurs in His dominion what He does not will, just as there occurs in it what He has forbidden." Know that what al-Ka'bi mentioned is not an answer to the argument; rather, it is a commitment to contradicting the apparent meaning of the text. Analogizing will to command is invalid, because this text indicates that nothing exists except what Allah wills, whereas the texts contain nothing indicating that nothing enters existence except what He commands. Thus the difference is clear.

Al-Qaffal (a commentator) answered it by saying: "Why, when you entered your orchard, did you not say: 'As Allah wills,' like a person's saying concerning the things present in this orchard: 'As Allah wills.'" Similar to this is His saying: ﴿They will say: "[They were] three, the fourth of them their dog."﴾ [18:22] and they were three. And His saying: ﴿And say: "Ḥiṭṭah."﴾ [7:161], meaning: say "this is ḥiṭṭah." If that is so, then what is meant by this thing present in the orchard is a thing whose existence Allah willed. On this interpretation it does not follow that everything Allah wills occurs, because this ruling is not general to all things but is specific to the things witnessed in the orchard. This interpretation of al-Qaffal's is far better than what al-Jubba'i and al-Ka'bi mentioned. 

I say: even on his answer, the problem for the Mu'tazila is not resolved, because the cultivation of that orchard may have been achieved through usurpation and severe injustice. Thus it is also not valid, according to the Mu'tazila, to say: "This has occurred by the will of Allah." Unless we say that what is meant is that these fruits came about by the will of Allah, but this is a restriction of the apparent text without evidence.

The second statement which the believer commanded the disbeliever to say is his saying: ﴿There is no power except through Allah.﴾ That is: no one has power over any matter except by the help and empowerment of Allah.

The intended meaning is that the believer said to the disbeliever: "Why did you not say, upon entering your garden: 'The matter is what Allah wills, and what exists is what Allah has decreed,' acknowledging that it and all good in it are by the will and grace of Allah, for its affair is in His hand: if He wills, He leaves it; if He wills, He ruins it? And why did you not say: 'There is no power except through Allah,' affirming that whatever strength you were given for its cultivation and the management of its affairs is by the aid and support of Allah? No one has strength in his body or in what his hand possesses except through Allah."

Then, when the believer had taught the disbeliever faith, he answered him concerning his boasting of wealth and kinsmen, saying: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children.﴾ Whoever reads *aqalla* (أقل) in the accusative has made *anā* (أنا) a separating pronoun (fasl) and *aqalla* the second object. Whoever reads it in the nominative has made *anā* the subject (mubtada'), *aqallu* the predicate (khabar), and the whole clause the second object of *tarani* (ترني).

Know that the mention of children here indicates that what is meant by "kinsmen" (nafar) in His saying ﴿and more powerful in kinsmen﴾ [18:34] is helpers and children. It is as if he says to him: "If you see me as less in wealth, children, and helpers in this fleeting world, then ﴿perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾ either in this world or in the Hereafter, ﴿and send upon your garden a reckoning from the heaven﴾, that is, a punishment and destruction. *Ḥusbān* is a verbal noun like *ghufrān* and *buṭlān*, meaning "reckoning": that is, a measure which Allah has determined and computed, namely the decree of its destruction. Al-Zajjaj (a grammarian and commentator) said: "a punishment of reckoning, and that reckoning is the reckoning of what your hands have earned." It was also said: *ḥusbānan* means "missiles," the singular of which is *ḥusbānah*, namely thunderbolts. ﴿So that it becomes smooth earth (ṣa'īdan zalaqan)﴾, that is, your garden becomes a smooth ground with no vegetation in it. *Ṣa'īd* is the surface of the earth; *zalaqan* means it becomes such that a foot slips upon it. Then He said: ﴿Or its water sinks away (ghawran)﴾, that is, it sinks and descends into the earth. ﴿Then you will not be able to seek it.﴾ That is, it will become such that you cannot restore it to its place.

The lexicographers said concerning His saying ﴿its water (ghawran)﴾: that is, *ghā'iran* (sunken). It is an adjective in the form of a verbal noun, as one says: "So-and-so is a *zawr* and a *ṣawm*," applying to the singular, the plural, the masculine and the feminine. And one says: "*nisā'un nawḥ*" meaning *nawā'iḥ* (women mourners).

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that He fulfilled what this believer had decreed, and said: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (ahīṭa bi-thamarihi)﴾. This is an expression for its total destruction. Its origin is from an enemy's encirclement, since when one is encircled, he is owned and dominated. It was then used for every destruction. From it is His saying: ﴿unless you are encompassed [by them]﴾ [12:66], and similar to it the saying: "*atā 'alayhi*" meaning he destroyed him, from "the enemy came upon them" when he came to them overpowering them.

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he began to turn his palms (yuqallibu kaffayhi)﴾. This is a metaphor for regret and grief, for whoever's grief is great claps one hand upon the other, or sometimes rubs one of them upon the other. He does this only out of remorse for what he spent on the garden in which his brother had admonished and rebuked him. ﴿And it was fallen upon its trellises (khāwiyatun 'alā 'urūshihā)﴾, that is, collapsed upon its trellises. It is possible that the meaning of "trellises" is the trellises of the vines: these trellises fell, then the walls fell upon them. It is also possible that "trellises" means the roofs, which fell upon the walls. The summary of the matter: this expression is a metaphor for its nullification and ruin.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And he said: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ The meaning is that when the believer said: ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾, this disbeliever recalled his words and said: ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord.﴾

If it is said: this statement suggests that his garden was destroyed only because of the ill omen of his polytheism, and this is not the case, because most kinds of affliction befall believers. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And were it not that the people would be one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways upon which they climb﴾ [43:33]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Affliction is reserved for the prophets, then the saints, then the most excellent, and then the next most excellent." Furthermore, when he said: ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord,﴾ he regretted polytheism and desired monotheism, so it was necessary that he become a believer. Why then did He say after it: ﴿And he had no group to help him against Allah, nor was he [able to be] victorious﴾?

The answer to the first question is that his grief was great because he had spent his life in pursuit of this world and had turned away throughout his life from seeking religion. When this world was utterly lost, deprivation of both this world and religion remained upon him. For this reason his grief was great.

The answer to the second question is that he regretted polytheism only because he believed that if he had been a monotheist and not a polytheist, his garden would have remained for him. Thus he desired monotheism and turned away from polytheism only for the sake of seeking [worldly gain]<br>

[p. 110]

the world, and for this reason his monotheism was not accepted by Allah.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And he had no group to help him against Allah.﴾ In this verse there are two discussions.

The first discussion: Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿and there was not (lam yakun) for him a group﴾ with the *yā'* (masculine), because *fi'ah* (group) is a collective noun, and when it precedes the pronoun it is permissible to use the masculine; and also because it respects the sense. The others read it with the *tā'* (feminine), dotted with two dots above, because the pronoun refers to the word *fi'ah*.

The second discussion: What is meant by His saying ﴿who would help him against Allah﴾ is that no group came into existence for him that could help him against Allah. That is, Allah alone, exalted is He, is able to help him, and no one other than Him can help him. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾

First matter: The reciters differed in three places in this verse.

The first: concerning the word *walāyah* (guardianship). In the reading of Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī it is with a *kasrah* on the *wāw*, and in the reading of the rest it is with a *fatḥah*. It is reported from Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā' that he said: "Kasrah on the *wāw* is a solecism (laḥn)." The author of *al-Kashshāf* said: *al-walāyah* with a *fatḥah* means support and alliance, and with a *kasrah* means authority and dominion.

The second: Abū 'Amr and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿al-ḥaqq﴾ with a *ḍammah* (nominative), the sense being "There, the guardianship is the Truth, belonging to Allah." The rest read it with a *kasrah* (genitive) as an adjective of Allah.

The third: Ibn Kathīr, Abū 'Amr, Nāfi', al-Kisā'ī and Ibn 'Āmir read *'uquban* with a *ḍammah* on the *qāf*. 'Āṣim and Ḥamzah read *'uqbā* with the *qāf* sukun.

Second matter: ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah﴾ has several interpretations:

The first: When He mentioned the story of the two men that He mentioned, we knew that victory and the praiseworthy outcome belonged to the believer over the disbeliever. We understood that this is how it is with regard to every believer and every disbeliever. So He said: ﴿There, guardianship belongs to Allah, the Truth,﴾ that is, in such a time and such a situation, guardianship belongs to Allah: He gives support to His friends, so He makes them prevail over their enemies, and He entrusts the affair of the disbelievers to them. Thus His saying *hunālika* ("there") is an indication of the place and the time in which Allah wills to manifest the honour of His friends and the humiliation of His enemies in them.

The second interpretation: the meaning is that in such a severe state, every needy and distressed person turns to Allah and seeks refuge in Him. That is, His saying ﴿And he said: "Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ is a word to which that disbeliever was compelled, and he said it out of distress at what his polytheism had brought upon him. Had it not been for that, he would not have said it.

The third interpretation: the meaning: there, guardianship belongs to Allah, by which He gives victory to His believing friends over the disbelievers, avenges them, and heals their hearts from their enemies. That is, He, exalted is He, gave victory to the believing brother by what He did to the disbeliever, and confirmed his words in His saying ﴿It may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden and send upon it a reckoning from the sky﴾. This is reinforced by His saying: ﴿He is best in reward and best in outcome,﴾ that is, for His friends.

The fourth interpretation: His saying *hunālika* refers to the Hereafter; that is, in that Hereafter guardianship belongs to Allah, like His saying: ﴿"To whom belongs the dominion today? To Allah"﴾ [40:16]. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He is best in reward﴾, that is, in the Hereafter, for whoever believes in Him and turns to Him; ﴿and best in outcome﴾, that is, He is best in consequence for whoever hopes in Him and acts for His sake. We have already mentioned that it was read as *'uqbā* with a *ḍammah* and sukun on the *qāf*, and *'uqbā* on the pattern *fu'lā*; all of them mean "outcome."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 32–44 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men: for one of them We made two gardens of grapevines, and We surrounded them with date palms, and between them We placed fields of crops.﴾ ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fall short of it in anything, and We caused a river to gush forth between them.﴾ ﴿And he had fruit, so he said to his companion while he was conversing with him, "I am greater than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾ ﴿And he entered his garden while he was wronging himself, and said, "I do not think that this will ever perish.﴾ ﴿And I do not think the Hour will be established. And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than it as a return."﴾ ﴿His companion said to him while he was conversing with him, "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then proportioned you as a man?"﴾ ﴿But as for me, He is Allah, my Lord, and I associate none with my Lord.﴾ ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What Allah wills [will be]; there is no power except in Allah"? If you see me as less than you in wealth and children,﴾ ﴿it may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden and send upon it a calamity from the heaven, so it becomes a barren slippery ground,﴾ ﴿or its water becomes sunken so you will not be able to seek it."﴾ ﴿And his fruit was encompassed [by ruin], and he began to turn his palms over [in regret] for what he had spent upon it while it was fallen upon its trellises, and he said, "I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord."﴾ ﴿And he had no company to support him other than Allah, nor was he [able to] defend himself.﴾ ﴿There, protection belongs to Allah, the Truth. He is best in reward and best in outcome.﴾

The purpose of this is that the disbelievers boasted of their wealth and their supporters against the poor among the Muslims. So Allah, exalted is He, explained that this is not something that necessitates boasting, since the poor man may become rich and the rich man poor. As for that by which boasting is due, it is obedience to Allah and His worship, and this is available to the poor among the believers. He explained this by presenting this parable mentioned in the verse, so He said: ﴿And present to them the parable of two men﴾, meaning: the situation of the disbelievers and the believers is likened to the situation of two men who were brothers among the Children of Israel, one of them a disbeliever named Barātūs and the other a believer named Yahūdhā. It was also said that they are the two mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A speaker among them said, "Indeed, I had a companion"﴾ (al-Saffat: 51). They inherited from their father eight thousand dinars, and each of them took half. The disbeliever bought land, and the believer said, "O Allah, I buy from You land in Paradise for a thousand," and gave it in charity. Then his brother built a house for a thousand, and the believer said, "O Allah, I buy from You a house in Paradise for a thousand," and gave it in charity. Then his brother married a woman for a thousand, and the believer said, "O Allah, I have made a thousand a dowry for the large-eyed maidens (ḥūr ʿīn)." Then his brother bought servants and estates for a thousand, and the believer said, "O Allah, I have bought from You the young boys for a thousand, so accept it as charity." Then he was afflicted with need, so he sat on his brother's path, and when his brother passed by him with his retinue, he approached him, but he drove him away and rebuked him for giving away his wealth in charity.

As for His saying: ﴿We made for one of them two gardens﴾, know that Allah, exalted is He, described that garden with attributes:

The first attribute: that it is a garden (jannah). A plantation was called a garden because what is hidden within it is concealed by the shade of the trees, and the root of the word is from concealment and covering.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿And We surrounded them with date palms﴾, meaning, We made the palms encircle the two gardens. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne (ḥāffīn min ḥawl al-ʿarsh)﴾ (al-Zumar: 75), meaning standing around the Throne encircling it. Al-ḥifāf is the side of a thing, and al-aḥiffah is its plural. So the meaning of the saying of one who says, "The people surrounded him (ḥaffa bihi al-qawm)," is that they became at its sides, which are its edges. The poet said:

He has glances at the two sides of his couch, when he turns them there is punishment and bounty.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: "They surrounded him (ḥaffūhu) when they went around him, and I surrounded him with them (ḥaffaftuhu bihim), meaning I made them surrounding him." It is transitive to one object, so the preposition bāʾ makes it take a second object, like His saying: "I covered him (ghashītuhu)" and "I covered him with it (ghashītuhu bihi)." He said: "This attribute is one that the landowners (ad-dahāqīn) prefer in their vineyards, which is that they make them surrounded by fruit-bearing trees, and this is also beautiful in appearance."

The third attribute: ﴿And We placed between them fields of crops﴾, and what is intended by it are several matters:

One: that this land should combine staple foods and fruits.

Second: that this land should be wide in its extents and far-spread in its sides, and yet nothing intervenes in it that would cut off part of it from part.

Third: that such land brings a different benefit at every time, another fruit, so its benefits were continuous and uninterrupted.

The fourth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Both gardens brought forth their produce and did not fall short of it in anything﴾. Kilā is a singular definite noun used to emphasize two masculine definite nouns, and kiltā is a singular noun used to emphasize two feminine definite nouns. When they are in construction with an apparent noun, both take the alif in all three cases, as in your saying: "The two brothers of yours (kilā akhawayka) came to me," "I saw both your brothers," and "I passed by both your brothers." Likewise: "Both your sisters (kiltā ukhtayka) came to me," "I saw both your sisters," and "I passed by both your sisters."
