Then He mentioned what indicates the superiority of those poor people over those wealthy disbelievers, saying: ﴿But the enduring good deeds are better in the sight of your Lord for reward, and better for hope.﴾ The statement of this proof is that the good things of this world are perishable and finite, while the good things of the Hereafter are lasting and enduring, and what is enduring is better than what is perishable and finite. This is known by necessity, especially when it is established that the good things of this world are base and worthless, and that the good things of the Hereafter are lofty and exalted, because the good things of this world are sensory, while the good things of the Hereafter are intellectual, and the intellectual is far more noble than the sensory, by the proofs mentioned in the explanation of His words: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾ (al-Nur: 35), in the explanation that intellectual perceptions are superior to sensory ones. Since this is so, the sum of intellectual and sensory felicities is the felicity of the Hereafter. Therefore it must be superior to the sensory, worldly felicities. And Allah knows best.

The exegetes have mentioned several opinions about "the enduring good deeds":

It has been said: they are our saying: "Subhan Allah (Glory be to Allah), al-Hamdu li-Allah (Praise be to Allah), la ilaha illa Allah (there is no god but Allah), and Allah Akbar (Allah is greatest)." Al-Shaykh al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, has a subtle explanation of these words. He said: It is reported that whoever says "Subhan Allah" receives ten rewards, and when he says "al-Hamdu li-Allah" they become twenty, and when he says "la ilaha illa Allah" they become thirty, and when he says "Allah Akbar" they become forty.

He said: The reality of this matter is that the highest level of reward is being absorbed in knowledge of Allah and in love for Him. When he says "Subhan Allah," he has recognized that He, glorified be He, is exalted above everything unworthy. The attainment of this knowledge is a great felicity and complete delight. When he says along with that "al-Hamdu li-Allah," he has affirmed that the Truth, glorified be He, together with being exalted above everything unworthy, is the source of bestowing everything fitting and of overflowing every good and perfection. Thus the degrees of knowledge have doubled, and for that reason we said the reward has doubled. When he says along with that "la ilaha illa Allah," he has affirmed that He who is exalted above everything unworthy is the source of everything fitting, and there is no existent like this except the One. Thus the levels of knowledge have become three, and for that reason the degrees of reward have become three. When he says "Allah Akbar," its meaning is that He is greater and more magnificent than that the intellect could reach the reality of His majesty and splendor. Thus the levels of knowledge have become four, and for that reason the degrees of reward have become four.

The second opinion: the enduring good deeds are the five daily prayers.

The third opinion: they are the good speech, as Allah said: ﴿And they were guided to good speech﴾ (al-Hajj: 24).

The fourth opinion: every deed and speech that calls you to occupy yourself with knowledge of Allah, with love for Him, and with serving Him, is among the enduring good deeds. Every deed and speech that calls you to occupy yourself with the conditions of creation is outside that category. This is because everything other than the Truth, glorified be He, is perishable in itself and destroyed in itself. Therefore, occupying oneself with it and turning to it is a vain deed and wasted striving. As for the Truth, He is lasting in Himself and does not accept cessation. Thus, occupation with knowledge of Allah, love for Him, and obedience to Him is what remains, enduring without ceasing or perishing.

* * *

Then He said, ﴿better in the sight of your Lord for reward, and better for hope﴾, meaning: every deed done seeking the face of Allah, there is no doubt that what is connected to it of reward, and what is connected to it of hope, will be good and superior, because the doer of those deeds hopes in this world for Allah's reward and his share in the Hereafter.

[Page 113]

﴿And on the Day We set the mountains moving, and you will see the earth laid bare, and We shall gather them and leave none of them behind.﴾ ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in ranks. "You have come to Us just as We created you the first time. Yet you claimed that We would never appoint a time for you."﴾ ﴿The Book will be placed, and you will see the guilty fearful of what is in it, and they will say, "Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves out no small deed or great, but has counted it all?" They will find what they did present there, and your Lord wrongs no one.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾. Having explained the baseness of this world and the nobility of the Resurrection, He followed this with the conditions of the Resurrection. The purpose of this is to refute the polytheists who boasted over the poor among the Muslims with their abundance of wealth and helpers. The scholars differed over what governs ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾, in several ways:

The first: the sense is "Mention to them: ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾," as a continuation of His saying: ﴿And set forth for them the parable of the life of this world﴾.

The second: the sense is "﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾ such and such will happen, and it will be said to them: ﴿You have come to Us just as We created you the first time﴾," because the verb of saying is implied in this place, so the meaning is that it will be said to them in this place.

The third: the sense is that ﴿and better in hope﴾ governs ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾. The first is the most apparent.

Having understood this, we say: He mentioned in the verse several kinds of the conditions of the Resurrection.

The first kind: His saying, ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾, and in it are two discussions.

The first discussion: Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Ibn Amir read ﴿tusayyaru﴾ (تُسَيَّرُ) in the passive form (fi'l ma lam yusamma fa'iluh, the verb whose agent is not named), and ﴿al-jibalu﴾ (الجِبالُ) in the nominative, attributing the verb ﴿tusayyaru﴾ to it, following His saying: ﴿And when the mountains are set moving﴾ (At-Takwir: 3). The rest read ﴿nusayyiru﴾ (نُسَيِّرُ), attributing the act of setting in motion to Himself, exalted is He, and ﴿al-jibala﴾ (الجِبالَ) in the accusative, as the object of ﴿nusayyiru﴾. The meaning is: We do that to them, following His saying: ﴿and We shall gather them and leave none of them behind﴾. The meaning is one, because when they are set in motion, the one who sets them in motion is none other than God, glorified is He.

The author of al-Kashshaf (Az-Zamakhshari) transmitted another reading, which is: ﴿tasiru al-jibalu﴾ (تَسِيرُ الجِبالُ), attributing ﴿tasiru﴾ to ﴿al-jibal﴾.

The second discussion: His saying, ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾: the wording of the verse contains nothing that indicates where they move to. So it may be said that He, exalted is He, sets them moving to the place He wills, and did not make that place known to His creation. But the truth is that the intended meaning is that He, exalted is He, sets them moving to nothingness, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will scatter them as dust. And He will leave it as a level plain, in which you will see no crookedness or curve﴾ (Ta-Ha: 105–107), and His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be pulverized to powder, and they will become scattered dust﴾ (Al-Waqi'ah: 5–6).

The second kind of the conditions of the Resurrection: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you will see the earth laid bare﴾, and concerning its explanation there are several meanings:

The first: nothing remains on its surface of buildings, nor of mountains, nor of trees. So it remains bare and manifest, with nothing covering it. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or curve﴾.

The second: the intended meaning of its being laid bare is that it brings forth what is in its belly, and casts out the dead who were buried in it. So it is laid bare in its hollow and its belly. The mention of the hollow is omitted, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it casts out what is within it and empties itself﴾ (Al-Inshiqaq: 4), and His saying: ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ (Az-Zalzalah: 2), and His saying: ﴿and they will all come forth before God﴾ (Ibrahim: 21).

The third: the faces of the earth were covered by the mountains and seas, so when God, exalted is He, annihilates the mountains and seas, the faces of those regions become bare after having been covered.

The third kind of the conditions of the Resurrection: His saying: ﴿and We shall gather them and leave none of them behind﴾. The meaning: We gathered them for the reckoning, and We left none of them behind, that is, We did not leave out any of the first or the last without gathering them for that Day. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed the former and the latter﴾ ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day﴾ (Al-Waqi'ah: 49–50). The meaning of ﴿lam nughadir﴾ (لَمْ نُغادِرْ) is "We did not leave", as it is said: ghadarahu and aghdarahu when one leaves him. From it comes al-ghadr (الغَدْر), which is abandoning fidelity, and from it al-ghadir (الغَدِير), because the torrents have left it; and from it the woman's braid is called al-ghadirah, because she places it behind her.

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the gathering of creation, He mentioned the manner of their presentation, saying: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in ranks﴾. There are two issues concerning this:

The first issue: concerning the explanation of ﴿saffan﴾ (صَفًّا), there are several meanings:

The first: all of creation will be presented before God in one rank, manifest, such that none of them screens another. Al-Qaffal said: It seems that ﴿al-saff﴾ returns to the meaning of manifestness and emergence, and from it the word al-safsaf (الصَّفْصَف) for the open plain is derived.

The second: it is not far-fetched that creation will be in rows, with some standing behind others, like the rows surrounding the Ka'bah, where some are behind others. On this interpretation, the meaning of His saying ﴿saffan﴾ is "rows" (ṣufūfan), like His saying: ﴿He brings you forth as a child﴾ (Ghafir: 67), meaning "as children".

The third: ﴿saffan﴾ means "standing", as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So mention the name of God over them while they stand in ranks﴾ (Al-Hajj: 36). They said: "standing".

The second issue: The Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ (Al-Fajr: 22), indicates that God, exalted is He, is present in that place, and the people of the Resurrection are presented before Him in rows. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You have indeed come to Us﴾ indicates that He, exalted is He, is present in that place. It was answered that God, exalted is He, made their standing in the place where He asks them about their deeds and reckons with them over them a presentation before Him, not that He is present in a place and they are presented before Him in order that He may see them after He had not been seeing them. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You have indeed come to Us just as We created you the first time﴾. The intended meaning is not equality in every respect, because they were created as small children without intellect and without obligation. Rather, the intended meaning is that He said to the polytheists who denied the resurrection and who boasted in this world over the poor believers with wealth and helpers: ﴿You have indeed come to Us just as We created you the first time﴾, naked, barefoot, without wealth or helpers. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you have indeed come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾ (Al-An'am: 94). And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said: I will surely be given wealth and children?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and he will come to Us alone﴾ (Maryam: 77–80). Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Yet you claimed that We would never appoint a time for you﴾, meaning: while you were powerful against the believers with wealth and helpers, you denied resurrection and the Last Day. Now you have left behind wealth and helpers in this world, and you have witnessed that the resurrection and the Last Day are true.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the Book will be placed﴾. The intended meaning is that the book of every person will be placed in his hand on this Day, either in the right hand or in the left. The intended meaning is the genus, which is the pages of deeds. ﴿And you will see the guilty fearful of what is in it﴾, meaning: fearful of what is in the Book of their wicked deeds, and fearful lest that be made manifest to the people of the place of standing, so that they are disgraced. In sum, they experience fear of punishment from the Truth and fear of disgrace before creation. They will say, "Woe to us!", calling out their destruction, which they brought upon themselves specifically from among all destructions: ﴿What is this Book that leaves out no small deed or great, but has counted it all?﴾ This is an expression of comprehensiveness, meaning that it leaves out none of the sins, whether small or great, without its being recorded in this Book. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers, who know what you do﴾ (Al-Infitar: 10–12), and His saying: ﴿Indeed We were having your deeds copied﴾ (Al-Jathiyah: 29). The feminine ta' (تاء التأنيث) is attached to ṣaghīrah and kabīrah on the assumption that the intended meaning is the small act and the great act. ﴿Except it has counted it﴾ means: except it has recorded and enumerated it. Some scholars said: They cried out about the minor sins before the major sins, because those minor sins are what led them to the major sins; so they were extremely wary of the minor sins.

﴿And they will find what they did present there﴾, that is, recorded in the pages, ready at hand, or the recompense of what they did. ﴿And your Lord wrongs no one﴾, its meaning being that He does not record against him what he did not do, nor increase his deserved punishment, and does not punish anyone for the crime of another.

Remaining in the verse are issues:

The first issue: Al-Jubba'i said: This verse indicates the falsity of the position of the Mujbirah (determinists) in several matters. The first: that if He punished His servants without an act having proceeded from them, He would be unjust. The second: that He does not punish children without sin. The third: the invalidity of their saying: God may do whatever He wills and punish without any crime, because creation is His creation. For if it were so, there would be no meaning to negating injustice from Him, since on the assumption that whatever He does He wills, it would not be injustice on His part, and His saying "He does not wrong" would have no benefit. It is said to him:

As for the answer to the first two: it is the counter-argument of knowledge and the motive (al-mu'arada bil-'ilm wal-da'i).

As for the answer to this third: it is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ (Maryam: 35), and this does not indicate that taking a son is valid for Him; so likewise here.

The second issue: It is related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "People will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection concerning three: Joseph, Job, and Solomon. He will summon the slave and say to him: What distracted you from Me? He will say: You made me a slave to a human being, and You did not free me. Then He will summon Joseph, peace be upon him, and say: This one was a slave like you, and that did not prevent him from worshipping Me. He will be commanded to the Fire. Then He will summon the afflicted, and when he says: You distracted me with affliction, He will summon Job, peace be upon him, and say: I afflicted this one with a greater affliction than Yours, and that did not prevent him from worshipping Me. He will be commanded to the Fire. Then the king will be brought in this world with what God gave him of wealth and abundance, and He will say: What did you do with what I gave you? He will say: Kingship distracted me from that. Then Solomon, peace be upon him, will be summoned, and He will say: This is My servant Solomon, to whom I gave more than I gave you, and that did not distract him from My worship. Go, for you have no excuse. And he will be commanded to the Fire." And it is related from Mu'adh, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: "The foot of the servant will not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked about four things: about his body, how he wore it out; about his life, how he spent it; about his wealth, from where he acquired it and how he spent it; and about his knowledge, how he acted upon it."

The third issue: The verse indicates the affirmation of minor and major sins among the sins. This is agreed upon among the Muslims, except that they differed over its explanation. The Mu'tazilah said: The major sin is that whose punishment exceeds the reward of its doer, and the minor sin is that whose punishment falls short of the reward of its doer. Know that this definition is valid only if it is established that the act necessitates reward and punishment, and that is, according to us, false for many reasons that we have mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, in refuting the doctrine of annulment (al-ihbat) and expiation (al-takfir). Rather, the truth according to us is that acts of obedience are confined to two kinds: exalting the command of God, and compassion toward the creation of God. So whatever is stronger in being ignorance of God is greater in being a major sin, and whatever is stronger in being harm to another is greater in being a sin or act of disobedience. This is the rule.

﴿And on the Day We set the mountains moving, and you will see the earth laid bare, and We shall gather them and leave none of them behind.﴾ ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in ranks. "You have come to Us just as We created you the first time. Yet you claimed that We would never appoint a time for you."﴾ ﴿The Book will be placed, and you will see the guilty fearful of what is in it, and they will say, "Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves out no small deed or great, but has counted it all?" They will find what they did present there, and your Lord wrongs no one.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾. Having explained the baseness of this world and the nobility of the Resurrection, He followed this with the conditions of the Resurrection. The purpose of this is to refute the polytheists who boasted over the poor among the Muslims with their abundance of wealth and helpers. The scholars differed over what governs ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾, in several ways:

The first: the sense is "Mention to them: ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾," as a continuation of His saying: ﴿And set forth for them the parable of the life of this world﴾.

The second: the sense is "﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾ such and such will happen, and it will be said to them: ﴿You have come to Us just as We created you the first time﴾," because the verb of saying is implied in this place, so the meaning is that it will be said to them in this place.

The third: the sense is that ﴿and better in hope﴾ governs ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾. The first is the most apparent.

Having understood this, we say: He mentioned in the verse several kinds of the conditions of the Resurrection.

The first kind: His saying, ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾, and in it are two discussions.

The first discussion: Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Ibn Amir read ﴿tusayyaru﴾ (تُسَيَّرُ) in the passive form (fi'l ma lam yusamma fa'iluh, the verb whose agent is not named), and ﴿al-jibalu﴾ (الجِبالُ) in the nominative, attributing the verb ﴿tusayyaru﴾ to it, following His saying: ﴿And when the mountains are set moving﴾ (At-Takwir: 3). The rest read ﴿nusayyiru﴾ (نُسَيِّرُ), attributing the act of setting in motion to Himself, exalted is He, and ﴿al-jibala﴾ (الجِبالَ) in the accusative, as the object of ﴿nusayyiru﴾. The meaning is: We do that to them, following His saying: ﴿and We shall gather them and leave none of them behind﴾. The meaning is one, because when they are set in motion, the one who sets them in motion is none other than God, glorified is He.

The author of al-Kashshaf (Az-Zamakhshari) transmitted another reading, which is: ﴿tasiru al-jibalu﴾ (تَسِيرُ الجِبالُ), attributing ﴿tasiru﴾ to ﴿al-jibal﴾.

The second discussion: His saying, ﴿on the Day We set the mountains moving﴾: the wording of the verse contains nothing that indicates where they move to. So it may be said that He, exalted is He, sets them moving to the place He wills, and did not make that place known to His creation. But the truth is that the intended meaning is that He, exalted is He, sets them moving to nothingness, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will scatter them as dust. And He will leave it as a level plain, in which you will see no crookedness or curve﴾ (Ta-Ha: 105–107), and His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be pulverized to powder, and they will become scattered dust﴾ (Al-Waqi'ah: 5–6).

The second kind of the conditions of the Resurrection: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you will see the earth laid bare﴾, and concerning its explanation there are several meanings:

The first: nothing remains on its surface of buildings, nor of mountains, nor of trees. So it remains bare and manifest, with nothing covering it. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or curve﴾.

The second: the intended meaning of its being laid bare is that it brings forth what is in its belly, and casts out the dead who were buried in it. So it is laid bare in its hollow and its belly. The mention of the hollow is omitted, and its evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it casts out what is within it and empties itself﴾ (Al-Inshiqaq: 4), and His saying: ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ (Az-Zalzalah: 2), and His saying: ﴿and they will all come forth before God﴾ (Ibrahim: 21).

The third: the faces of the earth were covered by the mountains and seas, so when God, exalted is He, annihilates the mountains and seas, the faces of those regions become bare after having been covered.

The third kind of the conditions of the Resurrection: His saying: ﴿and We shall gather them and leave none of them behind﴾. The meaning: We gathered them for the reckoning, and We left none of them behind, that is, We did not leave out any of the first or the last without gathering them for that Day. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Indeed the former and the latter﴾ ﴿will surely be gathered to the appointed time of a known day﴾ (Al-Waqi'ah: 49–50). The meaning of ﴿lam nughadir﴾ (لَمْ نُغادِرْ) is "We did not leave", as it is said: ghadarahu and aghdarahu when one leaves him. From it comes al-ghadr (الغَدْر), which is abandoning fidelity, and from it al-ghadir (الغَدِير), because the torrents have left it; and from it the woman's braid is called al-ghadirah, because she places it behind her.

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the gathering of creation, He mentioned the manner of their presentation, saying: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in ranks﴾. There are two issues concerning this:

The first issue: concerning the explanation of ﴿saffan﴾ (صَفًّا), there are several meanings:

The first: all of creation will be presented before God in one rank, manifest, such that none of them screens another. Al-Qaffal said: It seems that ﴿al-saff﴾ returns to the meaning of manifestness and emergence, and from it the word al-safsaf (الصَّفْصَف) for the open plain is derived.

The second: it is not far-fetched that creation will be in rows, with some standing behind others, like the rows surrounding the Ka'bah, where some are behind others. On this interpretation, the meaning of His saying ﴿saffan﴾ is "rows" (ṣufūfan), like His saying: ﴿He brings you forth as a child﴾ (Ghafir: 67), meaning "as children".

The third: ﴿saffan﴾ means "standing", as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So mention the name of God over them while they stand in ranks﴾ (Al-Hajj: 36). They said: "standing".

The second issue: The Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) said: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ (Al-Fajr: 22), indicates that God, exalted is He, is present in that place, and the people of the Resurrection are presented before Him in rows. Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You have indeed come to Us﴾ indicates that He, exalted is He, is present in that place. It was answered that God, exalted is He, made their standing in the place where He asks them about their deeds and reckons with them over them a presentation before Him, not that He is present in a place and they are presented before Him in order that He may see them after He had not been seeing them. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿You have indeed come to Us just as We created you the first time﴾. The intended meaning is not equality in every respect, because they were created as small children without intellect and without obligation. Rather, the intended meaning is that He said to the polytheists who denied the resurrection and who boasted in this world over the poor believers with wealth and helpers: ﴿You have indeed come to Us just as We created you the first time﴾, naked, barefoot, without wealth or helpers. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you have indeed come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾ (Al-An'am: 94). And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said: I will surely be given wealth and children?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and he will come to Us alone﴾ (Maryam: 77–80). Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Yet you claimed that We would never appoint a time for you﴾, meaning: while you were powerful against the believers with wealth and helpers, you denied resurrection and the Last Day. Now you have left behind wealth and helpers in this world, and you have witnessed that the resurrection and the Last Day are true.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the Book will be placed﴾. The intended meaning is that the book of every person will be placed in his hand on this Day, either in the right hand or in the left. The intended meaning is the genus, which is the pages of deeds. ﴿And you will see the guilty fearful of what is in it﴾, meaning: fearful of what is in the Book of their wicked deeds, and fearful lest that be made manifest to the people of the place of standing, so that they are disgraced. In sum, they experience fear of punishment from the Truth and fear of disgrace before creation. They will say, "Woe to us!", calling out their destruction, which they brought upon themselves specifically from among all destructions: ﴿What is this Book that leaves out no small deed or great, but has counted it all?﴾ This is an expression of comprehensiveness, meaning that it leaves out none of the sins, whether small or great, without its being recorded in this Book. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers, who know what you do﴾ (Al-Infitar: 10–12), and His saying: ﴿Indeed We were having your deeds copied﴾ (Al-Jathiyah: 29). The feminine ta' (تاء التأنيث) is attached to ṣaghīrah and kabīrah on the assumption that the intended meaning is the small act and the great act. ﴿Except it has counted it﴾ means: except it has recorded and enumerated it. Some scholars said: They cried out about the minor sins before the major sins, because those minor sins are what led them to the major sins; so they were extremely wary of the minor sins.

﴿And they will find what they did present there﴾, that is, recorded in the pages, ready at hand, or the recompense of what they did. ﴿And your Lord wrongs no one﴾, its meaning being that He does not record against him what he did not do, nor increase his deserved punishment, and does not punish anyone for the crime of another.

Remaining in the verse are issues:

The first issue: Al-Jubba'i said: This verse indicates the falsity of the position of the Mujbirah (determinists) in several matters. The first: that if He punished His servants without an act having proceeded from them, He would be unjust. The second: that He does not punish children without sin. The third: the invalidity of their saying: God may do whatever He wills and punish without any crime, because creation is His creation. For if it were so, there would be no meaning to negating injustice from Him, since on the assumption that whatever He does He wills, it would not be injustice on His part, and His saying "He does not wrong" would have no benefit. It is said to him:

As for the answer to the first two: it is the counter-argument of knowledge and the motive (al-mu'arada bil-'ilm wal-da'i).

As for the answer to this third: it is that He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not for God to take a son﴾ (Maryam: 35), and this does not indicate that taking a son is valid for Him; so likewise here.

The second issue: It is related from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "People will be called to account on the Day of Resurrection concerning three: Joseph, Job, and Solomon. He will summon the slave and say to him: What distracted you from Me? He will say: You made me a slave to a human being, and You did not free me. Then He will summon Joseph, peace be upon him, and say: This one was a slave like you, and that did not prevent him from worshipping Me. He will be commanded to the Fire. Then He will summon the afflicted, and when he says: You distracted me with affliction, He will summon Job, peace be upon him, and say: I afflicted this one with a greater affliction than Yours, and that did not prevent him from worshipping Me. He will be commanded to the Fire. Then the king will be brought in this world with what God gave him of wealth and abundance, and He will say: What did you do with what I gave you? He will say: Kingship distracted me from that. Then Solomon, peace be upon him, will be summoned, and He will say: This is My servant Solomon, to whom I gave more than I gave you, and that did not distract him from My worship. Go, for you have no excuse. And he will be commanded to the Fire." And it is related from Mu'adh, from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that he said: "The foot of the servant will not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked about four things: about his body, how he wore it out; about his life, how he spent it; about his wealth, from where he acquired it and how he spent it; and about his knowledge, how he acted upon it."

The third issue: The verse indicates the affirmation of minor and major sins among the sins. This is agreed upon among the Muslims, except that they differed over its explanation. The Mu'tazilah said: The major sin is that whose punishment exceeds the reward of its doer, and the minor sin is that whose punishment falls short of the reward of its doer. Know that this definition is valid only if it is established that the act necessitates reward and punishment, and that is, according to us, false for many reasons that we have mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, in refuting the doctrine of annulment (al-ihbat) and expiation (al-takfir). Rather, the truth according to us is that acts of obedience are confined to two kinds: exalting the command of God, and compassion toward the creation of God. So whatever is stronger in being ignorance of God is greater in being a major sin, and whatever is stronger in being harm to another is greater in being a sin or act of disobedience. This is the rule.

Allah the Exalted says:

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord. Will you then take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me, while they are your enemy? Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves. And I would not take misleaders as helpers.﴾ ﴿And on the Day He will say, "Call upon My partners whom you claimed." So they will call upon them, but they will not respond to them, and We will place between them a barrier of destruction.﴾ ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will know that they are going to fall into it, and they will find no escape from it.﴾

And in this passage there are several issues:

Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 50–53 (part 2 of 2):

The third point is the meaning. Mention to them, O Muhammad, their state and the state of their deities on the Day of Resurrection, when Allah says to them: ﴿Call upon My partners﴾, that is, call upon those whom you claimed to be partners to Me, since you made them fit for worship. Allah, exalted is He, does not mention in this verse how they called upon the partners, because He explained that in another verse, namely that they said: ﴿We were following you. Can you then relieve us of some of the fire?﴾ (Ghafir: 47). Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But they will not respond to them﴾, meaning they did not answer them in what they called them to, did not ward off any harm from them, and did not bring any benefit to them. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will place between them a mawbiq﴾. On this there are several opinions:

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The mawbiq (place of destruction) is from waqiba, yabiqu, wubuqan and wabaqan, meaning he perished, and awbaqahu meaning another caused him to perish. It may be a verbal noun like al-mawrid and al-mawid. The explanation of this opinion is that these polytheists who took deities besides Allah, such as the angels and Jesus, called upon these, but they did not respond to them. Then a barrier was placed between them, so Allah caused these polytheists to enter Hell and caused Jesus to enter Paradise, and the angels went to where Allah willed, to the abode of honour. The mawbiq arose between those disbelievers and the angels and Jesus, peace be upon him, and it is that valley in Hell.

The second opinion: al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: "mawbiq" means enmity, and the meaning is an enmity which, in its intensity, is destruction. From this is the saying: "Let not your love be excessive, nor your hatred a ruin."

The third opinion: al-Farra' said: al-bayn means connection, that is, their connection in the world will be a destruction for them on the Day of Resurrection.

The fourth opinion: The mawbiq is a distant barrier, meaning: We placed between these disbelievers and the angels and Jesus a distant barrier in which a traveller perishes because of its great distance, for the disbelievers are at the bottom of Hell while those others are in the highest gardens. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are going to fall therein﴾. Regarding this "thinking" there are two views:

The first: that the zann (thinking) here means knowledge and certainty.

The second, which is closer: the meaning is that these disbelievers see the Fire from a distant place, so they think that they will be cast into it at that very moment without delay or respite, because of the intensity of what they hear of its raging and its roaring, as He said: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring﴾ (al-Furqan: 12). Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will not find from it any escape﴾, meaning they will not find any turning away from the Fire to anything else, because the angels will drive them into it.

The third point is the meaning. Allah the Exalted says:

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord. And in this passage there are several issues:

This verse, whose purpose in being mentioned is this very same meaning, is so because Iblis only became arrogant toward Adam because he took pride in his origin and lineage, and said: "You created me from fire and created him from clay, so I am more noble than him in origin and lineage. How then should I prostrate, and how should I humble myself before him?" These polytheists treated the poor among the Muslims with this very same treatment. They said: "How can we sit with these poor people, when we are from noble lineages and they are from lowly lineages, and we are rich while they are poor?" So Allah the Exalted mentioned this story here as a warning that this way of thinking is precisely the way of Iblis. Then He warned against it and against following it in His saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies?﴾ This is the aspect of the arrangement (nazm) of the verses, and it is a good and valid one. Al-Qadi mentioned another aspect, saying: when He had earlier mentioned the matter of the Resurrection and what occurs at the gathering and the placing of the Book, it was as if Allah wished to mention here that He will call out to the polytheists and say to them: "Where are My partners whom you claimed?" Since Allah the Exalted knew that Iblis is the one who leads a person to affirm these partners, He therefore, without doubt, placed his story in this verse to complete that purpose. Then al-Qadi said: Although Allah the Exalted repeated this story in many sūrahs, there is in each place of it a new benefit.

**The second issue:** Allah the Exalted made clear in this verse that Iblis was of the jinn. People differ on this matter in three opinions.

The first: he was of the angels. Being of the angels does not contradict being of the jinn, and there are aspects to this view:

The first: a tribe of the angels is called by this name, based on the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾ (al-Saffat 37:158) and ﴿And they have attributed to Allah partners among the jinn﴾ (al-An'am 6:100).

The second: the jinn were named jinn because they are hidden, and the angels are likewise hidden, so they are included among the jinn.

The third: he was a keeper of the Garden, and was attributed to the Garden, as they say "Kufi" and "Basri." It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he was among the gardeners (al-jannanin) who work in the Gardens, a group of angels who fashion the adornments of the people of the Garden from the time they were created. Al-Qadi narrated this in his Tafsir from Hisham, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second opinion: he was of the jinn, who are the devils, and who were created from fire, and he is their father.

The third opinion: the view of the one who said: he was of the angels, then he was transformed and changed.

The proof that he is not of the angels is that Allah the Exalted affirmed for him offspring and progeny in this verse, namely His saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me?﴾ and the angels have no offspring or progeny. Therefore it is necessary that Iblis not be of the angels. What remains is to say: Allah the Exalted commanded the angels to prostrate, so if Iblis was not of the angels, how did that command apply to him? And also, if he was not of the angels, how is his exception from them valid? We have answered all of this thoroughly.

The first: al-Farra' said: "fasaqa 'an amri rabbihi" means he came out of obedience to Him. The Arabs say "fasaqat al-ruṭbah min qishriha" (the date came out of its skin), and the mouse was named fuwaysiqah because it comes out of its hole from both openings. Ru'bah said:

They descend into Najd and into a deep valley, [as] those who have strayed (fawāsiq) from their course, deviating.

The second: al-Zajjaj related from al-Khalil and Sibawayh that he said: when he was commanded and disobeyed, the cause of his transgression was that very command. The meaning is that without that prior command, the transgression would not have occurred. For this reason it is fitting to say "fasaqa 'an amri rabbihi."

The third: Qutrub said: "fasaqa 'an amri rabbihi" means he rejected it, like the saying: "ask the village" and "ask the caravan."

The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And I would not take misleaders as helpers (ʿaḍud)﴾, that is, "and I would not take them." The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to clarify their misguidance. And His saying "ʿaḍudan" means helpers.

The second, which is closer to me: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers who said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "If you do not drive these poor people away from your gathering, we will not believe in you." So it was as if Allah the Exalted said: those who came with this corrupt proposal and baseless obstinacy were not partners with Me in the management of the world, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾, and I did not strengthen Myself through them in managing this world and the Hereafter. Rather they are a people like the rest of creation, so why did they undertake this corrupt proposal? A parallel to this: whoever puts great proposals to you, you say to him: "You are not the ruler of the land nor a prince of the kingdom, that we should accept from you these tremendous proposals, so why do you undertake them?" What confirms this is that the pronoun must refer to the nearest of the things mentioned, and in this verse the nearest mention is of those disbelievers, namely His saying: ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, and by "the wrongdoers" are meant those disbelievers.

The third: that what is meant by His saying: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾ is that these disbelievers were ignorant of what the Pen had written from eternity regarding the states of happiness and wretchedness. It was as if it were said to them: The happy one is the one whom Allah has judged to be happy from eternity, and the wretched one is the one whom Allah has judged to be wretched from eternity, and you are heedless of the states of eternity. It is as if Allah the Exalted said: "I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves." And if you are ignorant of this state, how can you judge for yourselves elevation, loftiness, and perfection, and for others lowliness and abasement? Rather, the matter may in this world and the Hereafter be the reverse of what you have judged.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers.﴾ That is: evil is the substitute from Allah, Iblis, for whoever takes him as a substitute, so that he obeys him in place of obeying Allah.

Then He said: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves.﴾ In this there are two issues:

**The first issue:** They differed about the pronoun in His saying "ma ashhadtuhum" (I did not make them witness): to what does it refer? There are several aspects:

The first, which is the view of most scholars: the meaning is "I did not make the ones you took as allies witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor did I make some of them witness the creation of others," like His saying: ﴿Kill yourselves﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:66), meaning: I did not make them witness so that I might be strengthened by them. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And I would not take misleaders as helpers (ʿaḍud)﴾, that is, "and I would not take them." The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to clarify their misguidance. And His saying "ʿaḍudan" means helpers.

The second, which is closer to me: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers who said to the Messenger (ﷺ): "If you do not drive these poor people away from your gathering, we will not believe in you." So it was as if Allah the Exalted said: those who came with this corrupt proposal and baseless obstinacy were not partners with Me in the management of the world, by the evidence of His saying: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾, and I did not strengthen Myself through them in managing this world and the Hereafter. Rather they are a people like the rest of creation, so why did they undertake this corrupt proposal? A parallel to this: whoever puts great proposals to you, you say to him: "You are not the ruler of the land nor a prince of the kingdom, that we should accept from you these tremendous proposals, so why do you undertake them?" What confirms this is that the pronoun must refer to the nearest of the things mentioned, and in this verse the nearest mention is of those disbelievers, namely His saying: ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾, and by "the wrongdoers" are meant those disbelievers.

The third: that what is meant by His saying: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾ is that these disbelievers were ignorant of what the Pen had written from eternity regarding the states of happiness and wretchedness. It was as if it were said to them: The happy one is the one whom Allah has judged to be happy from eternity, and the wretched one is the one whom Allah has judged to be wretched from eternity, and you are heedless of the states of eternity. It is as if Allah the Exalted said: "I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves." And if you are ignorant of this state, how can you judge for yourselves elevation, loftiness, and perfection, and for others lowliness and abasement? Rather, the matter may in this world and the Hereafter be the reverse of what you have judged.

**The second issue:** Al-Kashshaf's author said: it was read "wa-ma kunta" with a fatḥah (on the ta'), and the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The meaning: it would not be proper for you to be strengthened by them, nor is it fitting for you to take pride in them. ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, read "mutakhidh al-muḍillīn" with tanwin, in accordance with the original form. al-Hasan read "ʿuḍdan" with the ḍād sukūn and transferred its ḍammah to the ʿayn. It was also read "ʿaḍdan" with fatḥah and sukūn of the ḍād, "ʿuḍudan" with two ḍammahs, and "ʿaḍadan" with two fatḥahs, being the plural of ʿāḍid, like khādim and khadam, and rāṣid and raṣad, from ʿaḍadahu, meaning he strengthened him and helped him.

Know that when Allah the Exalted had established that the statement they made in boasting over the poor, following Iblis, was of this nature, He returned after that to describing the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and said: ﴿And on the Day He will say, "Call upon My partners whom you claimed."﴾ In this there are discussions:

**The first discussion:** Hamzah read "naqūlu" (We will say) with a nūn, as a conjunction with His saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ and ﴿allies instead of Me﴾ and ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves, and I would not take misleaders as helpers﴾. The rest read it with a yā' (yaqūlu).

**The second discussion:** The phrase "wa-dhkur yawma naqūlu" (and mention the Day when We will say) is a conjunction with His saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate"﴾.

Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 50–53 (part 2 of 2):

The third point is the meaning. Mention to them, O Muhammad, their state and the state of their deities on the Day of Resurrection, when Allah says to them: ﴿Call upon My partners﴾, that is, call upon those whom you claimed to be partners to Me, since you made them fit for worship. Call upon them so that they may intercede for you and help you. By "the partners" is meant the jinn. So they called upon them. Allah, exalted is He, does not mention in this verse how they called upon the partners, because He explained that in another verse, namely that they said: ﴿We were following you. Can you then relieve us of some of the fire?﴾ (Ghafir: 47). Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But they will not respond to them﴾, meaning they did not answer them in what they called them to, did not ward off any harm from them, and did not bring any benefit to them. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will place between them a mawbiq﴾. On this there are several opinions:

The first: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: The mawbiq (place of destruction) is from waqiba, yabiqu, wubuqan and wabaqan, meaning he perished, and awbaqahu meaning another caused him to perish. It may be a verbal noun like al-mawrid and al-mawid. The explanation of this opinion is that these polytheists who took deities besides Allah, such as the angels and Jesus, called upon these, but they did not respond to them. Then a barrier was placed between them, so Allah caused these polytheists to enter Hell and caused Jesus to enter Paradise, and the angels went to where Allah willed, to the abode of honour. The mawbiq arose between those disbelievers and the angels and Jesus, peace be upon him, and it is that valley in Hell.

The second opinion: al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: "mawbiq" means enmity, and the meaning is an enmity which, in its intensity, is destruction. From this is the saying: "Let not your love be excessive, nor your hatred a ruin."

The third opinion: al-Farra' said: al-bayn means connection, that is, their connection in the world will be a destruction for them on the Day of Resurrection.

The fourth opinion: The mawbiq is a distant barrier, meaning: We placed between these disbelievers and the angels and Jesus a distant barrier in which a traveller perishes because of its great distance, for the disbelievers are at the bottom of Hell while those others are in the highest gardens. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are going to fall therein﴾. Regarding this "thinking" there are two views:

The first: that the zann (thinking) here means knowledge and certainty.

The second, which is closer: the meaning is that these disbelievers see the Fire from a distant place, so they think that they will be cast into it at that very moment without delay or respite, because of the intensity of what they hear of its raging and its roaring, as He said: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place, they hear its raging and roaring﴾ (al-Furqan: 12). His saying ﴿will be cast into it﴾ means will be mixed with it, for when the mixing of one thing with another is strong and complete, it is called muwaqa'a (close contact). Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will not find from it any escape﴾, meaning they will not find any turning away from the Fire to anything else, because the angels will drive them into it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 54–56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every [kind of] example. But mankind is ever most contentious.﴾ ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them and from asking forgiveness of their Lord, except that there should befall them the precedent of the former peoples or that the punishment should come to them face to face.﴾ ﴿And We send not the messengers except as bringers of good tidings and warners. But those who disbelieve argue by falsehood to refute thereby the truth, and they take My signs and that with which they are warned in ridicule.﴾

Know that when those disbelievers boasted over the poor among the Muslims for the abundance of their wealth and their followers, and God, exalted is He, demonstrated through the many aspects that their saying was corrupt and their doubt false, and He mentioned in it the two examples mentioned earlier, He said after that: ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every [kind of] example.﴾ This refers to what has preceded, and tasrif (diversification) necessitates repetition, and the matter is indeed so, because He, exalted is He, answered their doubt which they had mentioned from many aspects, and despite those sufficient answers and matching examples, these disbelievers do not abandon false argument. So He said: ﴿But mankind is ever most contentious﴾, i.e., most of the things from which argument arises; and the placement of His saying (jadalan, "contentious") is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz). Some of the verifiers said: the verse indicates that the prophets, peace be upon them, argued with them about the religion until they themselves became arguers, because argument does not take place except from both sides, and this indicates that the view of taqlid (blind imitation) is false. Then He said: ﴿And nothing prevented the people from believing when guidance came to them and from asking forgiveness of their Lord﴾, and in this there are two discussions:

Section 175/120
The first discussion: The Mu'tazilah said: the verse indicates that there was nothing that prevents one from proceeding to belief, and this indicates the corruption of the saying of whoever says that a preventer has occurred. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: knowledge that he will not believe is contrary to the existence of belief; so when that knowledge exists, the preventer exists. Also, the presence of the motive toward disbelief exists, otherwise it would not be necessary, because a voluntary act without a motive is impossible, and the existence of the motive toward disbelief prevents the attainment of belief. When this is established, it becomes clear that what is meant is the quantity of the perceptible preventers.

The second discussion: The meaning is that when guidance came to them, which is the evidence indicating the validity of Islam, and it is established that there is no preventer for them from believing or from seeking forgiveness and repentance, and the opportunity is available and the excuses are removed, then why did they not proceed to belief? Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿except that there should befall them the precedent of the former peoples﴾, which is the punishment of annihilation, ﴿or that the punishment should come to them face to face﴾. Hamzah, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read qubulan with the qaf and the ba' both dammed, and it is the plural of qabil, meaning kinds of punishment that follow one another while they are alive; and it was said: "in front of them" and "visibly." The rest read qibalan with a kasra on the qaf and a fatha on the ba', meaning also "visibly." The author of al-Kashshaf related: qabalan with two fathas, meaning "confronting." The meaning is that they will not proceed to belief except at the descent of the punishment of annihilation, and so they perish; or that the varieties of punishment and affliction follow one another while they remain in the life of this world. Know that they will not proceed to belief except under these two conditions, because the sensible person does not accept the occurrence of these two matters, except that their state resembles the state of one who has made action contingent upon these two conditions. Then God, exalted is He, clarified that He sent the messengers only as bringers of good tidings of reward for obedience and warners of punishment for disobedience, so that they might believe willingly. And He made clear, along with these circumstances, that there exists among the disbelievers argument by falsehood for the purpose of refuting the truth, and this indicates that the prophets used to argue with them, as we have explained, that argument arises only from both sides. And God, exalted is He, also made clear that they took the signs of God, which are the Qur'an and the warnings of the prophets, in ridicule, and all of that indicates the dominance of ignorance and hardness. The grammarians said: "ma" in His saying ﴿and that with which they are warned﴾ may be a relative pronoun with the returning pronoun of the relative clause omitted, and it may be a verbal particle (masdariyyah) meaning "their warning."

[Page 121]

Know that when God, exalted is He, related the disbelievers' disputing with falsehood, He afterwards described them with attributes that necessitate disgrace and abandonment.

The first attribute: His saying, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have put forward?﴾ That is, there is no greater injustice than the disbelief of one to whom the signs and clear proofs come, so he turns away from them and forgets what his hands have put forward. That is, along with his turning away from reflecting on the proofs and clear evidences, he disregards the deeds he committed that were reprehensible and the false doctrines he held. The meaning of "forgetting" here is being preoccupied with, and neglectful of, his earlier disbelief.

The second attribute: His saying, ﴿Indeed We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness. And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever.﴾ The interpretation of this verse has already been discussed exhaustively in Surat al-An'am. What is remarkable is that His saying, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have put forward﴾, is the proof-text of the Qadariyya (those who affirm human free will and responsibility), while His saying, ﴿Indeed We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it﴾ through the end of the verse, is the proof-text of the Jabriyya (those who affirm that human beings are compelled). We rarely find in the Qur'an a verse belonging to one of these two groups without another verse belonging to the other group accompanying it. Experience reveals the truth of what we say. This is nothing but a severe trial from God, the Exalted, which He placed upon His servants, so that the learned, firmly grounded scholars might be distinguished from the mere imitators.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy.﴾ "Al-Ghafur" (the Forgiving) is one who is abundant in forgiveness, and this points to the repelling of harms. "Dhu al-rahmah" (the Possessor of mercy) means one characterized by mercy. The intensive form was mentioned for forgiveness and not for mercy, because forgiveness is the abandonment of harm, and He, exalted is He, has abandoned harms without limit while being capable of them. As for the act of mercy, it is finite, because abandoning what has no end is possible, whereas doing what has no end is impossible. It may also be said that the meaning is that He forgives abundantly because He is the Possessor of mercy and has no need for it, so He bestows it abundantly upon those in need.

He then cited as evidence His not punishing the people of Makkah immediately, without granting respite, despite their extreme enmity toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Then He said: ﴿Rather, for them is an appointed time, and they will never find other than Him a refuge.﴾ This appointed time is either the Day of Resurrection, or in this world, and that is the Day of Badr and the rest of the days of the conquest. His saying, ﴿they will never find other than Him a refuge﴾, means a place of escape or a shelter. It is said: "wa'ala" when one seeks refuge, and "wa'ala ilayhi" when one seeks refuge with him.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those cities — We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We made for their destruction an appointed time.﴾ He means the cities of the earlier peoples, such as Thamud, the people of Lut, and others, which He pointed to so that they might take heed. "Tilka" (those) is the subject, and "al-qura" (the cities) is an attribute, because demonstrative nouns may be described by types of kinds. "Ahlaknahum" (We destroyed them) is the predicate, and the meaning is: those are the people of the cities, We destroyed them when they did wrong, in the manner of the wrongdoing of the people of Makkah. ﴿And We made for their destruction an appointed time﴾, that is, We set for their destruction a specific time from which they would not be delayed, just as We set for the people of Makkah the Day of Badr. "Al-mahlik" means the act of destruction or its time. It was also read "limahlakihim" with a fatha on the mim and the lam either fatha or kasra, meaning for their destruction or the time of their destruction. "Al-maw'id" is either a time or a verbal noun. The meaning is: We hastened their destruction, and yet We did not refrain from setting a time for it, so that they might be closer to repentance.
