"Tilka" (those) is the subject, and "al-qura" (the cities) is an attribute, because demonstrative nouns may be described by types of kinds. "Ahlaknahum" (We destroyed them) is the predicate, and the meaning is: those are the people of the cities, We destroyed them when they did wrong, in the manner of the wrongdoing of the people of Makkah. ﴿And We made for their destruction an appointed time﴾, that is, We set for their destruction a specific time from which they would not be delayed, just as We set for the people of Makkah the Day of Badr. "Al-mahlik" means the act of destruction or its time. It was also read "limahlakihim" with a fatha on the mim and the lam either fatha or kasra, meaning for their destruction or the time of their destruction. "Al-maw'id" is either a time or a verbal noun. The meaning is: We hastened their destruction, and yet We did not refrain from setting a time for it, so that they might be closer to repentance.

[Page 121]

Know that when God, exalted is He, related the disbelievers' disputing with falsehood, He afterwards described them with attributes that necessitate disgrace and abandonment.

The first attribute: His saying, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have put forward?﴾ That is, there is no greater injustice than the disbelief of one to whom the signs and clear proofs come, so he turns away from them and forgets what his hands have put forward. That is, along with his turning away from reflecting on the proofs and clear evidences, he disregards the deeds he committed that were reprehensible and the false doctrines he held. The meaning of "forgetting" here is being preoccupied with, and neglectful of, his earlier disbelief.

The second attribute: His saying, ﴿Indeed We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears a deafness. And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever.﴾ The interpretation of this verse has already been discussed exhaustively in Surat al-An'am. What is remarkable is that His saying, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, then turns away from them and forgets what his hands have put forward﴾, is the proof-text of the Qadariyya (those who affirm human free will and responsibility), while His saying, ﴿Indeed We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it﴾ through the end of the verse, is the proof-text of the Jabriyya (those who affirm that human beings are compelled). We rarely find in the Qur'an a verse belonging to one of these two groups without another verse belonging to the other group accompanying it. Experience reveals the truth of what we say. This is nothing but a severe trial from God, the Exalted, which He placed upon His servants, so that the learned, firmly grounded scholars might be distinguished from the mere imitators.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving, the Possessor of mercy.﴾ "Al-Ghafur" (the Forgiving) is one who is abundant in forgiveness, and this points to the repelling of harms. "Dhu al-rahmah" (the Possessor of mercy) means one characterized by mercy. The intensive form was mentioned for forgiveness and not for mercy, because forgiveness is the abandonment of harm, and He, exalted is He, has abandoned harms without limit while being capable of them. As for the act of mercy, it is finite, because abandoning what has no end is possible, whereas doing what has no end is impossible. It may also be said that the meaning is that He forgives abundantly because He is the Possessor of mercy and has no need for it, so He bestows it abundantly upon those in need.

He then cited as evidence His not punishing the people of Makkah immediately, without granting respite, despite their extreme enmity toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Then He said: ﴿Rather, for them is an appointed time, and they will never find other than Him a refuge.﴾ This appointed time is either the Day of Resurrection, or in this world, and that is the Day of Badr and the rest of the days of the conquest. His saying, ﴿they will never find other than Him a refuge﴾, means a place of escape or a shelter. It is said: "wa'ala" when one seeks refuge, and "wa'ala ilayhi" when one seeks refuge with him.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And those cities — We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We made for their destruction an appointed time.﴾ He means the cities of the earlier peoples, such as Thamud, the people of Lut, and others, which He pointed to so that they might take heed. "Tilka" (those) is the subject, and "al-qura" (the cities) is an attribute, because demonstrative nouns may be described by types of kinds. "Ahlaknahum" (We destroyed them) is the predicate, and the meaning is: those are the people of the cities, We destroyed them when they did wrong, in the manner of the wrongdoing of the people of Makkah. ﴿And We made for their destruction an appointed time﴾, that is, We set for their destruction a specific time from which they would not be delayed, just as We set for the people of Makkah the Day of Badr. "Al-mahlik" means the act of destruction or its time. It was also read "limahlakihim" with a fatha on the mim and the lam either fatha or kasra, meaning for their destruction or the time of their destruction. "Al-maw'id" is either a time or a verbal noun. The meaning is: We hastened their destruction, and yet We did not refrain from setting a time for it, so that they might be closer to repentance.

[p. 122]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will continue for a long period."﴾ ﴿So when they reached the meeting place between them, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, freely.﴾ ﴿So when they had passed on, he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have certainly suffered weariness from this journey of ours."﴾ ﴿He said, "Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock, I forgot the fish; and none but Satan made me forget it, that I should mention it. And it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner."﴾ ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they returned, retracing their footsteps.﴾

Know that this is the beginning of a third story which Allah the Exalted mentions in this surah. It is that Moses, peace be upon him, went to al-Khidr, peace be upon him, in order to learn knowledge from him. Although this account is independent in itself, it serves the purpose of the two preceding stories. As for the benefit of this story in refuting the disbelievers who boasted over the poor among the Muslims by their abundance of wealth and helpers, it is that Moses, peace be upon him, despite the abundance of his knowledge and his deeds, the loftiness of his station, and his possession of all the causes of complete nobility, went to al-Khidr to seek knowledge and humbled himself before him. This indicates that humility is better than arrogance. As for the benefit of this story in relation to the story of the People of the Cave, it is that the Jews said to the Meccan disbelievers: "If Muhammad informs you about this story, then he is a prophet; otherwise he is not." This is of no consequence, because being a prophet from Allah the Exalted does not necessarily entail that one knows all stories and events. Just as Moses, peace be upon him, being a truthful prophet from Allah did not prevent Allah's command to him to go to al-Khidr in order to learn from him. It is thus evident from what we have mentioned that this story is an independent story in itself, and yet it is beneficial in establishing the purpose of the two preceding stories.

The second issue: Most scholars hold that the Moses mentioned in this verse is Moses son of Imran, the bearer of the manifest miracles and the owner of the Torah. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Nawf, the son of Ka'b's wife, claims that al-Khidr was not the companion of Moses son of Imran, but rather the companion of Moses son of Misha son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub." It was also said that he was a prophet before Moses son of Imran. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The enemy of Allah lied. Know that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had two sons, Ifra'im and Misha. Ifra'im begot Nun, and Nun begot Yusha' son of Nun, who was the companion of Moses and his successor after his death. As for the son of Misha, it was said that prophethood came to him before Moses son of Imran. The people of the Torah claim that he is the one who sought this knowledge in order to learn, and that al-Khidr is the one who tore the ship, killed the boy, and set up the wall, and Moses son of Misha was with him. This is the view of the majority of the Jews." Al-Qaffal argued for the correctness of our view that this Moses is the owner of the Torah, saying: "Allah the Exalted mentions Moses in His Book only meaning the owner of the Torah. So the unrestricted use of this name necessitates that it be understood in that sense. And if another person named Moses were intended, he would have to be identified by a description that makes him distinct and removes doubt. Just as, when the well-known figure in common usage is Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, a specific man, if we mention this name and mean another man, we would specify him, such as saying: 'Abu Hanifa al-Dinawari said.'" The argument of those who said that this Moses is not the owner of the Torah is that after Allah sent down the Torah to him, and spoke to him without an intermediary, and vindicated him against his opponents with mighty, overwhelming miracles, the like of which had not been granted to most of the great prophets, it is unlikely that He would send him afterward to learn benefit. This was answered: It is not unlikely that a scholar who is complete in most sciences would be ignorant of some matters, and therefore need to learn them from someone lesser than him, and this is a known and common matter.

The third issue: They differed concerning Moses's servant. Most held that he was Yusha' son of Nun. Al-Qaffal narrated from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, from Abu Hurayra, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "His servant is Yusha' son of Nun."

The second view is that Moses's servant was the brother of Yusha', and he was the companion of Moses, peace be upon him, on this journey.

The third view: 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd narrated from al-Hasan concerning the words of Allah: ﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease"﴾ that he said: "He means his slave." Al-Qaffal said: "The language permits this. It has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'Let none of you say "my slave (male) and my slave (female)," but let him say "my young man (fata) and my young woman (fataat)."' This indicates that they used to call a male slave a fata and a female slave a fataat."

The fourth issue: It was said that when Moses, peace be upon him, was given the tablets and Allah spoke to him, he said: "Who is more excellent than me and more knowledgeable?" It was said to him: "A servant of Allah who dwells on the islands of the sea, and he is al-Khidr." In another report: When Moses, peace be upon him, was given of knowledge what he was given, he thought that no one was like him. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him while he was on the seashore and said: "O Moses, look at this small bird that swoops down to the sea and dips its beak into it, then rises. You, in what you have been given of knowledge, are less than the amount this bird takes with its beak from the sea." The jurists of legal theory (al-usuliyyun) said: "This report is weak, because the prophets must know that the knowledge of Allah has no end, and that the knowledge of created beings must be finite. Every finite quantity admits of something greater than it, so there is no degree of knowledge except that above it there is a degree. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ When these premises are known, it is highly improbable that a rational person would be certain that there is no one more knowledgeable than himself, especially Moses, peace be upon him, given his abundant knowledge of the realities of things and his great freedom from blameworthy traits such as self-admiration, bewilderment, and arrogance."

The third report: It was said that Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord: "Which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "Which of Your servants is most just?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow desire." He said: "Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people in addition to his own knowledge, perhaps he will hear a word that guides him to guidance or turns him back from ruin." Moses, peace be upon him, said: "If among Your servants there is someone more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him." He said: "The most knowledgeable than you is al-Khidr." He said: "Where shall I seek him?" He said: "On the shore, at the rock." He said: "O Lord, how can I reach him?" He said: "Take a fish in a basket; wherever you lose it, there he is." So he said to his servant: "When you lose the fish, inform me." They set out walking, and Moses slept. The fish stirred and leapt into the sea. When the time for the morning meal came, Moses asked for the fish, and his servant informed him that it had fallen into the sea. So he returned from that place to the place where the fish had leapt into the sea, and there he found a man covered with his garment. Moses, peace be upon him, greeted him. He said: "And how is greeting in your land?" So he introduced himself to him. He said: "O Moses, I am upon a knowledge that Allah taught me which you do not know, and you are upon a knowledge that Allah taught you which I do not know." When they boarded the ship, a sparrow came and perched on its edge and pecked into the water. Al-Khidr said: "My knowledge and your knowledge do not diminish the knowledge of Allah by an amount equal to what this sparrow took from the sea." I say: The ratio of that small quantity which the sparrow took from that water to the entirety of the sea's water is the ratio of a finite to a finite, while the ratio of the knowledge of all created beings to the knowledge of Allah the Exalted is the ratio of a finite to an infinite. Where is one of these two ratios from the other?

[p. 124]

And Allah knows the realities of matters best. Let us return to the exegesis. As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿I will not cease﴾, al-Zajjaj said: "His words ﴿I will not cease﴾ do not mean 'I will not depart,' for if that were so he would not have traversed any land." I say: It is possible to answer this by saying that ceasing from something means abandoning it and turning away from it. It is said: "So-and-so ceased (zala) from his path in generosity," meaning he abandoned it. So his words "I will not cease" mean "I will not cease from journeying and going," that is, "I will not abandon this action and this deed." I say: The well-known view among the majority is that his words "I will not cease" mean "I will not depart." The Arabs say: "I will not cease (la abrah), I will not stop (la azal), I will not leave off (la anfakk), and I will not fail (la aftu')," all with one meaning. Al-Qaffal said: "They said: the origin of their saying 'la abrah' is from al-barah (open space, clearing), just as the origin of 'la azal' is from al-zawal (ceasing). It is said: zala yazal and yazul, just as it is said: dama yadam and yadum, and mata yamat and yamut. Except that the form used with this word is yazal. So his words 'la abrah' mean 'I will remain,' because al-barah is non-existence; thus 'la abrah' is the negation of non-existence, and therefore it is an affirmation. So his words 'la azal wa la abrah' indicate continuity and steadfastness in the action." If it is asked: If his words "la abrah" mean "la azal," then there must be a predicate; we answer: the predicate is omitted because the situation and the discourse both indicate it. As for the situation, it was a situation of journeying. As for the discourse, his words "until I reach the meeting place of the two seas" are a set limit which requires something of which it is the limit. So the meaning is: "I will not cease traveling until I reach the meeting place of the two seas." It is also possible that the meaning is: "I will not cease from what I am upon, that is, I will hold firmly to the journey and the quest and will not abandon or leave it until I reach," just as you say: "I will not leave the place." As for the meeting place of the two seas, it is the place where Moses was promised a meeting with al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. It is the confluence of the Persian and Byzantine seas on the eastern side. It has been said to be other than this, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates the identification of these two seas. If something is established by a sound report, then so be it; otherwise it is preferable to remain silent about it. Some people said: "The two seas are Moses and al-Khidr, because they were two seas of knowledge." It is also read "mijma'a" with a kasra on the mim. Then He said: ﴿or I will continue for a long period﴾, that is, I will travel for a long time. It was said: a huqb (period) is eighty years. We have discussed this term in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (ahqaban)﴾ (al-Naba' 23). The essence of the matter is this: Allah, mighty and majestic, had informed Moses of the state of this scholar, but had not informed him of the exact location. So Moses, peace be upon him, said: "I will continue on until the two seas join and become one sea, or I will continue for a long time until I find this scholar." This is an announcement from Moses that he had prepared himself to endure severe fatigue and great hardship in travel for the sake of seeking knowledge. This is an indication that if a student traveled from the east to the west for the sake of a single question, that would be justified for him.

Then He said: ﴿So when they reached the meeting place between them﴾. The meaning is: they set out until they reached the meeting place between them. Regarding the pronoun in his words "between them," to what does it refer? There are two views:

The first: "the meeting place between them" means the meeting place of the two seas, and this seems to be an allusion to the words of Moses: ﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾; that is, Allah fulfilled what he had said.

The second view: the meaning is that they reached the place where Moses and his companion, whom he was seeking, would meet. For that place where the forgetting of the fish occurred is the place where al-Khidr lived or lived nearby. And for this reason, when Moses and his servant returned after remembering the fish, they came to it, and this is a good meaning. The exegetes follow the first view.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They forgot their fish﴾, and concerning this there are several discussions:

[Page 125]

**Discussion 1:** The narrations indicate that God informed Musa, peace be upon him, that this scholar's place was the meeting point of the two seas. However, God made the fish's coming back to life a sign of his specific dwelling. This is like someone seeking a person and being told: "His place is such-and-such a quarter in al-Rayy. When you reach that quarter, ask so-and-so about his house. Wherever he takes you, follow him, and you will reach him." Similarly here, it was said to him: "His place is the meeting point of the two seas. When you arrive there, you will see the fish come back to life and leap into the sea." It is possible that he was told: "There is where his place is." It is also possible that he was told: "Go in accordance with the fish's going, and you will find him."

Having understood this, we say: When Musa and his servant reached the meeting point of the two, the fish leapt into the sea and moved away. There are also narrations about how it leapt. It was said that the young man was washing the fish, because it had been salted, and it leapt and moved away. It was said that Yusha' performed ablution at that place, so water splashed onto the salted fish, and it came to life and leapt into the water. It was also said that a spring from Paradise burst forth there, and drops from that spring reached the fish, so it came to life and leapt into the sea. This is what is said about the description of the fish.

**Discussion 2:** The meaning of God's words ﴿they forgot their fish﴾ is that they forgot how to use this特殊 circumstance as evidence for reaching the sought goal. If it is objected: the salted fish returning to life is an astonishing condition, so since God made the occurrence of this astonishing condition a sign of reaching the sought goal, how can forgetting in this respect be conceived? The scholars answered that Yusha' had witnessed many overpowering miracles from Musa, peace be upon him, so this miracle no longer had a great impact on him, and therefore forgetting was permissible. I have another answer regarding this: when Musa, peace be upon him, regarded his own knowledge as great, God removed this necessary knowledge from the heart of his companion, as a reminder to Musa, peace be upon him, that knowledge is only attained through God's teaching and His preserving it upon the heart and the mind.

As for His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea, making a tunnel﴾, there are several views:

The first: the intended sense is: it moved in the sea, moving [in a tunnel]. But the verb "fa-ittakhadha" (it took) was placed in the position of "sariba" (it moved). Al-sarab means going, and from it is His words ﴿and one who goes freely by day﴾ (Al-Ra'd: 10).

The second: God stopped the flow of water over the sea and made it like an arch and a window, until the fish moved within it. When Musa and his servant passed the appointed place, which is reaching the rock, because of the forgetting mentioned, and they went far, became weary and hungry, ﴿he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered much fatigue from this journey of ours"﴾. ﴿He said﴾, the servant: ﴿"Do you see? When we took refuge at the rock"﴾. The hamza in "ara'ayta" is the interrogative hamza, and "ra'ayta" is in its original meaning. This speech came in the manner customary among people: when something astonishing happens to one of them, he says to his companion: "Did you see what happened to me?" Likewise here, it is as if he said: "Did you see what happened to me from it when we took refuge at the rock?" So the object of "ara'ayta" is omitted, because His words ﴿"Indeed I forgot the fish"﴾ indicate it. Then He said: ﴿"And none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it"﴾. There are discussions regarding this:

Discussion 1: This is a parenthetical clause that came between the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to. The construction is: "Indeed I forgot the fish, and it took its way into the sea astonishingly." The reason for this parenthetical clause is what serves as an excuse and cause for that forgetting.

Discussion 2: Al-Ka'bi said: His words ﴿"And none caused me to forget it except Satan"﴾ indicate that God did not create that forgetting and did not will it; otherwise, attributing it to God would be more fitting than attributing it to Satan, because if God created it in him, Satan's effort would have no effect on its existence or non-existence. Al-Qadi said: What is meant by forgetting is that a person's heart becomes occupied with his whisperings, which are from his own actions, rather than the forgetting that is contrary to remembrance, because that cannot be except from God, exalted is He.

Discussion 3: His words "an adhkurahu" (that I should mention it) are a substitution for the pronoun "-hu" in "ansanihi"; that is, "none caused me to forget its remembrance except Satan." Then He said: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, astonishingly﴾. There are several views regarding this:

The first: His words "ajaban" (astonishingly) are an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. It is as if it were said: "and it took its way into the sea in an astonishing manner." The reason it was astonishing is its transformation from the basket, its becoming alive, and its casting itself into the sea while they were heedless.

The second: What is meant by it is what we mentioned, that God made the water over it like an arch and like a passage.

The third: It was said that the speech was complete at His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea﴾, and then He said after it "ajaban" (astonishingly), and what is meant is his astonishment at that wonder which he saw, and at his forgetting of it. It was also said that His words "ajaban" are a report of Musa's astonishment, and it is not his own speech.

[Page 126]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking."﴾ That is, Musa said: "That is what we were seeking," because it was a sign of success in attaining the sought goal, which is meeting Khidr. The word "nabgh" originally was "nabghi," so the yā' was dropped for lightness, the kasra indicating it. Analogically it should not be dropped, because they only drop the yā' in nouns, and this is a verb. However, it is permissible, though analogically weak, to drop it, because it is dropped with a following sukūn, as in your saying: "What do we seek today?" Since it is dropped before the sukūn, it is also dropped before what is not a sukūn.

Then He said: ﴿so they went back, retracing their footsteps﴾, that is, they returned. His words ﴿qasasan﴾ (retracing) have two views:

One: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial, meaning they returned upon their traces, tracing their traces.

Two: it is a verbal noun for His words "fartadda 'ala athariha" (they went back, retracing their footsteps), because its meaning is "they followed their traces."

The summary of the speech: when they realized that they had passed beyond the place where that scholar dwelt, they turned back and returned to it. And God knows best.

[p. 122]

The argument of those who said that this Moses is not the owner of the Torah is that after Allah sent down the Torah to him, and spoke to him without an intermediary, and vindicated him against his opponents with mighty, overwhelming miracles, the like of which had not been granted to most of the great prophets, it is unlikely that He would send him afterward to learn benefit. This was answered: It is not unlikely that a scholar who is complete in most sciences would be ignorant of some matters, and therefore need to learn them from someone lesser than him, and this is a known and common matter.

The third issue: They differed concerning Moses's servant. Most held that he was Yusha' son of Nun. Al-Qaffal narrated from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, from Abu Hurayra, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "His servant is Yusha' son of Nun."

The second view is that Moses's servant was the brother of Yusha', and he was the companion of Moses, peace be upon him, on this journey.

The third view: 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd narrated from al-Hasan concerning the words of Allah: ﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease"﴾ that he said: "He means his slave." Al-Qaffal said: "The language permits this. It has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'Let none of you say "my slave (male) and my slave (female)," but let him say "my young man (fata) and my young woman (fataat)."' This indicates that they used to call a male slave a fata and a female slave a fataat."

The fourth issue: It was said that when Moses, peace be upon him, was given the tablets and Allah spoke to him, he said: "Who is more excellent than me and more knowledgeable?" It was said to him: "A servant of Allah who dwells on the islands of the sea, and he is al-Khidr." In another report: When Moses, peace be upon him, was given of knowledge what he was given, he thought that no one was like him. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him while he was on the seashore and said: "O Moses, look at this small bird that swoops down to the sea and dips its beak into it, then rises. You, in what you have been given of knowledge, are less than the amount this bird takes with its beak from the sea." The jurists of legal theory (al-usuliyyun) said: "This report is weak, because the prophets must know that the knowledge of Allah has no end, and that the knowledge of created beings must be finite. Every finite quantity admits of something greater than it, so there is no degree of knowledge except that above it there is a degree. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ When these premises are known, it is highly improbable that a rational person would be certain that there is no one more knowledgeable than himself, especially Moses, peace be upon him, given his abundant knowledge of the realities of things and his great freedom from blameworthy traits such as self-admiration, bewilderment, and arrogance."

The third report: It was said that Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord: "Which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "Which of Your servants is most just?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow desire." He said: "Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people in addition to his own knowledge, perhaps he will hear a word that guides him to guidance or turns him back from ruin." Moses, peace be upon him, said: "If among Your servants there is someone more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him." He said: "The most knowledgeable than you is al-Khidr." He said: "Where shall I seek him?" He said: "On the shore, at the rock." He said: "O Lord, how can I reach him?" He said: "Take a fish in a basket; wherever you lose it, there he is." So he said to his servant: "When you lose the fish, inform me." They set out walking, and Moses slept. The fish stirred and leapt into the sea. When the time for the morning meal came, Moses asked for the fish, and his servant informed him that it had fallen into the sea. So he returned from that place to the place where the fish had leapt into the sea, and there he found a man covered with his garment. Moses, peace be upon him, greeted him. He said: "And how is greeting in your land?" So he introduced himself to him. He said: "O Moses, I am upon a knowledge that Allah taught me which you do not know, and you are upon a knowledge that Allah taught you which I do not know." When they boarded the ship, a sparrow came and perched on its edge and pecked into the water. Al-Khidr said: "My knowledge and your knowledge do not diminish the knowledge of Allah by an amount equal to what this sparrow took from the sea." I say: The ratio of that small quantity which the sparrow took from that water to the entirety of the sea's water is the ratio of a finite to a finite, while the ratio of the knowledge of all created beings to the knowledge of Allah the Exalted is the ratio of a finite to an infinite. Where is one of these two ratios from the other?

[p. 124]

And Allah knows the realities of matters best. Let us return to the exegesis. As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿I will not cease﴾, al-Zajjaj said: "His words ﴿I will not cease﴾ do not mean 'I will not depart,' for if that were so he would not have traversed any land." I say: It is possible to answer this by saying that ceasing from something means abandoning it and turning away from it. It is said: "So-and-so ceased (zala) from his path in generosity," meaning he abandoned it. So his words "I will not cease" mean "I will not cease from journeying and going," that is, "I will not abandon this action and this deed." I say: The well-known view among the majority is that his words "I will not cease" mean "I will not depart." The Arabs say: "I will not cease (la abrah), I will not stop (la azal), I will not leave off (la anfakk), and I will not fail (la aftu')," all with one meaning. Al-Qaffal said: "They said: the origin of their saying 'la abrah' is from al-barah (open space, clearing), just as the origin of 'la azal' is from al-zawal (ceasing). It is said: zala yazal and yazul, just as it is said: dama yadam and yadum, and mata yamat and yamut. Except that the form used with this word is yazal. So his words 'la abrah' mean 'I will remain,' because al-barah is non-existence; thus 'la abrah' is the negation of non-existence, and therefore it is an affirmation. So his words 'la azal wa la abrah' indicate continuity and steadfastness in the action." If it is asked: If his words "la abrah" mean "la azal," then there must be a predicate; we answer: the predicate is omitted because the situation and the discourse both indicate it. As for the situation, it was a situation of journeying. As for the discourse, his words "until I reach the meeting place of the two seas" are a set limit which requires something of which it is the limit. So the meaning is: "I will not cease traveling until I reach the meeting place of the two seas." It is also possible that the meaning is: "I will not cease from what I am upon, that is, I will hold firmly to the journey and the quest and will not abandon or leave it until I reach," just as you say: "I will not leave the place." As for the meeting place of the two seas, it is the place where Moses was promised a meeting with al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. It is the confluence of the Persian and Byzantine seas on the eastern side. It has been said to be other than this, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates the identification of these two seas. If something is established by a sound report, then so be it; otherwise it is preferable to remain silent about it. Some people said: "The two seas are Moses and al-Khidr, because they were two seas of knowledge." It is also read "mijma'a" with a kasra on the mim. Then He said: ﴿or I will continue for a long period﴾, that is, I will travel for a long time. It was said: a huqb (period) is eighty years. We have discussed this term in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (ahqaban)﴾ (al-Naba' 23). The essence of the matter is this: Allah, mighty and majestic, had informed Moses of the state of this scholar, but had not informed him of the exact location. So Moses, peace be upon him, said: "I will continue on until the two seas join and become one sea, or I will continue for a long time until I find this scholar." This is an announcement from Moses that he had prepared himself to endure severe fatigue and great hardship in travel for the sake of seeking knowledge. This is an indication that if a student traveled from the east to the west for the sake of a single question, that would be justified for him.

Then He said: ﴿So when they reached the meeting place between them﴾. The meaning is: they set out until they reached the meeting place between them. Regarding the pronoun in his words "between them," to what does it refer? There are two views:

The first: "the meeting place between them" means the meeting place of the two seas, and this seems to be an allusion to the words of Moses: ﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾; that is, Allah fulfilled what he had said.

The second view: the meaning is that they reached the place where Moses and his companion, whom he was seeking, would meet. For that place where the forgetting of the fish occurred is the place where al-Khidr lived or lived nearby. And for this reason, when Moses and his servant returned after remembering the fish, they came to it, and this is a good meaning. The exegetes follow the first view.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They forgot their fish﴾, and concerning this there are several discussions:

[Page 125]

**Discussion 1:** The narrations indicate that God informed Musa, peace be upon him, that this scholar's place was the meeting point of the two seas. However, God made the fish's coming back to life a sign of his specific dwelling. This is like someone seeking a person and being told: "His place is such-and-such a quarter in al-Rayy. When you reach that quarter, ask so-and-so about his house. Wherever he takes you, follow him, and you will reach him." Similarly here, it was said to him: "His place is the meeting point of the two seas. When you arrive there, you will see the fish come back to life and leap into the sea." It is possible that he was told: "There is where his place is." It is also possible that he was told: "Go in accordance with the fish's going, and you will find him."

Having understood this, we say: When Musa and his servant reached the meeting point of the two, the fish leapt into the sea and moved away. There are also narrations about how it leapt. It was said that the young man was washing the fish, because it had been salted, and it leapt and moved away. It was said that Yusha' performed ablution at that place, so water splashed onto the salted fish, and it came to life and leapt into the water. It was also said that a spring from Paradise burst forth there, and drops from that spring reached the fish, so it came to life and leapt into the sea. This is what is said about the description of the fish.

**Discussion 2:** The meaning of God's words ﴿they forgot their fish﴾ is that they forgot how to use this特殊 circumstance as evidence for reaching the sought goal. If it is objected: the salted fish returning to life is an astonishing condition, so since God made the occurrence of this astonishing condition a sign of reaching the sought goal, how can forgetting in this respect be conceived? The scholars answered that Yusha' had witnessed many overpowering miracles from Musa, peace be upon him, so this miracle no longer had a great impact on him, and therefore forgetting was permissible. I have another answer regarding this: when Musa, peace be upon him, regarded his own knowledge as great, God removed this necessary knowledge from the heart of his companion, as a reminder to Musa, peace be upon him, that knowledge is only attained through God's teaching and His preserving it upon the heart and the mind.

As for His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea, making a tunnel﴾, there are several views:

The first: the intended sense is: it moved in the sea, moving [in a tunnel]. But the verb "fa-ittakhadha" (it took) was placed in the position of "sariba" (it moved). Al-sarab means going, and from it is His words ﴿and one who goes freely by day﴾ (Al-Ra'd: 10).

The second: God stopped the flow of water over the sea and made it like an arch and a window, until the fish moved within it. When Musa and his servant passed the appointed place, which is reaching the rock, because of the forgetting mentioned, and they went far, became weary and hungry, ﴿he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered much fatigue from this journey of ours"﴾. ﴿He said﴾, the servant: ﴿"Do you see? When we took refuge at the rock"﴾. The hamza in "ara'ayta" is the interrogative hamza, and "ra'ayta" is in its original meaning. This speech came in the manner customary among people: when something astonishing happens to one of them, he says to his companion: "Did you see what happened to me?" Likewise here, it is as if he said: "Did you see what happened to me from it when we took refuge at the rock?" So the object of "ara'ayta" is omitted, because His words ﴿"Indeed I forgot the fish"﴾ indicate it. Then He said: ﴿"And none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it"﴾. There are discussions regarding this:

Discussion 1: This is a parenthetical clause that came between the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to. The construction is: "Indeed I forgot the fish, and it took its way into the sea astonishingly." The reason for this parenthetical clause is what serves as an excuse and cause for that forgetting.

Discussion 2: Al-Ka'bi said: His words ﴿"And none caused me to forget it except Satan"﴾ indicate that God did not create that forgetting and did not will it; otherwise, attributing it to God would be more fitting than attributing it to Satan, because if God created it in him, Satan's effort would have no effect on its existence or non-existence. Al-Qadi said: What is meant by forgetting is that a person's heart becomes occupied with his whisperings, which are from his own actions, rather than the forgetting that is contrary to remembrance, because that cannot be except from God, exalted is He.

Discussion 3: His words "an adhkurahu" (that I should mention it) are a substitution for the pronoun "-hu" in "ansanihi"; that is, "none caused me to forget its remembrance except Satan." Then He said: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, astonishingly﴾. There are several views regarding this:

The first: His words "ajaban" (astonishingly) are an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. It is as if it were said: "and it took its way into the sea in an astonishing manner." The reason it was astonishing is its transformation from the basket, its becoming alive, and its casting itself into the sea while they were heedless.

The second: What is meant by it is what we mentioned, that God made the water over it like an arch and like a passage.

The third: It was said that the speech was complete at His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea﴾, and then He said after it "ajaban" (astonishingly), and what is meant is his astonishment at that wonder which he saw, and at his forgetting of it. It was also said that His words "ajaban" are a report of Musa's astonishment, and it is not his own speech.

[Page 126]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking."﴾ That is, Musa said: "That is what we were seeking," because it was a sign of success in attaining the sought goal, which is meeting Khidr. The word "nabgh" originally was "nabghi," so the yā' was dropped for lightness, the kasra indicating it. Analogically it should not be dropped, because they only drop the yā' in nouns, and this is a verb. However, it is permissible, though analogically weak, to drop it, because it is dropped with a following sukūn, as in your saying: "What do we seek today?" Since it is dropped before the sukūn, it is also dropped before what is not a sukūn.

Then He said: ﴿so they went back, retracing their footsteps﴾, that is, they returned. His words ﴿qasasan﴾ (retracing) have two views:

One: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial, meaning they returned upon their traces, tracing their traces.

Two: it is a verbal noun for His words "fartadda 'ala athariha" (they went back, retracing their footsteps), because its meaning is "they followed their traces."

The summary of the speech: when they realized that they had passed beyond the place where that scholar dwelt, they turned back and returned to it. And God knows best.

[p. 122]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will continue for a long period."﴾ ﴿So when they reached the meeting place between them, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, freely.﴾ ﴿So when they had passed on, he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have certainly suffered weariness from this journey of ours."﴾ ﴿He said, "Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock, I forgot the fish; and none but Satan made me forget it, that I should mention it. And it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner."﴾ ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they returned, retracing their footsteps.﴾

Know that this is the beginning of a third story which Allah the Exalted mentions in this surah. It is that Moses, peace be upon him, went to al-Khidr, peace be upon him, in order to learn knowledge from him. Although this account is independent in itself, it serves the purpose of the two preceding stories. As for the benefit of this story in refuting the disbelievers who boasted over the poor among the Muslims by their abundance of wealth and helpers, it is that Moses, peace be upon him, despite the abundance of his knowledge and his deeds, the loftiness of his station, and his possession of all the causes of complete nobility, went to al-Khidr to seek knowledge and humbled himself before him. This indicates that humility is better than arrogance. As for the benefit of this story in relation to the story of the People of the Cave, it is that the Jews said to the Meccan disbelievers: "If Muhammad informs you about this story, then he is a prophet; otherwise he is not." This is of no consequence, because being a prophet from Allah the Exalted does not necessarily entail that one knows all stories and events. Just as Moses, peace be upon him, being a truthful prophet from Allah did not prevent Allah's command to him to go to al-Khidr in order to learn from him. It is thus evident from what we have mentioned that this story is an independent story in itself, and yet it is beneficial in establishing the purpose of the two preceding stories.

The second issue: Most scholars hold that the Moses mentioned in this verse is Moses son of Imran, the bearer of the manifest miracles and the owner of the Torah. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Nawf, the son of Ka'b's wife, claims that al-Khidr was not the companion of Moses son of Imran, but rather the companion of Moses son of Misha son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub." It was also said that he was a prophet before Moses son of Imran. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The enemy of Allah lied. Know that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had two sons, Ifra'im and Misha. Ifra'im begot Nun, and Nun begot Yusha' son of Nun, who was the companion of Moses and his successor after his death. As for the son of Misha, it was said that prophethood came to him before Moses son of Imran. The people of the Torah claim that he is the one who sought this knowledge in order to learn, and that al-Khidr is the one who tore the ship, killed the boy, and set up the wall, and Moses son of Misha was with him. This is the view of the majority of the Jews." Al-Qaffal argued for the correctness of our view that this Moses is the owner of the Torah, saying: "Allah the Exalted mentions Moses in His Book only meaning the owner of the Torah. So the unrestricted use of this name necessitates that it be understood in that sense. And if another person named Moses were intended, he would have to be identified by a description that makes him distinct and removes doubt. Just as, when the well-known figure in common usage is Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, a specific man, if we mention this name and mean another man, we would specify him, such as saying: 'Abu Hanifa al-Dinawari said.'" The argument of those who said that this Moses is not the owner of the Torah is that after Allah sent down the Torah to him, and spoke to him without an intermediary, and vindicated him against his opponents with mighty, overwhelming miracles, the like of which had not been granted to most of the great prophets, it is unlikely that He would send him afterward to learn benefit. However, God made the fish's coming back to life a sign of his specific dwelling. This is like someone seeking a person and being told: "His place is such-and-such a quarter in al-Rayy. When you reach that quarter, ask so-and-so about his house. Wherever he takes you, follow him, and you will reach him." Similarly here, it was said to him: "His place is the meeting point of the two seas. When you arrive there, you will see the fish come back to life and leap into the sea." It is possible that he was told: "There is where his place is." It is also possible that he was told: "Go in accordance with the fish's going, and you will find him."

Having understood this, we say: When Musa and his servant reached the meeting point of the two, the fish leapt into the sea and moved away. There are also narrations about how it leapt. It was said that the young man was washing the fish, because it had been salted, and it leapt and moved away. It was said that Yusha' performed ablution at that place, so water splashed onto the salted fish, and it came to life and leapt into the water. It was also said that a spring from Paradise burst forth there, and drops from that spring reached the fish, so it came to life and leapt into the sea. This is what is said about the description of the fish.

**Discussion 2:** The meaning of God's words ﴿they forgot their fish﴾ is that they forgot how to use this特殊 circumstance as evidence for reaching the sought goal. If it is objected: the salted fish returning to life is an astonishing condition, so since God made the occurrence of this astonishing condition a sign of reaching the sought goal, how can forgetting in this respect be conceived? The scholars answered that Yusha' had witnessed many overpowering miracles from Musa, peace be upon him, so this miracle no longer had a great impact on him, and therefore forgetting was permissible. I have another answer regarding this: when Musa, peace be upon him, regarded his own knowledge as great, God removed this necessary knowledge from the heart of his companion, as a reminder to Musa, peace be upon him, that knowledge is only attained through God's teaching and His preserving it upon the heart and the mind.

As for His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea, making a tunnel﴾, there are several views:

The first: the intended sense is: it moved in the sea, moving [in a tunnel]. But the verb "fa-ittakhadha" (it took) was placed in the position of "sariba" (it moved). Al-sarab means going, and from it is His words ﴿and one who goes freely by day﴾ (Al-Ra'd: 10).

The second: God stopped the flow of water over the sea and made it like an arch and a window, until the fish moved within it. When Musa and his servant passed the appointed place, which is reaching the rock, because of the forgetting mentioned, and they went far, became weary and hungry, ﴿he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered much fatigue from this journey of ours"﴾. ﴿He said﴾, the servant: ﴿"Do you see? When we took refuge at the rock"﴾. The hamza in "ara'ayta" is the interrogative hamza, and "ra'ayta" is in its original meaning. This speech came in the manner customary among people: when something astonishing happens to one of them, he says to his companion: "Did you see what happened to me?" Likewise here, it is as if he said: "Did you see what happened to me from it when we took refuge at the rock?" So the object of "ara'ayta" is omitted, because His words ﴿"Indeed I forgot the fish"﴾ indicate it. Then He said: ﴿"And none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it"﴾. There are discussions regarding this:

Discussion 1: This is a parenthetical clause that came between the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to. The construction is: "Indeed I forgot the fish, and it took its way into the sea astonishingly." The reason for this parenthetical clause is what serves as an excuse and cause for that forgetting.

Discussion 2: Al-Ka'bi said: His words ﴿"And none caused me to forget it except Satan"﴾ indicate that God did not create that forgetting and did not will it; otherwise, attributing it to God would be more fitting than attributing it to Satan, because if God created it in him, Satan's effort would have no effect on its existence or non-existence. Al-Qadi said: What is meant by forgetting is that a person's heart becomes occupied with his whisperings, which are from his own actions, rather than the forgetting that is contrary to remembrance, because that cannot be except from God, exalted is He.

Discussion 3: His words "an adhkurahu" (that I should mention it) are a substitution for the pronoun "-hu" in "ansanihi"; that is, "none caused me to forget its remembrance except Satan." Then He said: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, astonishingly﴾. There are several views regarding this:

The first: His words "ajaban" (astonishingly) are an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. It is as if it were said: "and it took its way into the sea in an astonishing manner." The reason it was astonishing is its transformation from the basket, its becoming alive, and its casting itself into the sea while they were heedless.

The second: What is meant by it is what we mentioned, that God made the water over it like an arch and like a passage.

The third: It was said that the speech was complete at His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea﴾, and then He said after it "ajaban" (astonishingly), and what is meant is his astonishment at that wonder which he saw, and at his forgetting of it. It was also said that His words "ajaban" are a report of Musa's astonishment, and it is not his own speech.

[Page 126]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking."﴾ That is, Musa said: "That is what we were seeking," because it was a sign of success in attaining the sought goal, which is meeting Khidr. The word "nabgh" originally was "nabghi," so the yā' was dropped for lightness, the kasra indicating it. Analogically it should not be dropped, because they only drop the yā' in nouns, and this is a verb. However, it is permissible, though analogically weak, to drop it, because it is dropped with a following sukūn, as in your saying: "What do we seek today?" Since it is dropped before the sukūn, it is also dropped before what is not a sukūn.

Then He said: ﴿so they went back, retracing their footsteps﴾, that is, they returned. His words ﴿qasasan﴾ (retracing) have two views:

One: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial, meaning they returned upon their traces, tracing their traces.

Two: it is a verbal noun for His words "fartadda 'ala athariha" (they went back, retracing their footsteps), because its meaning is "they followed their traces."

The summary of the speech: when they realized that they had passed beyond the place where that scholar dwelt, they turned back and returned to it. And God knows best.

[p. 122]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas, or I will continue for a long period."﴾ ﴿So when they reached the meeting place between them, they forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, freely.﴾ ﴿So when they had passed on, he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have certainly suffered weariness from this journey of ours."﴾ ﴿He said, "Did you see? When we took refuge at the rock, I forgot the fish; and none but Satan made me forget it, that I should mention it. And it took its way into the sea in a wondrous manner."﴾ ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking." So they returned, retracing their footsteps.﴾

Know that this is the beginning of a third story which Allah the Exalted mentions in this surah. It is that Moses, peace be upon him, went to al-Khidr, peace be upon him, in order to learn knowledge from him. Although this account is independent in itself, it serves the purpose of the two preceding stories. As for the benefit of this story in refuting the disbelievers who boasted over the poor among the Muslims by their abundance of wealth and helpers, it is that Moses, peace be upon him, despite the abundance of his knowledge and his deeds, the loftiness of his station, and his possession of all the causes of complete nobility, went to al-Khidr to seek knowledge and humbled himself before him. This indicates that humility is better than arrogance. As for the benefit of this story in relation to the story of the People of the Cave, it is that the Jews said to the Meccan disbelievers: "If Muhammad informs you about this story, then he is a prophet; otherwise he is not." This is of no consequence, because being a prophet from Allah the Exalted does not necessarily entail that one knows all stories and events. Just as Moses, peace be upon him, being a truthful prophet from Allah did not prevent Allah's command to him to go to al-Khidr in order to learn from him. It is thus evident from what we have mentioned that this story is an independent story in itself, and yet it is beneficial in establishing the purpose of the two preceding stories.

The second issue: Most scholars hold that the Moses mentioned in this verse is Moses son of Imran, the bearer of the manifest miracles and the owner of the Torah. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Nawf, the son of Ka'b's wife, claims that al-Khidr was not the companion of Moses son of Imran, but rather the companion of Moses son of Misha son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub." It was also said that he was a prophet before Moses son of Imran. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The enemy of Allah lied. Know that Yusuf, peace be upon him, had two sons, Ifra'im and Misha. Ifra'im begot Nun, and Nun begot Yusha' son of Nun, who was the companion of Moses and his successor after his death. As for the son of Misha, it was said that prophethood came to him before Moses son of Imran. The people of the Torah claim that he is the one who sought this knowledge in order to learn, and that al-Khidr is the one who tore the ship, killed the boy, and set up the wall, and Moses son of Misha was with him. This is the view of the majority of the Jews." Al-Qaffal argued for the correctness of our view that this Moses is the owner of the Torah, saying: "Allah the Exalted mentions Moses in His Book only meaning the owner of the Torah. So the unrestricted use of this name necessitates that it be understood in that sense. And if another person named Moses were intended, he would have to be identified by a description that makes him distinct and removes doubt. Just as, when the well-known figure in common usage is Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, a specific man, if we mention this name and mean another man, we would specify him, such as saying: 'Abu Hanifa al-Dinawari said.'" The argument of those who said that this Moses is not the owner of the Torah is that after Allah sent down the Torah to him, and spoke to him without an intermediary, and vindicated him against his opponents with mighty, overwhelming miracles, the like of which had not been granted to most of the great prophets, it is unlikely that He would send him afterward to learn benefit. This was answered: It is not unlikely that a scholar who is complete in most sciences would be ignorant of some matters, and therefore need to learn them from someone lesser than him, and this is a known and common matter.

The third issue: They differed concerning Moses's servant. Most held that he was Yusha' son of Nun. Al-Qaffal narrated from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, from Abu Hurayra, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "His servant is Yusha' son of Nun."

The second view is that Moses's servant was the brother of Yusha', and he was the companion of Moses, peace be upon him, on this journey.

The third view: 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd narrated from al-Hasan concerning the words of Allah: ﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease"﴾ that he said: "He means his slave." Al-Qaffal said: "The language permits this. It has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'Let none of you say "my slave (male) and my slave (female)," but let him say "my young man (fata) and my young woman (fataat)."' This indicates that they used to call a male slave a fata and a female slave a fataat."

The fourth issue: It was said that when Moses, peace be upon him, was given the tablets and Allah spoke to him, he said: "Who is more excellent than me and more knowledgeable?" It was said to him: "A servant of Allah who dwells on the islands of the sea, and he is al-Khidr." In another report: When Moses, peace be upon him, was given of knowledge what he was given, he thought that no one was like him. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him while he was on the seashore and said: "O Moses, look at this small bird that swoops down to the sea and dips its beak into it, then rises. You, in what you have been given of knowledge, are less than the amount this bird takes with its beak from the sea." The jurists of legal theory (al-usuliyyun) said: "This report is weak, because the prophets must know that the knowledge of Allah has no end, and that the knowledge of created beings must be finite. Every finite quantity admits of something greater than it, so there is no degree of knowledge except that above it there is a degree. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ When these premises are known, it is highly improbable that a rational person would be certain that there is no one more knowledgeable than himself, especially Moses, peace be upon him, given his abundant knowledge of the realities of things and his great freedom from blameworthy traits such as self-admiration, bewilderment, and arrogance."

The third report: It was said that Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord: "Which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "Which of Your servants is most just?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow desire." He said: "Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people in addition to his own knowledge, perhaps he will hear a word that guides him to guidance or turns him back from ruin." Moses, peace be upon him, said: "If among Your servants there is someone more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him." He said: "The most knowledgeable than you is al-Khidr." He said: "Where shall I seek him?" He said: "On the shore, at the rock." He said: "O Lord, how can I reach him?" He said: "Take a fish in a basket; wherever you lose it, there he is." So he said to his servant: "When you lose the fish, inform me." They set out walking, and Moses slept. The fish stirred and leapt into the sea. When the time for the morning meal came, Moses asked for the fish, and his servant informed him that it had fallen into the sea. So he returned from that place to the place where the fish had leapt into the sea, and there he found a man covered with his garment. Moses, peace be upon him, greeted him. He said: "And how is greeting in your land?" So he introduced himself to him. He said: "O Moses, I am upon a knowledge that Allah taught me which you do not know, and you are upon a knowledge that Allah taught you which I do not know." When they boarded the ship, a sparrow came and perched on its edge and pecked into the water. Al-Khidr said: "My knowledge and your knowledge do not diminish the knowledge of Allah by an amount equal to what this sparrow took from the sea." I say: The ratio of that small quantity which the sparrow took from that water to the entirety of the sea's water is the ratio of a finite to a finite, while the ratio of the knowledge of all created beings to the knowledge of Allah the Exalted is the ratio of a finite to an infinite. Where is one of these two ratios from the other?

[p. 124]

And Allah knows the realities of matters best. Let us return to the exegesis. As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿I will not cease﴾, al-Zajjaj said: "His words ﴿I will not cease﴾ do not mean 'I will not depart,' for if that were so he would not have traversed any land." I say: It is possible to answer this by saying that ceasing from something means abandoning it and turning away from it. It is said: "So-and-so ceased (zala) from his path in generosity," meaning he abandoned it. So his words "I will not cease" mean "I will not cease from journeying and going," that is, "I will not abandon this action and this deed." I say: The well-known view among the majority is that his words "I will not cease" mean "I will not depart." The Arabs say: "I will not cease (la abrah), I will not stop (la azal), I will not leave off (la anfakk), and I will not fail (la aftu')," all with one meaning. Al-Qaffal said: "They said: the origin of their saying 'la abrah' is from al-barah (open space, clearing), just as the origin of 'la azal' is from al-zawal (ceasing). It is said: zala yazal and yazul, just as it is said: dama yadam and yadum, and mata yamat and yamut. Except that the form used with this word is yazal. So his words 'la abrah' mean 'I will remain,' because al-barah is non-existence; thus 'la abrah' is the negation of non-existence, and therefore it is an affirmation. So his words 'la azal wa la abrah' indicate continuity and steadfastness in the action." If it is asked: If his words "la abrah" mean "la azal," then there must be a predicate; we answer: the predicate is omitted because the situation and the discourse both indicate it. As for the situation, it was a situation of journeying. As for the discourse, his words "until I reach the meeting place of the two seas" are a set limit which requires something of which it is the limit. So the meaning is: "I will not cease traveling until I reach the meeting place of the two seas." It is also possible that the meaning is: "I will not cease from what I am upon, that is, I will hold firmly to the journey and the quest and will not abandon or leave it until I reach," just as you say: "I will not leave the place." As for the meeting place of the two seas, it is the place where Moses was promised a meeting with al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. It is the confluence of the Persian and Byzantine seas on the eastern side. It has been said to be other than this, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates the identification of these two seas. If something is established by a sound report, then so be it; otherwise it is preferable to remain silent about it. Some people said: "The two seas are Moses and al-Khidr, because they were two seas of knowledge." It is also read "mijma'a" with a kasra on the mim. Then He said: ﴿or I will continue for a long period﴾, that is, I will travel for a long time. It was said: a huqb (period) is eighty years. We have discussed this term in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (ahqaban)﴾ (al-Naba' 23). The essence of the matter is this: Allah, mighty and majestic, had informed Moses of the state of this scholar, but had not informed him of the exact location. So Moses, peace be upon him, said: "I will continue on until the two seas join and become one sea, or I will continue for a long time until I find this scholar." This is an announcement from Moses that he had prepared himself to endure severe fatigue and great hardship in travel for the sake of seeking knowledge. This is an indication that if a student traveled from the east to the west for the sake of a single question, that would be justified for him.

Then He said: ﴿So when they reached the meeting place between them﴾. The meaning is: they set out until they reached the meeting place between them. Regarding the pronoun in his words "between them," to what does it refer? There are two views:

The first: "the meeting place between them" means the meeting place of the two seas, and this seems to be an allusion to the words of Moses: ﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾; that is, Allah fulfilled what he had said.

The second view: the meaning is that they reached the place where Moses and his companion, whom he was seeking, would meet. For that place where the forgetting of the fish occurred is the place where al-Khidr lived or lived nearby. And for this reason, when Moses and his servant returned after remembering the fish, they came to it, and this is a good meaning. The exegetes follow the first view.
