This is the view of the majority of the Jews." Al-Qaffal argued for the correctness of our view that this Moses is the owner of the Torah, saying: "Allah the Exalted mentions Moses in His Book only meaning the owner of the Torah. So the unrestricted use of this name necessitates that it be understood in that sense. And if another person named Moses were intended, he would have to be identified by a description that makes him distinct and removes doubt. Just as, when the well-known figure in common usage is Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, a specific man, if we mention this name and mean another man, we would specify him, such as saying: 'Abu Hanifa al-Dinawari said.'" The argument of those who said that this Moses is not the owner of the Torah is that after Allah sent down the Torah to him, and spoke to him without an intermediary, and vindicated him against his opponents with mighty, overwhelming miracles, the like of which had not been granted to most of the great prophets, it is unlikely that He would send him afterward to learn benefit. This was answered: It is not unlikely that a scholar who is complete in most sciences would be ignorant of some matters, and therefore need to learn them from someone lesser than him, and this is a known and common matter.

The third issue: They differed concerning Moses's servant. Most held that he was Yusha' son of Nun. Al-Qaffal narrated from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, from Abu Hurayra, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "His servant is Yusha' son of Nun."

The second view is that Moses's servant was the brother of Yusha', and he was the companion of Moses, peace be upon him, on this journey.

The third view: 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd narrated from al-Hasan concerning the words of Allah: ﴿And when Moses said to his servant, "I will not cease"﴾ that he said: "He means his slave." Al-Qaffal said: "The language permits this. It has been reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: 'Let none of you say "my slave (male) and my slave (female)," but let him say "my young man (fata) and my young woman (fataat)."' This indicates that they used to call a male slave a fata and a female slave a fataat."

The fourth issue: It was said that when Moses, peace be upon him, was given the tablets and Allah spoke to him, he said: "Who is more excellent than me and more knowledgeable?" It was said to him: "A servant of Allah who dwells on the islands of the sea, and he is al-Khidr." In another report: When Moses, peace be upon him, was given of knowledge what he was given, he thought that no one was like him. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him while he was on the seashore and said: "O Moses, look at this small bird that swoops down to the sea and dips its beak into it, then rises. You, in what you have been given of knowledge, are less than the amount this bird takes with its beak from the sea." The jurists of legal theory (al-usuliyyun) said: "This report is weak, because the prophets must know that the knowledge of Allah has no end, and that the knowledge of created beings must be finite. Every finite quantity admits of something greater than it, so there is no degree of knowledge except that above it there is a degree. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ When these premises are known, it is highly improbable that a rational person would be certain that there is no one more knowledgeable than himself, especially Moses, peace be upon him, given his abundant knowledge of the realities of things and his great freedom from blameworthy traits such as self-admiration, bewilderment, and arrogance."

The third report: It was said that Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord: "Which of Your servants is most beloved to You?" He said: "The one who remembers Me and does not forget Me." He said: "Which of Your servants is most just?" He said: "The one who judges by the truth and does not follow desire." He said: "Which of Your servants is most knowledgeable?" He said: "The one who seeks the knowledge of people in addition to his own knowledge, perhaps he will hear a word that guides him to guidance or turns him back from ruin." Moses, peace be upon him, said: "If among Your servants there is someone more knowledgeable than me, then guide me to him." He said: "The most knowledgeable than you is al-Khidr." He said: "Where shall I seek him?" He said: "On the shore, at the rock." He said: "O Lord, how can I reach him?" He said: "Take a fish in a basket; wherever you lose it, there he is." So he said to his servant: "When you lose the fish, inform me." They set out walking, and Moses slept. The fish stirred and leapt into the sea. When the time for the morning meal came, Moses asked for the fish, and his servant informed him that it had fallen into the sea. So he returned from that place to the place where the fish had leapt into the sea, and there he found a man covered with his garment. Moses, peace be upon him, greeted him. He said: "And how is greeting in your land?" So he introduced himself to him. He said: "O Moses, I am upon a knowledge that Allah taught me which you do not know, and you are upon a knowledge that Allah taught you which I do not know." When they boarded the ship, a sparrow came and perched on its edge and pecked into the water. Al-Khidr said: "My knowledge and your knowledge do not diminish the knowledge of Allah by an amount equal to what this sparrow took from the sea." I say: The ratio of that small quantity which the sparrow took from that water to the entirety of the sea's water is the ratio of a finite to a finite, while the ratio of the knowledge of all created beings to the knowledge of Allah the Exalted is the ratio of a finite to an infinite. Where is one of these two ratios from the other?

[p. 124]

And Allah knows the realities of matters best. Let us return to the exegesis. As for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿I will not cease﴾, al-Zajjaj said: "His words ﴿I will not cease﴾ do not mean 'I will not depart,' for if that were so he would not have traversed any land." I say: It is possible to answer this by saying that ceasing from something means abandoning it and turning away from it. It is said: "So-and-so ceased (zala) from his path in generosity," meaning he abandoned it. So his words "I will not cease" mean "I will not cease from journeying and going," that is, "I will not abandon this action and this deed." I say: The well-known view among the majority is that his words "I will not cease" mean "I will not depart." The Arabs say: "I will not cease (la abrah), I will not stop (la azal), I will not leave off (la anfakk), and I will not fail (la aftu')," all with one meaning. Al-Qaffal said: "They said: the origin of their saying 'la abrah' is from al-barah (open space, clearing), just as the origin of 'la azal' is from al-zawal (ceasing). It is said: zala yazal and yazul, just as it is said: dama yadam and yadum, and mata yamat and yamut. Except that the form used with this word is yazal. So his words 'la abrah' mean 'I will remain,' because al-barah is non-existence; thus 'la abrah' is the negation of non-existence, and therefore it is an affirmation. So his words 'la azal wa la abrah' indicate continuity and steadfastness in the action." If it is asked: If his words "la abrah" mean "la azal," then there must be a predicate; we answer: the predicate is omitted because the situation and the discourse both indicate it. As for the situation, it was a situation of journeying. As for the discourse, his words "until I reach the meeting place of the two seas" are a set limit which requires something of which it is the limit. So the meaning is: "I will not cease traveling until I reach the meeting place of the two seas." It is also possible that the meaning is: "I will not cease from what I am upon, that is, I will hold firmly to the journey and the quest and will not abandon or leave it until I reach," just as you say: "I will not leave the place." As for the meeting place of the two seas, it is the place where Moses was promised a meeting with al-Khidr, peace be upon them both. It is the confluence of the Persian and Byzantine seas on the eastern side. It has been said to be other than this, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates the identification of these two seas. If something is established by a sound report, then so be it; otherwise it is preferable to remain silent about it. Some people said: "The two seas are Moses and al-Khidr, because they were two seas of knowledge." It is also read "mijma'a" with a kasra on the mim. Then He said: ﴿or I will continue for a long period﴾, that is, I will travel for a long time. It was said: a huqb (period) is eighty years. We have discussed this term in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿remaining therein for ages (ahqaban)﴾ (al-Naba' 23). The essence of the matter is this: Allah, mighty and majestic, had informed Moses of the state of this scholar, but had not informed him of the exact location. So Moses, peace be upon him, said: "I will continue on until the two seas join and become one sea, or I will continue for a long time until I find this scholar." This is an announcement from Moses that he had prepared himself to endure severe fatigue and great hardship in travel for the sake of seeking knowledge. This is an indication that if a student traveled from the east to the west for the sake of a single question, that would be justified for him.

Then He said: ﴿So when they reached the meeting place between them﴾. The meaning is: they set out until they reached the meeting place between them. Regarding the pronoun in his words "between them," to what does it refer? There are two views:

The first: "the meeting place between them" means the meeting place of the two seas, and this seems to be an allusion to the words of Moses: ﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾; that is, Allah fulfilled what he had said.

The second view: the meaning is that they reached the place where Moses and his companion, whom he was seeking, would meet. For that place where the forgetting of the fish occurred is the place where al-Khidr lived or lived nearby. And for this reason, when Moses and his servant returned after remembering the fish, they came to it, and this is a good meaning. The exegetes follow the first view.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They forgot their fish﴾, and concerning this there are several discussions:

[Page 125]

**Discussion 1:** The narrations indicate that God informed Musa, peace be upon him, that this scholar's place was the meeting point of the two seas. However, God made the fish's coming back to life a sign of his specific dwelling. This is like someone seeking a person and being told: "His place is such-and-such a quarter in al-Rayy. When you reach that quarter, ask so-and-so about his house. Wherever he takes you, follow him, and you will reach him." Similarly here, it was said to him: "His place is the meeting point of the two seas. When you arrive there, you will see the fish come back to life and leap into the sea." It is possible that he was told: "There is where his place is." It is also possible that he was told: "Go in accordance with the fish's going, and you will find him."

Having understood this, we say: When Musa and his servant reached the meeting point of the two, the fish leapt into the sea and moved away. There are also narrations about how it leapt. It was said that the young man was washing the fish, because it had been salted, and it leapt and moved away. It was said that Yusha' performed ablution at that place, so water splashed onto the salted fish, and it came to life and leapt into the water. It was also said that a spring from Paradise burst forth there, and drops from that spring reached the fish, so it came to life and leapt into the sea. This is what is said about the description of the fish.

**Discussion 2:** The meaning of God's words ﴿they forgot their fish﴾ is that they forgot how to use this特殊 circumstance as evidence for reaching the sought goal. If it is objected: the salted fish returning to life is an astonishing condition, so since God made the occurrence of this astonishing condition a sign of reaching the sought goal, how can forgetting in this respect be conceived? The scholars answered that Yusha' had witnessed many overpowering miracles from Musa, peace be upon him, so this miracle no longer had a great impact on him, and therefore forgetting was permissible. I have another answer regarding this: when Musa, peace be upon him, regarded his own knowledge as great, God removed this necessary knowledge from the heart of his companion, as a reminder to Musa, peace be upon him, that knowledge is only attained through God's teaching and His preserving it upon the heart and the mind.

As for His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea, making a tunnel﴾, there are several views:

The first: the intended sense is: it moved in the sea, moving [in a tunnel]. But the verb "fa-ittakhadha" (it took) was placed in the position of "sariba" (it moved). Al-sarab means going, and from it is His words ﴿and one who goes freely by day﴾ (Al-Ra'd: 10).

The second: God stopped the flow of water over the sea and made it like an arch and a window, until the fish moved within it. When Musa and his servant passed the appointed place, which is reaching the rock, because of the forgetting mentioned, and they went far, became weary and hungry, ﴿he said to his servant, "Bring us our morning meal; we have indeed suffered much fatigue from this journey of ours"﴾. ﴿He said﴾, the servant: ﴿"Do you see? When we took refuge at the rock"﴾. The hamza in "ara'ayta" is the interrogative hamza, and "ra'ayta" is in its original meaning. This speech came in the manner customary among people: when something astonishing happens to one of them, he says to his companion: "Did you see what happened to me?" Likewise here, it is as if he said: "Did you see what happened to me from it when we took refuge at the rock?" So the object of "ara'ayta" is omitted, because His words ﴿"Indeed I forgot the fish"﴾ indicate it. Then He said: ﴿"And none caused me to forget it except Satan, that I should mention it"﴾. There are discussions regarding this:

Discussion 1: This is a parenthetical clause that came between the conjoined element and what it is conjoined to. The construction is: "Indeed I forgot the fish, and it took its way into the sea astonishingly." The reason for this parenthetical clause is what serves as an excuse and cause for that forgetting.

Discussion 2: Al-Ka'bi said: His words ﴿"And none caused me to forget it except Satan"﴾ indicate that God did not create that forgetting and did not will it; otherwise, attributing it to God would be more fitting than attributing it to Satan, because if God created it in him, Satan's effort would have no effect on its existence or non-existence. Al-Qadi said: What is meant by forgetting is that a person's heart becomes occupied with his whisperings, which are from his own actions, rather than the forgetting that is contrary to remembrance, because that cannot be except from God, exalted is He.

Discussion 3: His words "an adhkurahu" (that I should mention it) are a substitution for the pronoun "-hu" in "ansanihi"; that is, "none caused me to forget its remembrance except Satan." Then He said: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, astonishingly﴾. There are several views regarding this:

The first: His words "ajaban" (astonishingly) are an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. It is as if it were said: "and it took its way into the sea in an astonishing manner." The reason it was astonishing is its transformation from the basket, its becoming alive, and its casting itself into the sea while they were heedless.

The second: What is meant by it is what we mentioned, that God made the water over it like an arch and like a passage.

The third: It was said that the speech was complete at His words ﴿and it took its way into the sea﴾, and then He said after it "ajaban" (astonishingly), and what is meant is his astonishment at that wonder which he saw, and at his forgetting of it. It was also said that His words "ajaban" are a report of Musa's astonishment, and it is not his own speech.

[Page 126]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿He said, "That is what we were seeking."﴾ That is, Musa said: "That is what we were seeking," because it was a sign of success in attaining the sought goal, which is meeting Khidr. The word "nabgh" originally was "nabghi," so the yā' was dropped for lightness, the kasra indicating it. Analogically it should not be dropped, because they only drop the yā' in nouns, and this is a verb. However, it is permissible, though analogically weak, to drop it, because it is dropped with a following sukūn, as in your saying: "What do we seek today?" Since it is dropped before the sukūn, it is also dropped before what is not a sukūn.

Then He said: ﴿so they went back, retracing their footsteps﴾, that is, they returned. His words ﴿qasasan﴾ (retracing) have two views:

One: it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial, meaning they returned upon their traces, tracing their traces.

Two: it is a verbal noun for His words "fartadda 'ala athariha" (they went back, retracing their footsteps), because its meaning is "they followed their traces."

The summary of the speech: when they realized that they had passed beyond the place where that scholar dwelt, they turned back and returned to it. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 18, verses 65–66 (part 1 of 2):

[The words of God Most High: "And they found a servant from among Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and had taught knowledge from Our presence." "Musa said to him, 'May I follow you on the condition that you teach me from what you have been taught, [so as to be] a guide to right conduct?'" "He said, 'Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me.'" "And how can you be patient about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?" "He said, 'You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter.'" "He said, 'If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you.']

In the verse there are several issues.

First issue: His words, "And they found a servant from among Our servants" (Q 18:65). On this there are two discussions.

First discussion: Most scholars said that this servant was a prophet, and they argued for this with several points.

The first: He, exalted is He, said, "We had given him mercy from Us and taught him." Mercy here means prophethood, as evidenced by His words, "Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?" (Surah al-Zukhruf: 32), and His words, "You did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you, except as a mercy from your Lord" (Surah al-Qasas: 86). The intended meaning of this mercy is prophethood. A critic may say: We accept that prophethood is a mercy, but it does not follow that every mercy is prophethood.

The second argument: His words, "And We taught him knowledge from Our presence." This indicates that He taught him without the mediation of any teacher or any guide. Whoever God teaches without human mediation must be a prophet who knows matters through revelation from God. This argument is weak, because necessary knowledge (*'ulum darurIyyah*) is acquired immediately from God, and that does not indicate prophethood.

The third argument: Musa, peace be upon him, said, "May I follow you on the condition that you teach me." A prophet does not follow a non-prophet in teaching. This too is weak, because a prophet does not follow a non-prophet in the sciences by virtue of which he became a prophet, but in other sciences he does.

[p. 127]

The fourth argument: That servant displayed superiority over Musa when he said to him, "And how can you be patient about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?" Musa, however, displayed humility toward him when he said, "I will not disobey you in any matter." All of this indicates that this scholar was above Musa, and whoever is not a prophet cannot be above a prophet. This too is weak, because it is possible that a non-prophet is above a prophet in sciences upon which his prophethood does not depend. So why do you say that this is not permissible? If they say: because it entails causing aversion (*tanfir*), we say: then sending Musa to learn from him after God had revealed the Torah to him and spoken to him without intermediary entails causing aversion. If they say: this does not entail aversion, then the same applies to what they have mentioned.

The fifth argument: al-Asamm (ibn Ali al-Asamm) argued for his prophethood from his words in the course of the story, "And I did not do it of my own accord" (Q 18:82). Its meaning is: I did it by the revelation of God. This indicates prophethood. This too is a weak proof, and its weakness is evident.

The sixth argument: It is narrated that when Musa, peace be upon him, reached him, he said, "Peace be upon you." He said, "And upon you peace, O prophet of the Children of Israel." Musa, peace be upon him, said, "Who informed you of this?" He said, "The One who sent you to me." They said: This indicates that he knew this only through revelation, and revelation does not occur except with prophethood. The critic may say: Why is it not permissible that this was of the category of *karamat* (miracles granted to saints) and *ilhamat* (inspirations)?

Second discussion: Most scholars said that this servant was al-Khidr. They said: He was named al-Khidr because whenever he stood on a spot, that spot would turn green (*akhdar*). Al-Jubba'i said: Reports have made clear that al-Khidr was sent after Musa, peace be upon him, from among the Children of Israel. If that is correct, then this servant cannot be al-Khidr. Also, even assuming that this servant is al-Khidr, and it has been established that he must be a prophet, this would imply that al-Khidr was higher in rank than Musa, the owner of the Torah. This is because we have explained that the words mentioned in these verses indicate that he was superior to Musa, and that Musa displayed humility toward him. However, it is impermissible that al-Khidr was higher in rank than Musa, because al-Khidr either is said to have been from the Children of Israel or not from the Children of Israel. If we say that he was from the Children of Israel, then he was from the *ummah* (community) of Musa, as God says in quoting Musa to Pharaoh, "Send with us the Children of Israel" (Surah al-Shu'ara: 17), and a community cannot be in a higher state than its prophet. If we say that he was not from the Children of Israel, then he could not be better than Musa, as God says to the Children of Israel, "And that I preferred you over the worlds" (Surah al-Baqarah: 47). These words strengthen the view of those who say that this Musa is not Musa, the owner of the Torah.

Third issue: His words, "And We taught him knowledge from Our presence" indicate that those sciences were acquired by him from God directly, without intermediary. The Sufis named the knowledge acquired through unveilings (*mukashafat*) "ladunni knowledge" ('ulum laduniyyah, knowledge bestowed directly from God). Shaykh Abu Hamid al-Ghazali has a treatise proving ladunni knowledge. I say: The thorough treatment of this topic is that we say: When we perceive a matter and conceive of a reality among realities, either we pass a judgment on it, which is assent (*tasdiq*), or we do not pass judgment, which is conception (*tasawwur*). Each of these two categories is either theoretical, acquired without effort or seeking, or acquired (*kasbi*). As for theoretical sciences, they arise in the soul and the intellect without acquisition or seeking, such as our conception of pain and pleasure, existence and non-existence, and our assent that affirmation and negation cannot both be true or both be false, and that one is half of two. As for acquired sciences, they are those that are not present in the essence of the soul from the beginning, but there must be a means through which one reaches the acquisition of those sciences. This means is of two kinds:

[p. 128]

The first: that a person labors to combine those self-evident theoretical sciences, so that through combining them he reaches the knowledge of unknown things. This method is called *nazar* (reflection), *tafakkur* (thinking), *tadabbur* (contemplation), *ta'ammul* (deliberation), *tarawwi* (consideration), and *istidlal* (inference). This kind of acquiring knowledge is the method that is not completed except through striving and seeking.

The second kind: that a person, through disciplines (*riyadat*) and spiritual struggles (*mujahadat*), strives to make the sensory and imaginative faculties weak. When they become weak, the intellectual faculty grows strong, the divine lights shine in the essence of the intellect, and cognitions arise and sciences are perfected without the intermediary of striving and seeking through reflection and contemplation. This is what is called ladunni knowledge.

Having understood this, we say: The essences of rational souls differ in their quiddity. Sometimes a soul is a luminous, divine, exalted soul, little attached to bodily pulls and physical urges. Therefore it is always highly prepared to receive holy emanations and divine lights, and so those lights overflow upon it from the unseen world in complete perfection. This is what is meant by ladunni knowledge, and it is what is meant by His words, "We had given him mercy from Us and taught him knowledge from Our presence." As for the soul that has not reached purity of essence and brightness of substance, it is a deficient, dull soul that cannot acquire cognitions and sciences except through a human intermediary who is made to teach and learn. The first kind, in relation to the second kind, is like the sun in relation to partial lights, like the sea in relation to partial streams, and like the Greatest Spirit in relation to partial spirits. This is a brief pointer to this approach, and behind it are secrets that cannot be mentioned in this book.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "Musa said to him, 'May I follow you on the condition that you teach me from what you have been taught, [so as to be] a guide to right conduct?'" On this there are two issues.

First issue: Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read *rashadan* (رَشَدًا) with a fatha on the ra' and the shin. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is narrated with a damma on the ra' and the shin. The rest read it with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin (رُشْدًا). Al-Qaffal said: These are dialectal variants with one meaning. It is said *rushd* and *rashad*, like *nukr* and *nakr*, just as it is said *suqm* and *saqam*, *shughl* and *shaghl*, *bukhl* and *bakhal*, and *'udm* and *'adam*. His words, *rushdan* (رُشْدًا), mean knowledge that is rightly guided. Al-Qaffal said: His words *rushdan* may have two meanings:

One: that *rushd* refers to al-Khidr, meaning from what God has taught you and guided you with.

The second: that it refers to Musa, and the meaning would be: so that you teach me and guide me from what you have been taught.

Second issue: Know that these verses indicate that Musa, peace be upon him, observed many kinds of courtesy and gentleness when he wished to learn from al-Khidr:

The first: He made himself a follower of him, for he said, "May I follow you?"

The second: He asked permission for establishing this following, for he said: Will you permit me to make myself a follower of you? This is an immense expression of humility.

The third: He said, "On the condition that you teach me." This is an acknowledgment on his own part of ignorance and of his teacher's knowledge.

The fourth: He said, "Teach me from what you have been taught." The particle *min* (مِن) denotes partiality, so he requested that he teach him some of what God had taught him. This too indicates humility, as if he were saying: I do not ask you to make me equal to you in knowledge, but I ask you to give me a part of the parts of your knowledge, just as a poor man asks a rich man to give him a portion of his wealth.

The fifth: His words, "from what you have been taught," are an acknowledgment that God taught him that knowledge.

The sixth: His words, "[so as to be] a guide to right conduct," are a request from him for guidance and direction. Guidance is that which, if it were not attained, error and misguidance would result.

The seventh: His words, "Teach me from what you have been taught," mean that he asked him to treat him in the same manner that God had treated him. It implies that your favor upon me in this teaching would be like God's favor upon you in this teaching. For this reason it was said: I am a slave to whoever has taught me a single letter.

The eighth: Following (*mutabi'ah*) is the act of performing the same action as another, because it is that person's action. When we say, "There is no god but Allah," the Jews who came before us used to say this same word, yet it is not obligatory for us to be followers of them in saying this word, because we do not say it because they said it, but because there is evidence that it must be said. However, when we perform these five prayers in conformity with the practice of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, we perform them only because he, peace be upon him, performed them. Therefore we are indeed followers of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in performing these prayers. Having established this, we say: His words, "May I follow you?" indicate that he would perform the same actions as that teacher merely because that teacher performs them. This indicates that the student must, at the outset, submit and refrain from disputing and objecting.

The ninth: His words, "I follow you," indicate a request to follow him absolutely, in all matters, without being restricted to some things rather than others.

The tenth: it is established by reports that al-Khadir first recognized that he (Musa) was the Prophet of the Children of Israel, and that he is Musa, the bearer of the Tawrat (Torah), the man whom God, exalted and majestic, addressed directly without an intermediary, and whom He favored with overwhelming and dazzling miracles. Then, despite these lofty positions and elevated, noble ranks, peace be upon him, he displayed these many kinds of humility. This indicates that he, peace be upon him, came seeking knowledge with the utmost intensity, and this is what befits him, because whoever's grasp of the sciences is greater, his knowledge of their delight and happiness is greater, so his pursuit of them is more intense, and his veneration of the people of knowledge is more complete and more profound.

The eleventh: he said, ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me?﴾ He thereby affirmed that he would be a follower of him first, and then he requested, second, that he teach him. This is from him a beginning with service, and then, in the second rank, a request for instruction.

The twelfth: he said, ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me?﴾ He sought nothing in exchange for this following and this instruction, as if he were saying: I do not ask you, in return for this following, for wealth or status, and my only aim is the pursuit of knowledge.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 18, verses 65–66 (part 1 of 2):

[The words of God Most High: "And they found a servant from among Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us and had taught knowledge from Our presence." "Musa said to him, 'May I follow you on the condition that you teach me from what you have been taught, [so as to be] a guide to right conduct?'" "He said, 'Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me.'" "And how can you be patient about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?" "He said, 'You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter.'" "He said, 'If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you.']

In the verse there are several issues.

First issue: His words, "And they found a servant from among Our servants" (Q 18:65). On this there are two discussions.

First discussion: Most scholars said that this servant was a prophet, and they argued for this with several points.

The first: He, exalted is He, said, "We had given him mercy from Us and taught him." Mercy here means prophethood, as evidenced by His words, "Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord?" (Surah al-Zukhruf: 32), and His words, "You did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you, except as a mercy from your Lord" (Surah al-Qasas: 86). The intended meaning of this mercy is prophethood. A critic may say: We accept that prophethood is a mercy, but it does not follow that every mercy is prophethood.

The second argument: His words, "And We taught him knowledge from Our presence." This indicates that He taught him without the mediation of any teacher or any guide. Whoever God teaches without human mediation must be a prophet who knows matters through revelation from God. This argument is weak, because necessary knowledge (*'ulum darurIyyah*) is acquired immediately from God, and that does not indicate prophethood.

The third argument: Musa, peace be upon him, said, "May I follow you on the condition that you teach me." A prophet does not follow a non-prophet in teaching. This too is weak, because a prophet does not follow a non-prophet in the sciences by virtue of which he became a prophet, but in other sciences he does.

[p. 127]

The fourth argument: That servant displayed superiority over Musa when he said to him, "And how can you be patient about that which you do not encompass in knowledge?" Musa, however, displayed humility toward him when he said, "I will not disobey you in any matter." All of this indicates that this scholar was above Musa, and whoever is not a prophet cannot be above a prophet. This too is weak, because it is possible that a non-prophet is above a prophet in sciences upon which his prophethood does not depend. So why do you say that this is not permissible? If they say: because it entails causing aversion (*tanfir*), we say: then sending Musa to learn from him after God had revealed the Torah to him and spoken to him without intermediary entails causing aversion. If they say: this does not entail aversion, then the same applies to what they have mentioned.

The fifth argument: al-Asamm (ibn Ali al-Asamm) argued for his prophethood from his words in the course of the story, "And I did not do it of my own accord" (Q 18:82). Its meaning is: I did it by the revelation of God. This indicates prophethood. This too is a weak proof, and its weakness is evident.

The sixth argument: It is narrated that when Musa, peace be upon him, reached him, he said, "Peace be upon you." He said, "And upon you peace, O prophet of the Children of Israel." Musa, peace be upon him, said, "Who informed you of this?" He said, "The One who sent you to me." They said: This indicates that he knew this only through revelation, and revelation does not occur except with prophethood. The critic may say: Why is it not permissible that this was of the category of *karamat* (miracles granted to saints) and *ilhamat* (inspirations)?

Second discussion: Most scholars said that this servant was al-Khidr. They said: He was named al-Khidr because whenever he stood on a spot, that spot would turn green (*akhdar*). Al-Jubba'i said: Reports have made clear that al-Khidr was sent after Musa, peace be upon him, from among the Children of Israel. If that is correct, then this servant cannot be al-Khidr. Also, even assuming that this servant is al-Khidr, and it has been established that he must be a prophet, this would imply that al-Khidr was higher in rank than Musa, the owner of the Torah. This is because we have explained that the words mentioned in these verses indicate that he was superior to Musa, and that Musa displayed humility toward him. However, it is impermissible that al-Khidr was higher in rank than Musa, because al-Khidr either is said to have been from the Children of Israel or not from the Children of Israel. If we say that he was from the Children of Israel, then he was from the *ummah* (community) of Musa, as God says in quoting Musa to Pharaoh, "Send with us the Children of Israel" (Surah al-Shu'ara: 17), and a community cannot be in a higher state than its prophet. If we say that he was not from the Children of Israel, then he could not be better than Musa, as God says to the Children of Israel, "And that I preferred you over the worlds" (Surah al-Baqarah: 47). These words strengthen the view of those who say that this Musa is not Musa, the owner of the Torah.

Third issue: His words, "And We taught him knowledge from Our presence" indicate that those sciences were acquired by him from God directly, without intermediary. The Sufis named the knowledge acquired through unveilings (*mukashafat*) "ladunni knowledge" ('ulum laduniyyah, knowledge bestowed directly from God). Shaykh Abu Hamid al-Ghazali has a treatise proving ladunni knowledge. I say: The thorough treatment of this topic is that we say: When we perceive a matter and conceive of a reality among realities, either we pass a judgment on it, which is assent (*tasdiq*), or we do not pass judgment, which is conception (*tasawwur*). Each of these two categories is either theoretical, acquired without effort or seeking, or acquired (*kasbi*). As for theoretical sciences, they arise in the soul and the intellect without acquisition or seeking, such as our conception of pain and pleasure, existence and non-existence, and our assent that affirmation and negation cannot both be true or both be false, and that one is half of two. As for acquired sciences, they are those that are not present in the essence of the soul from the beginning, but there must be a means through which one reaches the acquisition of those sciences. This means is of two kinds:

[p. 128]

The first: that a person labors to combine those self-evident theoretical sciences, so that through combining them he reaches the knowledge of unknown things. This method is called *nazar* (reflection), *tafakkur* (thinking), *tadabbur* (contemplation), *ta'ammul* (deliberation), *tarawwi* (consideration), and *istidlal* (inference). This kind of acquiring knowledge is the method that is not completed except through striving and seeking.

The second kind: that a person, through disciplines (*riyadat*) and spiritual struggles (*mujahadat*), strives to make the sensory and imaginative faculties weak. When they become weak, the intellectual faculty grows strong, the divine lights shine in the essence of the intellect, and cognitions arise and sciences are perfected without the intermediary of striving and seeking through reflection and contemplation. This is what is called ladunni knowledge.

Having understood this, we say: The essences of rational souls differ in their quiddity. Sometimes a soul is a luminous, divine, exalted soul, little attached to bodily pulls and physical urges. Therefore it is always highly prepared to receive holy emanations and divine lights, and so those lights overflow upon it from the unseen world in complete perfection. This is what is meant by ladunni knowledge, and it is what is meant by His words, "We had given him mercy from Us and taught him knowledge from Our presence." As for the soul that has not reached purity of essence and brightness of substance, it is a deficient, dull soul that cannot acquire cognitions and sciences except through a human intermediary who is made to teach and learn. The first kind, in relation to the second kind, is like the sun in relation to partial lights, like the sea in relation to partial streams, and like the Greatest Spirit in relation to partial spirits. This is a brief pointer to this approach, and behind it are secrets that cannot be mentioned in this book.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "Musa said to him, 'May I follow you on the condition that you teach me from what you have been taught, [so as to be] a guide to right conduct?'" On this there are two issues.

First issue: Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read *rashadan* (رَشَدًا) with a fatha on the ra' and the shin. From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is narrated with a damma on the ra' and the shin. The rest read it with a damma on the ra' and sukun on the shin (رُشْدًا). Al-Qaffal said: These are dialectal variants with one meaning. It is said *rushd* and *rashad*, like *nukr* and *nakr*, just as it is said *suqm* and *saqam*, *shughl* and *shaghl*, *bukhl* and *bakhal*, and *'udm* and *'adam*. His words, *rushdan* (رُشْدًا), mean knowledge that is rightly guided. Al-Qaffal said: His words *rushdan* may have two meanings:

One: that *rushd* refers to al-Khidr, meaning from what God has taught you and guided you with.

The second: that it refers to Musa, and the meaning would be: so that you teach me and guide me from what you have been taught.

Second issue: Know that these verses indicate that Musa, peace be upon him, observed many kinds of courtesy and gentleness when he wished to learn from al-Khidr:

The first: He made himself a follower of him, for he said, "May I follow you?"

The second: He asked permission for establishing this following, for he said: Will you permit me to make myself a follower of you? This is an immense expression of humility.

The third: He said, "On the condition that you teach me." This is an acknowledgment on his own part of ignorance and of his teacher's knowledge.

The fourth: He said, "Teach me from what you have been taught." The particle *min* (مِن) denotes partiality, so he requested that he teach him some of what God had taught him. This too indicates humility, as if he were saying: I do not ask you to make me equal to you in knowledge, but I ask you to give me a part of the parts of your knowledge, just as a poor man asks a rich man to give him a portion of his wealth.

The fifth: His words, "from what you have been taught," are an acknowledgment that God taught him that knowledge.

The sixth: His words, "[so as to be] a guide to right conduct," are a request from him for guidance and direction. Guidance is that which, if it were not attained, error and misguidance would result.

The seventh: His words, "Teach me from what you have been taught," mean that he asked him to treat him in the same manner that God had treated him. It implies that your favor upon me in this teaching would be like God's favor upon you in this teaching. For this reason it was said: I am a slave to whoever has taught me a single letter.

The eighth: Following (*mutabi'ah*) is the act of performing the same action as another, because it is that person's action. When we say, "There is no god but Allah," the Jews who came before us used to say this same word, yet it is not obligatory for us to be followers of them in saying this word, because we do not say it because they said it, but because there is evidence that it must be said. However, when we perform these five prayers in conformity with the practice of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, we perform them only because he, peace be upon him, performed them. Therefore we are indeed followers of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in performing these prayers. Having established this, we say: His words, "May I follow you?" indicate that he would perform the same actions as that teacher merely because that teacher performs them. This indicates that the student must, at the outset, submit and refrain from disputing and objecting.

The ninth: His words, "I follow you," indicate a request to follow him absolutely, in all matters, without being restricted to some things rather than others.

The tenth: it is established by reports that al-Khadir first recognized that he (Musa) was the Prophet of the Children of Israel, and that he is Musa, the bearer of the Tawrat (Torah), the man whom God, exalted and majestic, addressed directly without an intermediary, and whom He favored with overwhelming and dazzling miracles. Then, despite these lofty positions and elevated, noble ranks, peace be upon him, he displayed these many kinds of humility. This indicates that he, peace be upon him, came seeking knowledge with the utmost intensity, and this is what befits him, because whoever's grasp of the sciences is greater, his knowledge of their delight and happiness is greater, so his pursuit of them is more intense, and his veneration of the people of knowledge is more complete and more profound.

The eleventh: he said, ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me?﴾ He thereby affirmed that he would be a follower of him first, and then he requested, second, that he teach him. This is from him a beginning with service, and then, in the second rank, a request for instruction.

The twelfth: he said, ﴿May I follow you on condition that you teach me?﴾ He sought nothing in exchange for this following and this instruction, as if he were saying: I do not ask you, in return for this following, for wealth or status, and my only aim is the pursuit of knowledge.

Then He, exalted is He, related about al-Khidr that he said: ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me﴾ ﴿And how can you be patient about that which you have not encompassed in knowledge?﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the learner is of two kinds. One is a learner who has none of the knowledge, has not engaged in idle talk and dispute (qil wa qal), and has not accustomed himself to questioning (taqrir) and objection (i'tiraD). The other has acquired many sciences and has engaged in inference (istidlal) and objection.

Then this second kind of learner wishes to associate with a person more perfect than himself, in order to reach the degree of completeness and perfection. Learning in this second category is very difficult and arduous. That is because when he sees something or hears a statement, it may be, outwardly, reprehensible, while in reality it is true and correct.

So this learner, because he has become accustomed to idle talk and has grown used to discourse and disputation, is deceived by the outward appearance. And because of his lack of perfection, he does not grasp its inner meaning and reality. At that point he proceeds to contention, objection and argument, and that is something that is burdensome to hear for the complete, deeply learned teacher.

When such an incident happens twice or three times, complete aversion and intense dislike arise. This is what al-Khidr pointed to with his words: ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me﴾, indicating that he (Moses) had become accustomed to speech and had grown used to affirmation, negation, inference and objection. And his words: ﴿And how can you be patient about that which you have not encompassed in knowledge?﴾ indicate that he was not knowledgeable of the realities of things as they are. We have mentioned that whenever these two matters occur together, silence becomes difficult, teaching becomes hard, and the matter ultimately ends in aversion, dislike, and the severing of ties and mutual repulsion.

The second issue: Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued from His words: ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me﴾ that capacity (istita'ah) does not exist before the act. They said: If the capacity to perform the act existed before the act occurred, then the capacity to be patient would have existed in Moses, peace be upon him, before patience occurred. Then his statement ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me﴾ would necessarily become false. Since that is invalid, we know that capacity does not exist before the act. Al-Jubba'i (a Mu'tazili theologian) answered regarding this that what is meant by this statement is that patience is burdensome for him, not that he is incapable of it. It is said in common usage: "So-and-so cannot look at so-and-so" or "cannot sit with him" when that is burdensome for him. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They were not able to hear﴾, meaning that listening was difficult for them. It is said to him: This is a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence, and it is not permissible.

I say: What reinforces this argument mentioned by our companions is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how can you be patient about that which you have not encompassed in knowledge?﴾ He considered patience regarding what a person does not comprehend in its reality to be improbable. And if capacity existed before the act, then the capacity for knowledge would exist before that knowledge was acquired. And if that were so, then patience in the absence of that knowledge would not be improbable, because the one capable of an act is not deemed unlikely to undertake that act. Since God ruled its improbability, we know that capacity does not exist before the act.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related about Musa that he said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter.﴾ And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Those who criticize the infallibility (ʿișmah) of the prophets, by Allah's protection, have used this verse as evidence. They said: Al-Khidr said to Musa, ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me﴾, and Musa said, ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, patient, and I will not disobey you in any matter.﴾ Each of these two statements contradicts the other, so one of them must be a lie, and in either case a lie would have to proceed from the prophets, peace be upon them. The answer is that his statement, ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me﴾, is to be understood as referring to the majority and the most likely case, and on this interpretation nothing they mentioned follows.

The second issue: The expression "in kāna kadhā" (if it be so) indicates doubt. So his statement, ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, patient﴾, means: "You will find me patient, if Allah wills my being patient." This implies that doubt arises as to whether Allah wills that he be patient or not.

There is no doubt that patience in a situation of suspension (of judgment) is obligatory. This implies that Allah, exalted is He, may not will from the servant what He has made obligatory upon him, and this indicates the soundness of our statement that Allah, exalted is He, may command a thing while not willing it. The Muʿtazilah said: This phrase is only mentioned out of observance of courtesy (adab) regarding what a person wishes to do in the future. It is said to them: If this courtesy's meaning is sound, then the claim is established; and if it is corrupt, then what courtesy is there in mentioning this false statement?

The third issue: His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and I will not disobey you in any matter﴾, indicates that the apparent form of a command (amr) implies obligation (wujūb), because one who abandons what is commanded is disobedient by the indication of this verse, and the disobedient deserves punishment, due to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 23]. This indicates that the apparent form of a command implies obligation.

All of this indicates that it is obligatory upon the student to show humility to the utmost degree. As for the teacher, if he sees that harshness toward the student would benefit him and guide him to good, then it is obligatory for him to mention it, for silence about it would place the student in delusion and pride, and that would prevent him from learning. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 71–73:

﴿So they set out, until when they boarded the ship, he made a hole in it. He said, "Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? Indeed you have done a grave thing."﴾ ﴿He said, "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot, and do not impose on me hardship in my affair."﴾

Know that Musa and that scholar, when they had agreed upon the stipulated condition mentioned, set out and reached a place where they needed to board a ship. So they boarded it, and that scholar proceeded to make a hole in the ship. I say: perhaps he made a hole in a plank of the ship, so that by means of that hole the ship would become visibly defective, and so that drowning would not quickly reach its people. At that point Musa said to him: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people?﴾ And in this there are two discussions.

The first discussion: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (لِيَغْرَقَ أهْلُها) with a fatha on the ya', attributing the drowning to the people, while the rest read ﴿لِتُغْرِقَ أهْلَها﴾ in the second-person address, and the implied meaning is: "that you might drown the people of this ship."

The second discussion: when Musa, peace be upon him, witnessed that matter which was outwardly reprehensible, he forgot the earlier condition, and for this reason he said what he said. Those who object to the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, have argued from this verse in two respects:

The first: it is established by proof that that scholar was one of the prophets. Then Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people?﴾ If Musa spoke truly in this statement, this indicates that a great sin proceeded from that prophet; and if he lied, this indicates that a lie proceeded from Musa, peace be upon him.

The second: he (Musa) had committed himself not to object to that scholar, and firm covenants were made concerning this; then he (Musa) broke those covenants, and that is a sin.

As for the answer to the first: when Musa, peace be upon him, witnessed from him an action outside the ordinary, he said this statement, not because he believed that he had done something ugly, but because he wished to understand its reality and its cause. It may be said of a wondrous matter whose cause is not known that it is "imr" (a grave matter), from the saying: "amira al-amr" when it became great. And the poet said:

A calamity, a great calamity...

As for the answer to the second: he acted on the basis of forgetfulness. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 74–76:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they set out until, when they met a boy, he killed him. [Moses] said, "Have you killed an innocent soul without [its having killed] another? You have certainly done a terrible thing."﴾ ﴿[Khidr] said, "Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?"﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as your companion. You have even received an excuse from me."﴾

Know that the word ghulam (boy) may apply to a young man who has reached maturity, as evidence of which it is said: "The opinion of the shaykh (elder) is better than the sight of the ghulam," where the shaykh is set as the opposite of the ghulam, and this indicates that the ghulam is the young man. Its root is from al-ightilam (sexual arousal), which is intense desire, and that occurs only in youth. As for the application of this term to a small child, it is clear. The Qur'an does not specify how they met him: was he playing with a group of young boys, or was he alone? Was he a Muslim or an unbeliever? Was he isolated? Was he mature or a child? The name ghulam is more fitting for a child, and although it may include an adult, His saying ﴿without [its having killed] another soul﴾ is more fitting for an adult than for a child, because a child is not killed even if he kills. Furthermore, did he kill him by cutting off his head, or by striking his head against the wall, or by another means? There is nothing in the wording of the Qur'an that indicates any of these categories. Accordingly, Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Have you killed an innocent soul without [its having killed] another? You have certainly done a terrible thing.﴾ In this there are several discussions:

The first discussion: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (zakiyyatan) with an alif (zakiyatan? no: zakiyatan with alif, i.e., "zakiyatan" as "zākiyatan"), and the rest read (zakiyyatan) without an alif. Al-Kisa'i said: al-zākiyah and al-zakiyyah are two dialects, and their meaning is "pure." Abu 'Amr said: al-zākiyah is the one who has not sinned, and al-zakiyyah is the one who sinned and then repented.

The second discussion: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that Moses, peace be upon him, found it strange that one would kill a soul except in retaliation for a soul; but the matter is not so, because his blood may be made lawful by some other cause. The answer is that the strongest cause is that one.

The third discussion: nukr (terrible) is greater than imr (an extraordinary thing) in ugliness. This points to the fact that killing the boy is uglier than tearing the ship, because that was not the destruction of a soul, since it was possible that drowning would not occur; but here destruction certainly occurred, so it was more reprehensible. It is also said that His saying ﴿You have certainly done an extraordinary thing (shay'an imra)﴾ means "a wonder," and nukr is greater than wonder. It is also said that nukr is what the intellects deny and souls recoil from, so it is more emphatic in condemning a thing than imr. Some said: imr is greater, because tearing the ship leads to the destruction of many souls, whereas this killing is only the destruction of one person. Also, imr is a great calamity, so it is more emphatic than nukr. He, exalted is He, related that this scholar did nothing more than remind him of what he had pledged to him, saying: ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ This is the very same as what he had said in the first case, except that here he added the word "you" (laka), because this word emphasizes the rebuke. Accordingly, Moses said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, then do not keep me as your companion﴾, despite knowing how intensely he desired to accompany him. This is the speech of one deeply regretful. Then he said: ﴿You have even received an excuse from me﴾, meaning that he praises him in this manner, since he bore with him twice, first and second, despite the short time. Three points remain concerning the recitation of this verse:

The first: Nafi' according to the narration of Warsh and Qalun, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read (nukuran) with a damma on the kaf throughout the Qur'an, and the rest read it with a sukun on the kaf wherever it occurs; both are dialects.

The second: All read (la tusahibni) with an alif except Ya'qub, who read (la taskhbni) from sahiba, and the meaning is the same.

The third: Regarding (ladunni) there are several readings:

The first: the reading of Nafi' and Abu Bakr in some narrations from 'Asim: (min ladunni) with a light nun and a damma on the dal.

The second: Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs from 'Asim: (ladunni) with a doubled nun and a damma on the dal.

The third: Abu Bakr from 'Asim with ishmam and without prolonging.

The fourth: (min ludhni) with a damma on the lam and a sukun on the dal in some narrations from 'Asim. All these readings are dialects in this word.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 18, verses 77–78:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So they set out, until when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food, but they refused to entertain them. Then they found therein a wall about to collapse, so he repaired it. [Musa] said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ ﴿[The other] said: "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience."﴾

Know that the town was Antioch (Antakiyyah), and it was said that it was al-Aylah. Here there are some questions.

The first question: Asking for food is not the custom of noble people. So how did Musa, along with that scholar, undertake it? Because it was Musa's custom to present his need and ask for food. Do you not see that Allah related of him, in the story of Musa at the water of Madyan, that he said: ﴿My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾ [al-Qasas: 24]?

The answer: The undertaking of a hungry person to ask for food is a permissible matter in all the sacred laws. Indeed, it may even become obligatory when there is fear of severe harm.

The second question: Why did He say: ﴿until when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food﴾ when it would have been required to say: "asked them for food"?

The answer: Repetition may be for emphasis, like the saying of the poet:

*I wish the crow, on the morning it caws constantly, were a crow with its throat cut.*

The third question: Entertaining a guest is among the recommended acts (mandubat, acts whose performance is rewarded but whose omission is not sinful). So leaving it is leaving a recommended act, and that is not a reprehensible matter. How then is it permissible for Musa, peace be upon him, despite his high station, to become so severely angry at them that, because of it, he broke the covenant he had made with that scholar in his words: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, then do not accompany me﴾? Likewise, this kind of intense anger over not eating for a single night is not befitting even of the lowliest of people, let alone the one whom Allah spoke to directly.

The answer: As for your saying that entertaining a guest is recommended, we say: it may be recommended, but it may also be obligatory, namely when the guest has reached such a degree of hunger that, if he does not eat, he would die. When the situation is as we have described, the intense anger was not caused by abstaining from eating for one day. If they say: he had not reached the point of death, as is shown by his saying: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it,﴾ and he was seeking a wage for repairing that wall, and if he had reached the point of death from hunger, he would not have been able to do that work; so how could it be valid for him to seek a wage? We say: perhaps that hunger was severe, but it had not reached the limit of death. Then the Exalted said: ﴿but they refused to entertain them﴾, and in this there are two discussions.

The first discussion: *yudayyifuhuma* (they entertain them as guests). One says *dayyafahu* when he has a guest for him. Its original meaning is "he inclined toward him," from *dafa al-sahm 'an al-gharad* (the arrow deviated from the target). Its counterpart is *zarahu* from *al-izwiraar* (turning away). *Adafahu* and *dayyafahu* mean "he hosted him" or "made him his guest." It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "They were people of a town of base character."

The second discussion: I have seen in the books of narratives that when the people of that town heard the revelation of this verse, they were ashamed, and they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a load of gold and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we will pay this gold so that you change the *ba'* (ب) into a *ta'* (ت), so that the reading becomes thus: (*fa-atawu an yudayyifuhuma*)," meaning "they came (*atawu*) to entertain them," that is, the coming of the people of that town to them was for the purpose of hospitality. They said: "Our aim in this is that this baseness be removed from us." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refused and said: "Changing this single dot entails the entry of falsehood into the speech of Allah, and that entails a defect in divinity. So we know that changing a single dot in the Qur'an entails the invalidity of both lordship and servanthood."

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Then they found therein a wall about to collapse, so he repaired it.﴾ That is, they saw in the town a leaning wall. If it is said: How is it permissible to describe a wall with *irada* (wanting, intending), when wanting is one of the attributes of living beings? We say: this expression came by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*), and it has counterparts in poetry. He said:

*The spear wants the chest of Abu Baraa, and shies away from the blood of the Banu Uqayl.*

Al-Farra' recited:

*If a time that gathers my scattered affairs, indeed it is a time that intends kindness.*

And al-Ra'i said:

*In a desert waste I split their skulls, splitting like axes when they want to be blades.*

A counterpart of this in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿And when the anger subsided from Musa﴾ [al-A'raf: 154], and His saying: ﴿that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82], and His saying: ﴿They said, "We come willingly"﴾ [Fussilat: 11].

His saying: ﴿*an yanqaddh* (about to collapse)﴾: one says *inqadda* when its falling happens quickly, from *inqidad al-tair* (the swooping of a bird). It is the form *infa'ala*, the intransitive counterpart of *qadadtuhu*. It was also said that *inqadda* is a verb derived from *naqd* (breaking), like *ihmarra* from *humrah* (redness). It is also read as *an yunqada*, from *naqd*, and as *an yanqaad*, from *inqaadat al-'ayn*, when the eye splits lengthwise.

As for His saying: ﴿so he repaired it﴾, it was said: he tore it down and then rebuilt it. It was said: he set it upright with his hand. It was said: he wiped it with his hand, and it stood up and became straight, and that was one of his miracles.

Know that when that scholar did this, and the situation was one of compulsion and need for food, then because of that necessity, Musa forgot what he had said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, then do not accompany me.﴾ Therefore he said: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it,﴾ that is, you could have asked for a wage for your work, which you could spend on obtaining food and on obtaining other necessary needs. The first: Musa, peace be upon him, had stipulated that if he asked him another question after this, the parting would take place, when he said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, then do not accompany me.﴾ So when he mentioned this question, that scholar parted from him and said: ﴿This is the parting between me and you,﴾ meaning: this is the promised parting.

The second: His saying *hadha* refers to the third question, that is: this objection is the cause of the parting.

The second question: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿This is the parting between me and you﴾? The answer: Its meaning is: this is a separation that has occurred between me and you. The verbal noun (*masdar*) has been attributed to the time/place (*zarf*). So the meaning would be: this is the separation of our connection, meaning our union, like the saying of one who says: "May Allah disgrace the liar among me and you," meaning one of us. So when one says: "What is its *ta'wil*?" the meaning is: "What is its outcome?"

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 18, verses 77–78:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So they set out, until when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food, but they refused to entertain them. Then they found therein a wall about to collapse, so he repaired it. [Musa] said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ ﴿[The other] said: "This is the parting between me and you. I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience."﴾

Know that the town was Antioch (Antakiyyah), and it was said that it was al-Aylah. Here there are some questions.

The first question: Asking for food is not the custom of noble people. So how did Musa, along with that scholar, undertake it? Because it was Musa's custom to present his need and ask for food. Do you not see that Allah related of him, in the story of Musa at the water of Madyan, that he said: ﴿My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾ [al-Qasas: 24]?

The answer: The undertaking of a hungry person to ask for food is a permissible matter in all the sacred laws. Indeed, it may even become obligatory when there is fear of severe harm.

The second question: Why did He say: ﴿until when they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food﴾ when it would have been required to say: "asked them for food"?

The answer: Repetition may be for emphasis, like the saying of the poet:

*I wish the crow, on the morning it caws constantly, were a crow with its throat cut.*

The third question: Entertaining a guest is among the recommended acts (mandubat, acts whose performance is rewarded but whose omission is not sinful). So leaving it is leaving a recommended act, and that is not a reprehensible matter. How then is it permissible for Musa, peace be upon him, despite his high station, to become so severely angry at them that, because of it, he broke the covenant he had made with that scholar in his words: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, then do not accompany me﴾? Likewise, this kind of intense anger over not eating for a single night is not befitting even of the lowliest of people, let alone the one whom Allah spoke to directly.

The answer: As for your saying that entertaining a guest is recommended, we say: it may be recommended, but it may also be obligatory, namely when the guest has reached such a degree of hunger that, if he does not eat, he would die. When the situation is as we have described, the intense anger was not caused by abstaining from eating for one day. If they say: he had not reached the point of death, as is shown by his saying: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it,﴾ and he was seeking a wage for repairing that wall, and if he had reached the point of death from hunger, he would not have been able to do that work; so how could it be valid for him to seek a wage? We say: perhaps that hunger was severe, but it had not reached the limit of death. Then the Exalted said: ﴿but they refused to entertain them﴾, and in this there are two discussions.

The first discussion: *yudayyifuhuma* (they entertain them as guests). One says *dayyafahu* when he has a guest for him. Its original meaning is "he inclined toward him," from *dafa al-sahm 'an al-gharad* (the arrow deviated from the target). Its counterpart is *zarahu* from *al-izwiraar* (turning away). *Adafahu* and *dayyafahu* mean "he hosted him" or "made him his guest." It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "They were people of a town of base character."

The second discussion: I have seen in the books of narratives that when the people of that town heard the revelation of this verse, they were ashamed, and they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a load of gold and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we will pay this gold so that you change the *ba'* (ب) into a *ta'* (ت), so that the reading becomes thus: (*fa-atawu an yudayyifuhuma*)," meaning "they came (*atawu*) to entertain them," that is, the coming of the people of that town to them was for the purpose of hospitality. They said: "Our aim in this is that this baseness be removed from us." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refused and said: "Changing this single dot entails the entry of falsehood into the speech of Allah, and that entails a defect in divinity. So we know that changing a single dot in the Qur'an entails the invalidity of both lordship and servanthood."

We say: this expression came by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*), and it has counterparts in poetry. He said:

Al-Farra' recited:
