Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 79:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to some poor people who worked on the sea. I wished to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force﴾ ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers, and we feared lest he would burden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾ ﴿so we wished that their Lord would replace him for them with one better than him in purity and nearer in compassion﴾ ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and beneath it was a treasure belonging to them. Their father had been righteous. So your Lord wished that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord. I did not do it of my own accord. That is the interpretation of what you could not bear with patience﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that these three matters share one thing, namely that the rulings of the Prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, are based on outward appearances, as he (peace be upon him) said: "We judge by the outward, and Allah takes care of the inward (sara'ir)."

This scholar's rulings were not based on the outward appearances of affairs, but on the real causes existing in reality itself. That is because the outward appearance is that it is forbidden to dispose of people's property and lives: in the first matter, and in the second, without an apparent cause that permits that disposal. For damaging the boat is a diminution of a person's ownership without an apparent cause, and killing the boy is the destruction of a protected soul without an apparent cause, and undertaking to erect that leaning wall in the third matter is bearing toil and hardship without an apparent cause. In these three matters, the ruling of that scholar was not based on apparent, known causes, but on causes that are considered in reality itself. This indicates that that scholar had been given by Allah a rational power by which he was able to oversee the inner dimensions of affairs and to perceive by it the realities of things. Thus the rank of Moses (peace be upon him) in knowing the laws and rulings was building matters upon outward appearances, whereas this scholar's rank was standing upon the inner dimensions of things, the realities of affairs, and perceiving their hidden secrets. By this path it became clear that his rank in knowledge was above the rank of Moses (peace be upon him). Having understood this, we say: the three matters are based on one principle, namely that when two harms conflict, the lesser must be borne to prevent the greater. This is the accepted principle in the three matters.

As for the first matter: that scholar knew that if he did not damage that boat, that king would seize it, and its benefits would be entirely lost to its owners. So there arose a conflict between damaging and defecting it, whereby it would remain with its owners, and not damaging it, whereby the king would seize it and its benefits would be entirely lost to its owners. There is no doubt that the first harm is smaller, so it was obligatory to bear it to prevent the second, which is greater than both.

As for the second matter: likewise, because the boy's remaining alive was a corruption to the parents in their religion and in their worldly life. Perhaps he knew through revelation that the harms arising from killing that boy were less than the harms arising from the occurrence of those corruptions to the two parents. For this reason he proceeded to kill him.

The third matter: likewise, because the hardship resulting from undertaking to erect that wall is less harmful than its falling; for if it had fallen, the wealth of those orphans would have been lost, and that involves severe harm. The conclusion is that that scholar was specially endowed with standing upon the inner dimensions of things and with perceiving their realities as they are in themselves, and he was specially endowed with founding the real rulings upon those inner states. As for Moses (peace be upon him), he was not like that, but his rulings were based on the outward appearances of affairs; therefore the disparity between them in knowledge became evident. If someone says: the sum of the matter is that He, may He be exalted, made him perceive the inner dimensions of things and their realities in themselves, and this kind of knowledge cannot be learned, and Moses (peace be upon him) went to him only to learn knowledge from him; so it was obligatory for that scholar to show him knowledge that could be learned, and these three matters are sciences that cannot be learned; so what is the benefit in mentioning and displaying them? The answer: knowledge of the outward dimensions of things can be acquired on the basis of knowing the outward laws, whereas knowledge of the inner dimensions of things can only be acquired on the basis of purifying the inner self, stripping the soul, and cleansing the heart of bodily attachments. For this reason He, may He be exalted, said in describing the knowledge of that scholar: ﴿And We taught him knowledge from Us﴾ (al-Kahf: 65). Then, when Moses (peace be upon him) had perfected his rank in the knowledge of the Law, Allah sent him to this scholar so that Moses (peace be upon him) would know that the perfection of rank lies in a person passing from the knowledge of the Law, which is based on outward appearances, to the knowledge of the inner dimensions, which is based on overseeing inner dimensions and perceiving the realities of affairs.

The second issue: Know that that scholar answered the first matter with his saying: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to some poor people who worked on the sea. I wished to damage it, for behind them was a king who seized every boat by force﴾. In it there are several benefits:

The first benefit: that boat belonged to people who were needy, making their living by it on the sea, and Allah, exalted is He, named them "masakin" (the poor). Know that al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, argued from this verse that the condition of the faqir (one in dire need) in hardship and need is worse than that of the miskin; for He, exalted is He, called them masakin although they owned that boat.

The second benefit: the meaning of that scholar in this statement is that my purpose in damaging that boat was not to drown its people; rather my purpose was that that oppressive king used to seize boats that were free of defects, so I made this boat defective so that the oppressor would not seize it, for the harm of this damage is easier than the harm resulting from that seizure. If it is asked: is it permissible for a stranger to dispose of another's property for such a purpose?

We say: this is among the matters whose rulings vary according to the difference of the laws. Perhaps this meaning was permissible in that law; as for in our law, such a ruling is not far-fetched, for if we know that highwaymen take all of a person's property, and if we give the highwayman part of that wealth, the rest is saved, then it is good for us to give part of that person's property to the highwayman so that the rest is saved; and this would be counted by us as a kindness to that owner.

The third benefit: that damage had to be carried out in a manner whereby that boat was not entirely destroyed, for if it were so, the harm resulting from its seizure would not be greater than the harm resulting from its damage, and then its damage would not be permissible.

The fourth benefit: the word "wara'" in His saying ﴿and behind them﴾ has two opinions:

The first: that what is meant by it is "and in front of them there was a king who seized," thus said al-Farra'.

And its explanation is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Before them is Hell﴾ (al-Jathiyah: 10), meaning "in front of them." Likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they leave behind them a heavy day﴾ (al-Insan: 27). Its verification is that everything that is hidden from you has been concealed from you, and you are concealed from it; so everything that is absent from you is "wara'aka" (behind you). The front and before of a thing, when it is absent from you and concealed from you, is not far from the application of the word "wara'" to it.

The second opinion: it is possible that the king was from behind the place from which the boat's owner would sail, and the boat's return was toward him.

**The second question, the killing of the boy.** The scholar answered it by saying: ﴿As for the boy, his parents were believers﴾. It has been said that this boy had reached maturity (bulugh), that he was a highway robber, and that he committed reprehensible deeds. His parents needed to ward off people's evil from him, to defend him, and to deny anyone who accused him of any of these reprehensible acts. That would have led them into wrongdoing (fisq), and perhaps that wrongdoing would have led to disbelief (kufr). It has also been said that he was a child, but God Most High knew that if he reached maturity these corruptions would arise from him.

As for His words, ﴿so We feared that he would overburden them with rebellion and disbelief﴾: "fear" (khashyah) here means dread and the predominance of assumption (ghalabat al-zann). God Most High had permitted the scholar to kill anyone whose corruption of this kind was strongly presumed to arise from him.

As for His words, ﴿that he would overburden them with rebellion﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: the meaning is that this boy would drive his parents toward rebellion and disbelief, as in His words, ﴿and do not burden me in my affair with hardship﴾ (Al-Kahf: 73), meaning: do not force me into hardship and constraint. This is because his parents, out of love for the child, need to defend him, and perhaps they would need to go along with him in those reprehensible deeds.

The second: the meaning is that this child kept company with them in the manner of rebellious disbelievers. If it is asked: is it permissible to kill a person on the basis of such an assumption? We say: if that assumption is confirmed by revelation from God, it is permissible. Then God Most High said: ﴿so We intended that their Lord replace him for them with one better than him in purity﴾. That is: We intended that God Most High grant them a child better than this boy in purity (zakāh), meaning in religion and righteousness. It has been said that the mention of zakāh here is in contrast to Moses's words, peace be upon him: ﴿Have you killed an innocent soul without [its having killed] another?﴾. So the scholar said: We intended that God grant these two parents, in place of this son, a child who would be better than him in the way you mentioned concerning purity. The meaning of zakāh here would be purity. It is as if Moses, peace be upon him, had said: "Have you killed a pure soul, because it had not reached the limit of maturity, and so it was pure and clean of sins?" The scholar replied: although that soul was pure and clean in its present state, God knew of it that, once it reached maturity, it would commit rebellion and disbelief. So We intended to give them a child greater in purity and cleanness than him, one of whom God knows that, at maturity, he will not commit any of these forbidden acts.

Whoever said that this boy had reached maturity holds that the meaning of describing his soul as pure is that nothing had appeared from him that would necessitate killing him.

Then He said: ﴿and nearer in compassion﴾, meaning that this replacement would be nearer in tenderness and compassion toward his parents, by being more dutiful and more caring toward them. Ruhm means compassion and tenderness. It is narrated that they had a daughter, who married a prophet, and she gave birth to a prophet through whose hands God guided a great community.

**Two points of recitation (qira'ah) remain among the issues of this verse:**

The first: Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited (يُبَدِّلَهُما) with a fatha on the bā' and a shaddah on the dāl. Likewise in Surat al-Tahrim: (أنْ يُبَدِّلَهُ أزْواجًا), and in Surat al-Qalam: (عَسى رَبُّنا أنْ يُبَدِّلَنا). The rest recited it with a sukūn on the bā' and a light dāl. Both are dialects: abdala yubdilu and baddala yubaddilu.

The second: Ibn 'Amir, in one of the two transmissions from Abu 'Amr, recited (رُحُمًا) with a ḍammah on the ḥā'. The rest recited it with a sukūn on it. Both are dialects, like nukr and nukur, and shughl and shughul.

**As for the third question, the erection of the wall:** the scholar answered it by saying that the reason for doing so was that there was a treasure beneath that wall, and it belonged to two orphans in that town, whose father had been righteous. Since that wall was about to collapse, and if it had fallen the treasure would have been lost, God willed to preserve that treasure for those two orphans, out of care for their right and out of regard for the righteousness of their father. So He commanded me to erect that wall in order to safeguard these interests.

In the verse there are several benefits.

The first benefit: God named that place a town (qaryah) when He said, ﴿When they came to the people of a town﴾, and He also called it a city (madinah) when He said, ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city﴾.

The second benefit: The scholars differed about this treasure (kanz). It was said that it was wealth, and this is the sound view, for two reasons. The first is that what is understood from the word kanz is wealth. The second is that His words, ﴿and they would extract their treasure﴾, indicate that this treasure was wealth. It was also said that it was knowledge, based on His words, ﴿and their father had been righteous﴾, since a righteous man's treasure is knowledge and not wealth, because hoarding wealth does not befit righteousness. This is based on the saying of God the Exalted: ﴿Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of Allah — give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [At-Tawbah: 34]. It was also said that it was a tablet of gold on which was written: "I am amazed at one who believes in divine decree (qadar) yet grieves; I am amazed at one who believes in provision yet toils; I am amazed at one who believes in death yet rejoices; I am amazed at one who believes in reckoning yet is heedless; I am amazed at one who knows the world and its turning with its people yet feels secure in it. There is no god but Allah; Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah."

The third benefit: His words, ﴿and their father had been righteous﴾, indicate that the righteousness of fathers brings care for the conditions of their children. It is narrated from Ja'far ibn Muhammad that there were seven generations of fathers between the two boys and the righteous father. It is narrated from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali that he said to one of the Kharijites (a dissenting sect) in a discussion that took place between them: "By what did Allah preserve the wealth of the two boys?" He replied: "By the righteousness of their father." He said: "Then are my father and my grandfather better than him?" He replied: "Allah has informed us that you are a contentious people."

It is also mentioned that the righteous father used to have people deposit their trusts with him, and he would return them to them safely.

If it is asked: Did either of the two orphans know of the treasure's existence beneath that wall, or did neither of them know? If the former, it would be impossible for them to leave the wall to collapse. If the latter, how could they, after reaching maturity, extract that treasure and benefit from it?

The answer: Perhaps the two orphans were unaware of it, but their guardian (wasi) knew of it. Then that guardian went away, and the wall came close to collapse in his absence. When the scholar had established these answers, he said: ﴿a mercy from your Lord﴾, meaning: I did these deeds only so that God's mercy would appear, because all of them return to one principle, which is bearing the lesser harm to prevent the greater harm, as we have explained.

Then he said: ﴿And I did it not upon my own order﴾, meaning: I did not do what you saw of these matters by my own command, judgment, or opinion. Rather, I did it by the command and revelation of Allah, because undertaking to diminish people's property and shed their blood is not permissible except by revelation and a decisive text.

A question remains in the verse. He said: ﴿So I intended to damage it﴾, and He said: ﴿so we intended that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity﴾, and He said: ﴿So your Lord intended that they reach their maturity﴾. How did the attribution of these three intentions differ, when all of them concern one story and one act?

The answer: When he mentioned the defect, he attributed it to his own intention, saying: "I intended to damage it." When he mentioned the killing, he expressed himself with the plural form, as an indication that he was among the great in the sciences of wisdom, and so he would not undertake this killing except for a lofty wisdom. When he mentioned the care for the interests of the two orphans on account of their father's righteousness, he attributed it to God the Exalted, because the one who takes charge of the interests of children out of regard for the rights of their fathers is none other than Allah, glorified and exalted.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 83–85:

Page 139
His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say: "I will recite to you a remembrance of him."﴾ ﴿Indeed, We established him on the earth and gave him of every thing a means.﴾ ﴿So he followed a means.﴾

Know that this is the fourth story among the stories mentioned in this surah, and it contains several issues.

The first issue: We have mentioned at the beginning of this surah that the Jews instructed the polytheists to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the story of the People of the Cave, the story of Dhul-Qarnayn, and the Spirit. Therefore, what is meant by His saying, ﴿They ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn﴾, is that question.

The second issue: People have differed about who Dhul-Qarnayn was, and they have mentioned several opinions.

The first: that he is Alexander the son of Philip the Greek. They said: The evidence for this is that the Qur'an indicates that the man called Dhul-Qarnayn had a kingdom that reached the farthest west, as shown by His saying, ﴿until, when he reached the setting place of the sun, he found it setting in a murky spring﴾ [al-Kahf: 86]. Also, his kingdom reached the farthest east, as shown by His saying, ﴿until, when he reached the rising place of the sun﴾ [al-Kahf: 90]. Also, his kingdom reached the farthest north, as evidenced by the fact that Gog and Magog are a people of the Turks who dwell in the farthest north, and by the fact that the barrier mentioned in the Qur'an is said in the books of history to have been built in the farthest north. So this man called Dhul-Qarnayn in the Qur'an, the Qur'an has indicated that his kingdom reached the farthest west, east and north, and this is the whole of the inhabited part of the earth. Such a sweeping kingdom is certainly contrary to customary norms, and if it were so, his remembrance would have to remain perpetuated throughout time and would not remain hidden and concealed. The king who is famous in the books of history as having had a kingdom reaching this extent is none other than Alexander. That is because, when his father died, he united the kings of Rome, who had been separate groups, then he united the kings of the West and subdued them, and pressed on until he reached the Green Sea (the Mediterranean). Then he returned to Egypt, built Alexandria and named it after himself. Then he entered al-Sham and headed for the Children of Israel, came to Bayt al-Maqdis, and slaughtered at its altar. Then he turned toward Armenia and the Gate of Gates (Bab al-Abwab), and the Iraqis, the Copts and the Berbers submitted to him. Then he headed toward Dara son of Dara and defeated him several times until his bodyguard killed him; thus Alexander seized the realms of the Persians. Then he headed for India and China, raided distant peoples, returned to Khurasan and built many cities, returned to Iraq, fell ill at Shahrazur, and died there.

Since it has been established by the Qur'an that Dhul-Qarnayn was a man who ruled the earth entirely, or nearly so, and it has been established by the science of history that the one whose situation was this was none other than Alexander, it is necessary to conclude with certainty that what is meant by Dhul-Qarnayn is Alexander the son of Philip the Greek. Then they mentioned several reasons for his being given this name:

The first: he was given this title because he reached the two horns of the sun, that is, its rising and its setting, just as Ardashir son of Bahman was titled "the long-handed," because his command was effective wherever he willed.

The second: the Persians said that Dara the Elder had married a daughter of Philip. When he drew near to her, he found an offensive odour from her, so he returned her to her father Philip. She had become pregnant by him with Alexander, and after she returned to her father she gave birth to Alexander. Alexander remained with Philip, and Philip showed that he was his son, though in reality he was the son of Dara the Elder. They said: The evidence for this is that when Alexander reached Dara son of Dara, while he still had a breath of life, he placed his head in his lap and said to Dara: "O my father, tell me who did this to you so that I may avenge you upon him!" This is what the Persians said. They said: On this assumption, Alexander's father was Dara the Elder and his mother was a daughter of Philip, so he was born of two different origins, the Persians and the Romans. They mentioned this only because they wanted to make him descend from the lineage of the kings of the non-Arabs, so that no king like him would be of a lineage other than the lineage of the kings of the non-Arabs. In reality this is a lie. Alexander said to Dara, "O my father," only as a gesture of humility, and Dara was honoured by that address.

The second opinion: Abu al-Rayhan al-Harawi the astrologer said in his book which he called "The Remaining Traces of Past Generations": It has been said that Dhul-Qarnayn was Abu Karib Shimr ibn Ubayr ibn Afriqish al-Himyari, for his kingdom reached the eastern and western ends of the earth. He is the one whom one of the poets from Himyar took pride in, when he said:

Before me Dhul-Qarnayn was a Muslim, a king who rose high on the earth, not weak-minded,
He reached the east and the west, seeking the means of kingship from a noble lord.

Then Abu al-Rayhan said: This opinion is likely to be closer to the truth, because the Adhwa' were from Yemen, and their names are not free of "Dhu Kadhi al-Nadi," "Dhu Nuwas," "Dhu al-Nun," and others.

The third opinion: he was a righteous servant whom Allah empowered over the earth, gave knowledge and wisdom, and clothed with awe, though we do not know who he was. Then they mentioned several reasons for his being called Dhul-Qarnayn:

The first: Ibn al-Kawwa asked Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, about Dhul-Qarnayn, and said: Was he a king or a prophet? He said: "Neither a king nor a prophet; he was a righteous servant who was struck on his right horn in obedience to Allah, and died; then Allah revived him, and he was struck on his left horn, and died; then Allah revived him. Thus he was called Dhul-Qarnayn, and the kingdom was his."

The second: He was called Dhul-Qarnayn because two generations of people passed away in his time.

The third: It has been said that the two sides of his head were of copper.

The fourth: There was on his head something resembling two horns.

The fifth: His crown had two horns.

The sixth: From the Prophet (ﷺ): "He was called Dhul-Qarnayn because he traversed the two horns of the world, meaning its east and its west."

The seventh: He had two horns, that is, two braids.

The eighth: Allah the Exalted subjected to him light and darkness, so when he travelled, light guided him from in front of him, and darkness drove him on from behind him.

The ninth: It is possible that he was given this title for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram, as if he butts his opponents.

The tenth: He saw in a dream that he ascended to the heavens and grasped the two extremities of the sun, its horns and its sides, so he was called Dhul-Qarnayn for this reason.

The eleventh: He was called this because he entered light and darkness.

The fourth opinion: that Dhul-Qarnayn was one of the angels. It is related from Umar that he heard a man say, "O Dhul-Qarnayn!" and he said: "O Allah, forgive us! Are you not content to be named after the prophets, that you must be named after the angels!"

This is the sum of what has been said on this subject. The first opinion is the most apparent, because of the evidence we have mentioned, namely that such a great king must be well known among the people of the world, and the one who is well known for such a great kingdom is Alexander. Therefore it is necessary that what is meant by Dhul-Qarnayn is precisely him. However, there is a strong difficulty in this: he was a student of the sage Aristotle and was upon his doctrine, so Allah's exalting him would necessitate ruling that Aristotle's doctrine is true and correct, and that is something with no way to it. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: They differed over whether Dhul-Qarnayn was among the prophets or not. Some of them said he was a prophet, and they argued for this with several points:

The first: His saying, ﴿Indeed, We established him on the earth﴾. The better interpretation of it is that it refers to establishment in religion, and complete establishment in religion is prophethood.

The second: His saying, ﴿and gave him of every thing a means﴾. Among "every thing" is prophethood, so the generality in His saying ﴿and gave him of every thing a means﴾ requires that He gave him a means in prophethood.

The third: His exalted saying, ﴿We said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either punish them or take towards them a goodly course"﴾ [al-Kahf: 86]. Whoever Allah speaks with must necessarily be a prophet. Others said he was a righteous servant and was not a prophet.

The fourth issue: Concerning the particle sin in His saying ﴿sa-atlu﴾ ("I will recite"), its meaning is: "I will do this, if Allah the Exalted grants me success in it, and reveals to me a revelation concerning it, and informs me of the manner of that situation." As for His saying, ﴿Indeed, We established him on the earth﴾, this establishment may be understood to mean establishment by means of prophethood, and it may be understood to mean establishment by means of kingship, in that he ruled the eastern and western parts of the earth. The first is preferable, because establishment by means of prophethood is higher than establishment by means of kingship, and it is better to interpret the speech of Allah in its most perfect and excellent sense. Then He said, ﴿and gave him of every thing a means﴾. They said: The word sabab (means) in its original linguistic sense is an expression for a rope, and then it was borrowed for everything by which one reaches a goal, and it includes knowledge, power and instruments. So His saying ﴿and gave him of every thing a means﴾ means: We gave him, from every thing, of the affairs by which he could attain the acquisition of that thing. Then those who said he was a prophet said: Among "every thing" is prophethood, so this verse indicates that Allah the Exalted gave him the path by which he could reach the attainment of prophethood. Those who denied that he was a prophet said: What is meant is that He gave him, from every thing he needed in setting right his kingdom, a means. However, one might say: specifying the general is contrary to the apparent sense, so one should not resort to it except with evidence. Then He said, ﴿So he followed a means﴾, meaning that when Allah the Exalted had given him a means to every thing, whenever he wished something he followed a means that would bring him to it and bring it near to him. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (fa-ittaba'a) with a doubled ta', and likewise (thumma ittaba'a), meaning he took a path and travelled. The rest read fa-atba'a with a cut alif and a sukun on the ta', without doubling.

The fourth: There was on his head something resembling two horns.

The fifth: His crown had two horns.

The sixth: From the Prophet (ﷺ): "He was called Dhul-Qarnayn because he traversed the two horns of the world, meaning its east and its west."

The seventh: He had two horns, that is, two braids.

The eighth: Allah the Exalted subjected to him light and darkness, so when he travelled, light guided him from in front of him, and darkness drove him on from behind him.

The ninth: It is possible that he was given this title for his bravery, just as a brave man is called a ram, as if he butts his opponents.

The tenth: He saw in a dream that he ascended to the heavens and grasped the two extremities of the sun, its horns and its sides, so he was called Dhul-Qarnayn for this reason.

The eleventh: He was called this because he entered light and darkness.

The fourth opinion: that Dhul-Qarnayn was one of the angels. It is related from Umar that he heard a man say, "O Dhul-Qarnayn!" and he said: "O Allah, forgive us! Are you not content to be named after the prophets, that you must be named after the angels!"

This is the sum of what has been said on this subject. The first opinion is the most apparent, because of the evidence we have mentioned, namely that such a great king must be well known among the people of the world, and the one who is well known for such a great kingdom is Alexander. Therefore it is necessary that what is meant by Dhul-Qarnayn is precisely him. However, there is a strong difficulty in this: he was a student of the sage Aristotle and was upon his doctrine, so Allah's exalting him would necessitate ruling that Aristotle's doctrine is true and correct, and that is something with no way to it. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: They differed over whether Dhul-Qarnayn was among the prophets or not. Some of them said he was a prophet, and they argued for this with several points:

The first: His saying, ﴿Indeed, We established him on the earth﴾. The better interpretation of it is that it refers to establishment in religion, and complete establishment in religion is prophethood.

The second: His saying, ﴿and gave him of every thing a means﴾. Among "every thing" is prophethood, so the generality in His saying ﴿and gave him of every thing a means﴾ requires that He gave him a means in prophethood.

The third: His exalted saying, ﴿We said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, either punish them or take towards them a goodly course"﴾ [al-Kahf: 86]. Whoever Allah speaks with must necessarily be a prophet. Others said he was a righteous servant and was not a prophet.

The rest read fa-atba'a with a cut alif and a sukun on the ta', without doubling.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 86–88:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Until, when he reached the setting-place of the sun, he found it setting in a murky spring, and he found near it a people. We said: "O Dhu'l-Qarnayn, either you punish them, or you adopt towards them a good course."﴾ ﴿He said: "As for him who does wrong, we shall punish him, then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment."﴾ ﴿"But as for him who believes and does righteous deeds, he shall have a reward, the best, and we shall speak to him of our command with ease."﴾

Know that the meaning is that he intended to reach the setting-place, so he followed a means that would bring him to it, until he reached it. As for His statement, ﴿he found it setting in a murky spring﴾, there are several discussions:

The first: Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read ﴿فِي عَيْنٍ حامِيَةٍ﴾ (in a hot spring) with an alif and without a hamzah, meaning "hot." It is also reported from Abu Dharr that he said: "I was riding behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a camel, and he saw the sun when it set, and he said: 'Do you know, O Abu Dharr, where this sets?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It sets in a hot spring.'" This is the recitation (qira'ah) of Ibn Mas'ud and Talhah, and of Ibn 'Amir. The rest read ﴿حَمِئَةٍ﴾ (murky), which is the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas. It happened that Ibn 'Abbas was with Mu'awiyah, and Mu'awiyah recited ﴿حامِيَةٍ﴾ with an alif, so Ibn 'Abbas said: "﴿حَمِئَةٍ﴾." Mu'awiyah then said to 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar: "How do you recite?" He said: "As the Commander of the Believers recites." Then he turned to Ka'b al-Ahbar: "How do you find the sun setting?" He said: "In water and mud. So we find it in the Torah." The murky (ḥamiʾah) is that which contains water and black sludge. Know that there is no contradiction between ﴿حَمِئَةٍ﴾ and ﴿حامِيَةٍ﴾; it is permissible that the spring combines both descriptions together.

The second: It has been established by proof that the earth is a sphere and that the heaven encompasses it, and there is no doubt that the sun is in the orbit (falak). Also He said: ﴿and he found near it a people﴾, and it is known that the sitting of a people close to the sun is not possible. Also, the sun is many times larger than the earth, so how is its entry into one of the springs of the earth conceivable? If this is established, we say: the interpretation of His statement ﴿it sets in a murky spring﴾ is in several respects:

The first: When Dhu'l-Qarnayn reached its place in the west, and no inhabited places remained beyond it, he found the sun as if it were setting in a dark depression. Although it is not so in reality, just as the one riding the sea sees the sun as if it sets in the sea when he does not see the shore, while in reality it sets beyond the sea. This is the interpretation that Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i mentioned in his tafsir.

The second: The western side of the earth has dwellings surrounded by the sea. The one looking at the sun imagines that it sets in those seas. There is no doubt that the western seas are very hot, so they are hot, and they are also murky because of the abundance of black sludge and water in them. So His statement ﴿it sets in a murky spring﴾ is an indication that the western side of the earth is surrounded by the sea, and it is a place of intense heat.

The third: The people of reports (ahl al-akhbar) said: the sun sets in a spring abundant in water and sludge. This is far-fetched, because when we observe a lunar eclipse and consider it, and we see that the people of the west say: this eclipse happened at the beginning of the night, and we see that the people of the east say: it happened at the beginning of the day, we know that the beginning of the night for the people of the west is the beginning of the second day for the people of the east. Rather, that time which is the beginning of the night for us is the time of 'asr in one land, the time of zuhr in another land, the time of forenoon (ḍaḥwah) in a third land, the time of sunrise in a fourth land, and midnight in a fifth land. Since these states are known after induction and consideration, and we know that the sun is rising and visible at all these times, what is said, that it sets in mud and sludge, would be a statement contrary to certainty, and the speech of Allah the Exalted is free of this accusation. Thus nothing remains but to resort to the interpretation we have mentioned.

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and he found near it a people﴾. To what does the pronoun in His statement ʿindahā ("near it") refer? In this there are two opinions:

The first: that it refers to the sun, and the feminine is for the sun, because when a person imagined that the sun sets there, the inhabitants of this place were as if they lived near the sun.

The second opinion: that the pronoun refers to the hot spring, and according to this opinion the interpretation is what we have mentioned. Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿We said: "O Dhu'l-Qarnayn, either you punish them, or you adopt towards them a good course."﴾ There are discussions concerning this:

The first: His statement, the Exalted, ﴿We said: "O Dhu'l-Qarnayn, either you punish them, or you adopt towards them a good course"﴾ indicates that He, the Exalted, spoke with him without an intermediary, and this indicates that he was a prophet. This wording is interpreted to mean that He addressed him through the tongues of some prophets, and this is a departure from the apparent meaning.

The second discussion: The people of reports said wondrous things about the description of that place. Ibn Jurayj said: there is a city there which has twelve thousand gates; were it not for the voices of its people, people would hear the crash of the sun when it sets.

The third discussion: His statement, the Exalted, ﴿We said: "O Dhu'l-Qarnayn, either you punish them, or you adopt towards them a good course"﴾ indicates that the inhabitants of the far west were disbelievers. So Allah gave Dhu'l-Qarnayn the choice regarding them between punishing them if they persisted in their disbelief, and bestowing favour upon them and pardoning them. This choice is in the sense of striving for the better of the two matters, just as He gave His Prophet ﷺ the choice between bestowing favour upon the polytheists and killing them. Most scholars said: this punishment is killing, and as for adopting a good course towards them, it is leaving them alive. Then Dhu'l-Qarnayn said: ﴿As for him who does wrong﴾, that is, who wronged himself by persisting in disbelief. The evidence that this is the intended meaning is that he mentioned in contrast: ﴿But as for him who believes and does righteous deeds﴾. Then he said: ﴿we shall punish him﴾, that is, with killing in this world. ﴿Then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment﴾, that is, a dreadful, abhorrent punishment. ﴿But as for him who believes and does righteous deeds, he shall have a reward, the best﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read ﴿جَزاءً الحُسْنى﴾ with nasb (accusative) and tanwin, while the rest read it with raf' (nominative) and idafah (construct, annexation). According to the first recitation, the sense is: "So for him is the best as a reward," just as you say: "This garment is yours as a gift." As for the second recitation, there are two interpretations in tafsir:

The first: so for him is the reward of the good deed, and the good deed is faith and righteous action.

The second: that the sense is: so for him is the reward, the best recompense, and the meaning is: for him is this reward which is the best recompense, and the reward is described as the best recompense. The annexation of the described to its description is well known, as in His statement: ﴿And surely the abode of the Hereafter﴾ (al-An'am: 32) and ﴿the truth of certainty﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 95). Then He said: ﴿and we shall speak to him of our command with ease﴾, that is, we shall not command him with what is difficult and burdensome, but with what is easy and facilitated, from zakat, kharaj, and others. The estimate of this is: "ease" (yusr), as in His statement: (﴿a gentle word﴾) (al-Isra': 28). It is also recited as yusuran with two dammahs.

According to the first recitation, the sense is: "So for him is the best as a reward," just as you say: "This garment is yours as a gift." As for the second recitation, there are two interpretations in tafsir:

The first: so for him is the reward of the good deed, and the good deed is faith and righteous action.

The second: that the sense is: so for him is the reward, the best recompense, and the meaning is: for him is this reward which is the best recompense, and the reward is described as the best recompense. Then He said: ﴿and we shall speak to him of our command with ease﴾, that is, we shall not command him with what is difficult and burdensome, but with what is easy and facilitated, from zakat, kharaj, and others. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 89–91:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then he followed a path﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the rising place of the sun, he found it rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter from it﴾ ﴿Thus. And We had full knowledge of what was with him.﴾

Know that when Allah, may He be exalted, first explained that he (Dhu al-Qarnayn) had headed to the nearest of the inhabited places to the setting of the sun, He followed this with an explanation that he had headed to the nearest of the inhabited places to the rising of the sun. Allah the Exalted explained that he found the sun rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter from it. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: there is no tree, no mountain, and no buildings there that would block the rays of the sun from falling upon them. For this reason, when the sun rises, they enter into holes that extend deep into the earth or they dive into the water. Thus, at sunrise it becomes impossible for them to conduct their livelihood, and at sunset they occupy themselves with securing their livelihood needs. Their condition is the opposite of the conditions of the rest of creation.

The second opinion: its meaning is that they have no clothing, and they are always naked like the other animals. It is said in the books of astronomy (al-Hay'a) that the condition of most of the Zanj is like this, and the condition of everyone who lives in the lands near the equator is like this as well. It is mentioned in the books of tafsir that one of them said: "I traveled until I passed China, and I asked about these people. It was said: 'Between you and them is a journey of one day and one night.' So I reached them, and behold, one of them spreads out one of his ears and wears the other. When the sunrise drew near, I heard a sound like a clamor, and I fainted. Then I regained consciousness, and they were rubbing me with oil. When the sun rose, behold, it was above the water like oil. Then they brought us into a hole of theirs. When the day grew bright, they began to catch fish and throw it in the sun, and it would cook."

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Thus. And We had full knowledge of what was with him.﴾ Concerning this there are several aspects:

The first: that is, thus did Dhu al-Qarnayn follow these means until he reached what he reached, and We knew, when We granted him authority, what he possessed of fitness for that kingship and for being independent in it.

The second: thus did Allah arrange the affair of these people as He had informed His Messenger, peace be upon him, in this remembrance.

The third: thus was his conduct with the people of the rising place as it was with the people of the setting place. He judged concerning these as he judged concerning those, from punishing the wrongdoers and doing good to the believers.

The fourth: the speech is complete at His saying "thus," and the meaning is that He, the Exalted, said: He arranged the affair of these people as Dhu al-Qarnayn found them. Then He said after it: ﴿And We had full knowledge of what was with him﴾, meaning: We were aware that the matter was so.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 18, verses 92–95:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then he followed a way﴾ ﴿until, when he reached the place between the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could hardly understand any speech﴾ ﴿They said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the earth. So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set a barrier between us and them?"﴾ ﴿He said, "That in which my Lord has established me is better. So help me with strength, and I will make between you and them a rampart."﴾

Know that when Dhul-Qarnayn reached the east and the west, he followed another way and travelled the path until he reached the place between the two barriers. Allah had given him knowledge and power sufficient to undertake these matters. Here there are several discussions:

**The first:** Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *al-Saddayn* with a *damm* (ḍamma, vowel u) on the *sin* and *saddan* with a *fath* (fatha, vowel a) wherever it occurs. Hafs, from 'Asim, reads both with a *fath* throughout the Qur'an. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read both with a *damm* throughout the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *al-Saddayn* and *saddan* here with a *fath* on the *sin*, and with a *damm* in Ya-Sin in both places. Al-Kisa'i said: "They are two dialects." It has also been said: what is made by the hand of the children of Adam is *al-sadd* with a *fath* on the *sin*, and what is made by the making of Allah is *al-sudd* with a *damm* on the *sin*; its plural is *sudad*. This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn al-Anbari. The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's exegesis) said: *al-sudd* with a *damm* is a form (*fu'l*) in the sense of a passive participle (*maf'ul*), i.e. it is what Allah made and created; and *al-sadd* with a *fath* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) denoting an event that people bring about.

**The second:** The more apparent view is that the place of the two barriers is in the northern region. It has been said: they are two mountains between Armenia and Adharbayjan. It has also been said: this place is at the furthest end of the land of the Turks. Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari related in his *Tarikh* that the ruler of Adharbayjan, at the time of its conquest, sent a man to it from the direction of the Khazar, and he witnessed it and described it as a lofty structure behind a deep, firm and impregnable trench. Ibn Khurdadhbah mentioned in his book *al-Masalik wa al-Mamalik* that al-Wathiq billah saw in a dream as if he had opened this rampart. So he sent some of his servants to see it, and they set out from the Gate of Gates (Bab al-Abwab) until they reached it and witnessed it. They described it as a structure of iron bricks bound with molten copper, with a locked gate upon it. Then, when that man tried to return, the guide led them out to the lands adjoining Samarqand. Abu al-Rayhan said: what this implies is that its location is in the north-western quarter of the inhabited world. And Allah knows the reality of the matter best.

**The third:** When Dhul-Qarnayn reached what lay between the two barriers, he found beyond them, i.e. behind them, passing beyond them, ﴿a people﴾, i.e. a nation of humankind, ﴿who could hardly understand any speech﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *yufaqqihuna* with a *damm* on the *ya* and a *kasra* on the *qaf*, in the sense that it was not possible for them to make others understand. The rest read it with a *fath* on the *ya* and the *qaf*. The meaning is that they did not know any language other than their own, and they did not understand the tongue in which Dhul-Qarnayn spoke. Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "O Dhul-Qarnayn, indeed Gog and Magog are corrupters in the earth."﴾

If it is asked: how did Dhul-Qarnayn understand this speech from them after Allah had described them with His saying, ﴿who could hardly understand any speech﴾? The answer: there are two views concerning *kad* (to be nearly/hardly).

The first: its affirmation is a negation and its negation is an affirmation. So His saying, ﴿who could hardly understand any speech﴾ does not indicate that they understand nothing at all; rather it indicates that they may understand, but with difficulty and hardship.

The second view: *kad* means "to be near to", and according to this view His saying, ﴿who could hardly understand any speech﴾ means: they do not know, and they are not near to understanding. According to this view there must be an ellipsis (idmar), namely that it is said: they can hardly understand it except after approximation and hardship, by means of gesture and the like. This verse may be used as evidence for the correctness of the first view in the interpretation of *kad*.

**The fourth:** Concerning *Ya'juj* and *Ma'juj* there are two views:

The first: they are two non-Arabic (a'jami) proper names, as shown by their being diptotes (mamnu' min al-sarf).

The second view: they are derived words (mushtaqqan). 'Asim read *Ya'juj* and *Ma'juj* with *hamz* (*Ya'ujuj wa Ma'ujuj*). The rest read *Yajuj* and *Majuj*. It was also recited, in one narration, as *Ajuj* and *Ma'juj*. Those who hold that these two names are derived have mentioned several explanations:

The first: al-Kisa'i said: *Ya'juj* is derived from *ta'ajujj al-nar*, the blazing and flaming of fire; they were named thus because of their swiftness in movement. *Ma'juj* is from the surging of the sea (*mawj al-bahr*).

The second: *Ya'juj* is derived from *ta'ajujj al-milh*, meaning the intensity of its saltiness; they were named thus because of their vigour in movement.

The third: al-Qutaybi said: it is derived from the saying of people: *ajja al-zalim* in his walk, *ya'icc ajjan*, when he ran and you heard the rustling of his running.

The fourth: al-Khalil said: *al-Ajj* is a grain like lentils, and *al-Majj* is the spitting out of saliva. It is possible that they are derived from these two.

They differed as to which of the peoples they belong to. It has been said: they are from the Turks. It has also been said: *Ya'juj* are from the Turks, and *Ma'juj* are from the Jil and the Daylam. Then among people there are those who described them as short in stature and small in body, such that the height of one of them is a span; and among them are those who described them as tall of stature and large of body, and attributed to them claws like talons on their nails and molars like those of beasts of prey.

They differed as to the manner of their corruption in the earth. It has been said: they used to kill people. It has been said: they used to eat human flesh. It has been said: they used to go out in the spring and leave nothing green for them. In sum, the word *fasad* (corruption) is capable of all these divisions. And Allah knows best what He intends.

Then Allah the Exalted related of the people between the two barriers that they said to Dhul-Qarnayn: ﴿So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set a barrier between us and them?﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read *kharajan* (with alif), and the rest read *kharjan*. It has been said: *al-kharaj* and *al-kharj* are one and the same. It has also been said that they are two distinct things. According to this latter view they differ: it has been said: *al-kharj* without an alif is the reward (*al-ju'l*), because each of the people brings out something of his own, so this one brings out certain things and that one brings out other things. And *al-kharaj* is what the ruler collects every year.

Al-Farra' said: *al-kharaj* is the original noun, and *al-kharj* is like a verbal noun. Qutrub said: *al-kharj* is the poll-tax (*al-jizyah*), and *al-kharaj* is the land-tax.

Dhul-Qarnayn said: ﴿That in which my Lord has established me is better. So help me﴾, i.e. that which made me firmly established with abundant wealth and wide affluence is better than what you offer in tribute, so I have no need of it. This is like what Sulayman, peace be upon him, said: ﴿What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you﴾ [al-Naml: 36]. Ibn Kathir read *ma makkanani* with two *nun*s, indicating them clearly (al-idhhar), and the rest read it with a single *nun* doubled (al-idgham). Then Dhul-Qarnayn said: ﴿So help me with strength, and I will make between you and them a rampart.﴾ That is: I have no need of your wealth, but ﴿help me﴾ with men and tools with which I may build the barrier. It has also been said that the meaning is: help me with money which I may spend on this important matter, and I do not seek wealth to take for myself. *Al-radm* is the barrier. It is said: *radamtu al-bab*, meaning I blocked the door; and *radamtu al-thawb*, meaning I patched the garment, because it closes the tear with a patch. And *al-radm* is more intensive than *al-sadd*, from the saying: a garment is *mardum*, meaning patches have been placed upon it.

His saying ﴿alayhi qitran﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿afrigh﴾, and its underlying sense is "bring me qitran," so the first was omitted because the second indicates it, "pour over it qitran." Then he said, ﴿fa-ma istata'u﴾, where he dropped the taa' for lightness, since the taa' is close in articulation to the ta'. It has also been read ﴿fa-ma ista'u﴾ with the sin changed to sad. ﴿An yazhiruhu﴾ means "to climb over it," i.e., they were not able to ascend it because of its height and smoothness, nor to pierce it because of its hardness and thickness.

Then Dhu al-Qarnayn said, ﴿This is a mercy from my Lord.﴾ So his saying "this" refers to the barrier: this barrier is a blessing from God and a mercy upon His servants. Or "this" refers to the power and empowerment to construct it.

﴿But when the promise of my Lord comes﴾ means: when the Hour draws near, He will make it level, i.e., flattened and leveled with the ground. Everything that is spread out after being raised has become leveled (indakka). It has also been read ﴿dakka'*﴾ with the long vowel, meaning level ground. ﴿And the promise of my Lord is ever true.﴾ Here ends the narrative of Dhu al-Qarnayn.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 99–104:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We will leave them, that day, surging over one another, and the Horn will be blown, and We will gather them in a [complete] gathering﴾ ﴿And We will present Hell that day to the disbelievers, in presentation﴾ ﴿Those whose eyes were under a veil from My remembrance, and who were unable to hear﴾.

Know that the pronoun in His saying "some of them" (ba'duhum) refers to Ya'juj and Ma'juj. And His saying "that day" (yawma'idhin) has several interpretations:

The first: that the day of the barrier (yawm al-sadd) is when some of them surge over others, behind it, because they were prevented from coming out.

The second: that at the time of the emergence, some of them surge over others. It has been said that when they come out from behind the barrier, they surge, crowding into the lands; they come to the sea and drink its water and eat its creatures, then they eat the trees, and they eat the flesh of people. They are unable to reach Makkah, Madinah and Bayt al-Maqdis. Then God sends upon them creatures which enter their ears, and they die.

The third view: that what is meant by His saying "that day" is the Day of Resurrection. All of these are possible, but the closer view is that what is meant is the time when God makes that barrier crumble to dust (dakkan); at that point some of them surge over others. After that the Horn is blown, and that becomes one of the signs of the Resurrection. The discussion of the Horn has already passed and will come later. As for the presenting of Hell and its being exposed, until it becomes manifest with its terrors, that is in the manner of the punishment of the disbelievers, because of the great distress that overtakes them. God has made clear that He will reveal it to the disbelievers who were blind and deaf. As for the blindness, it is what is meant by His saying "whose eyes were under a veil from My remembrance," and what is meant by it is the intensity of their turning away from accepting the truth. As for the deafness, it is what is meant by His saying "and who were unable to hear," meaning that their condition is worse than deafness, because the deaf man may be able to hear when shouted at, whereas these have lost that ability entirely. The scholars (al-Ashab) have argued from His saying "and who were unable to hear" that ability (istita'ah) is together with the act, since when they did not hear, they were not able to. The judge (al-Qadi) said: what is meant is their aversion from hearing that speech and their finding it burdensome, like the saying of a man: "I cannot bear to look at so-and-so."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 105–106:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they may take My servants as allies apart from Me? Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Say: Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in respect of their deeds?﴾ ﴿Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think that they are doing good work.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and His meeting, so their deeds have become worthless, and We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ ﴿That is their recompense: Hell, because they disbelieved and took My signs and My messengers in mockery.﴾ And in it are issues:

The first issue: Know that when Exalted is He explained the state of the disbelievers, that they turned away from the Reminder and from listening to what the Messenger brought, He followed it with His saying: ﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they may take My servants as allies apart from Me?﴾ The meaning is: Do they suppose that they will benefit from what they worshipped while turning away from reflecting upon the signs and rebelling against accepting His command and the command of His Messenger? This is an interrogative in the manner of rebuke.

The second issue: Abu Bakr, not traced back to Asim, recited (Afa-hasbu alladhina kafaru) with a sukun on the sin and a raf' on the ba', and this is among the letters in which he differed from Asim. He mentioned that it is the recitation of the Commander of the Faithful Ali ibn Abi Talib. On this reading, "hasb" is a mubtada' (subject), "an yattakhidhu" is the khabar (predicate), and the meaning is: Is it sufficient for them and enough for them that they take such and such? As for the rest, they recited (Afa-hasiba) in the past tense, and on this reading there is an ellipsis, and the meaning is: Do those who disbelieve think that taking My servants as allies is beneficial?

The third issue: There are several views concerning "the servants." It was said: He meant Jesus and the angels. It was said: They are the devils, whom they befriend and obey. It was said: They are the idols, which He named servants, as in His saying: ﴿They are servants like you﴾. Then Exalted is He said: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell as a lodging for the disbelievers.﴾ Concerning "nuzul" there are two views:

The first: Al-Zajjaj said: it is the abode and the dwelling place.

The second: It is that which is prepared for the guest (nazil), and the guest is the visitor. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment.﴾ Then Exalted is He mentioned what draws attention to the folly of the people, and said: ﴿Say: Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in respect of their deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world.﴾ It was said that they are the monks, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Labouring, toiling﴾. It is narrated from Mujahid that they are the People of the Book. It is narrated from Ali that Ibn al-Kawwa asked him about them, and he said: They are the people of Harura. The principle is that it is said: this is one who performs deeds thinking them to be acts of obedience, while in themselves they are acts of disobedience; and even if they were acts of obedience, they are not accepted from them because of their disbelief. Those people performed those deeds seeking reward, and they exhausted themselves in them seeking recompense and success on the Day of Resurrection. So when they do not attain their aims, He made clear that they had been astray. Then Exalted is He explained their handiwork, and said: ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and His meeting, so their deeds have become worthless.﴾ In this there are two issues:

The first issue: The meeting with Allah is an expression for seeing Him, as evidenced by the usage: "I met so-and-so," meaning "I saw him." If it is said: meeting is an expression for arrival, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Then the waters met according to a decree that had been decreed﴾ [al-Qamar: 12], and that is impossible with respect to Allah, Exalted is He, so it must be interpreted as meeting the reward of Allah. The answer: although the word "liqa'" originally expresses arrival and encounter, its use for seeing is a clear, well-known metaphor; and what they say, that its intended meaning is meeting the reward of Allah, is not complete except by supplying an implied word. It is known that interpreting the word as the well-established metaphor is preferable to interpreting it in a way that requires an implied word.

The second issue: The Mu'tazilah cited His saying: ﴿So their deeds have become worthless﴾ as evidence that the doctrine of ihbat (the nullification of deeds) and takfir (expiation) is true. We have discussed this issue thoroughly in Surat al-Baqarah, so we will not repeat it. Then Exalted is He said: ﴿So We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection.﴾ Concerning this there are several aspects:

The first: We will hold them in contempt, and they will have no weight or value with Us.

The second: We will not set up a scale for them, because the scale is only placed for the people of good deeds and bad deeds among the monotheists, to distinguish the measure of acts of obedience and the measure of sins.

The third: Al-Qadi said: whoever's disobedience prevails, his acts of obedience become as though they had never been, so nothing of his obedience enters into the weighing. This explanation is based on his view of ihbat and takfir. Then Exalted is He said: ﴿That is their recompense: Hell﴾. So His saying "That" means: that which We have mentioned and detailed of the kinds of threat is their recompense for their worthless deeds, and His saying "Hell" is an explanatory apposition to "their recompense." Then Exalted is He made clear that this recompense is a reward for a combination of two matters:

One of them: their disbelief.

The second: that to their disbelief they added that they took the signs of Allah and His messengers in mockery, and they did not confine themselves to rejecting and denying them, but went so far as to ridicule them.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verses 107–109:**

Page 149

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Paradise (Firdaws) as a lodging﴾ ﴿abiding therein forever; they will not desire any transfer from it﴾.

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the threat, He followed it with the promise. And when He mentioned regarding the disbelievers that Hell is their lodging, He followed it with mention of what encourages faith and righteous action. So He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds will have the Gardens of Paradise (Firdaws) as a lodging﴾.

The second issue: The conjunction of "doing righteous deeds" to "faith" (by the particle wa, "and"), and the conjoined element differing from the element it is conjoined to, indicates that righteous deeds are distinct from faith.

The third issue: On the authority of Qatadah: Firdaws is the middle and best part of Paradise. On the authority of Ka'b: there is no higher garden among the gardens than the Garden of Firdaws, and in it are those who enjoin good and forbid evil. On the authority of Mujahid: Firdaws is the orchard, in Byzantine (Rumi) language. On the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: ("Paradise has one hundred degrees; between every two degrees is a distance of one hundred years, and Firdaws is the highest of them in degree, and from it flow the four rivers, and the Firdaws is above them. So when you ask Allah for Paradise, ask Him for Firdaws, for above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, and from it the rivers of Paradise gush forth.")

The fourth issue: Some have said that He, exalted is He, made the whole of Paradise a lodging for the believers. A generous host, when he first provides a lodging, must follow it with a robe of honor, and beyond Paradise in its entirety there is nothing except the vision of Allah. If it is said: Did He not, in the first verse, make the whole of Hell a lodging for the disbelievers, and there remains no other punishment beyond the whole of Hell? Likewise here He made the whole of Paradise a lodging for the believers, although there is nothing else beyond Paradise. The answer: We say that for the disbeliever, after the attainment of Hell, there is a higher rank than it, which is his being veiled from the vision of Allah, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿No! Indeed, they will be veiled from their Lord that Day﴾ ﴿Then indeed they will be burning in Hellfire﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15, 16]. Thus He made being burned by the Fire later in rank than being veiled from Allah. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿they will not desire any transfer from it﴾. The hiwal is the taḥawwul (transfer, change of place); it is said: "He moved from his place, ḥiwalan," just as one says "he returned to her love, ʿawdan." The meaning is: there is no increase upon the felicities and good things of Paradise, such that they would desire other things. This description indicates the utmost perfection, because a person in this world, when he reaches any degree of happiness, has his gaze aspiring to what is higher than it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 18, verse 110:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Were the sea ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would surely be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted, even if We brought the like of it as a supplement.﴾ ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me that your God is one God. So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned in this surah the kinds of proofs and clear signs, and explained the stories of the former people, He drew attention to the perfection of the state of the Qur'an, saying: ﴿Say: Were the sea ink for the words of my Lord﴾. The word midad (ink) is the name for that with which the inkwell is replenished of ink, and for that with which the lamp is replenished of oil. The meaning is: if the words of God's knowledge and His wisdoms were written, and the sea were ink for them (and the intended meaning of "sea" is the genus), the sea would be exhausted before the words are exhausted. The essence of the statement is that seas, however much they are imagined in vastness and greatness, are finite, while the known things of God are not finite, and the finite can never suffice for the infinite. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yanfada" with a ya' because the verb precedes the plural; the rest read it with a ta' because "kalimat" is feminine. It is related that Huyayy ibn Akhtab said: "In your Book is: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good﴾ (al-Baqarah: 269), and then you recite: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ (al-Isra': 85)." So this verse was revealed, meaning that this is much good, but it is a drop from the sea of God's words.

The second issue: The opponents used this verse to refute the position of our companions that the speech of God, exalted is He, is one. They said: it is explicit in affirming the words of God, exalted is He. Our companions interpreted "words" as the objects of God's knowledge, exalted is He. Al-Jubba'i said: Also His saying: ﴿before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾ indicates that the words of God, exalted is He, may be exhausted in general, and what is established as non-existent is impossible to be eternal. Also He said: ﴿even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾, and this indicates that He, exalted is He, is able to bring the like of His speech, and what is brought is originated, and what is like the originated is also originated. The response of our companions is that what is meant by it is the expressions indicating the objects of that eternal attribute.

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained the perfection of the speech of God, He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to adopt the way of humility, saying: ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you; it is revealed to me﴾, meaning: there is no distinction between me and you in any of the attributes, except that God, exalted is He, revealed to me that there is no god but God, the One, the Unique, the Eternal Refuge. The verse indicates two objectives:

The first: that the word "innama" (only) denotes restriction, and this is His saying: ﴿that your God is one God﴾.

The second: that the Deity, exalted is He, being one God can be established by transmitted (sam'i) proofs. We have established these two objectives in the other surahs with strong arguments. Then He said: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾. Hope (raja') is the expectation of benefits reaching him, and fear (khawf) is the expectation of harms reaching him. Our companions interpreted "the meeting with the Lord" as seeing Him, while the Mu'tazilah interpreted it as meeting God's reward. This debate has already passed. And it is remarkable that He, exalted is He, placed at the end of this surah what indicates the occurrence of the vision of God in three verses:

The first of them: His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord and in His meeting﴾ [al-Kahf: 105].

The second of them: His saying: ﴿For them the Gardens of Paradise are an abode of hospitality﴾ [al-Kahf: 107].

The third of them: His saying: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾. And there is no clearer explanation than this. Then He said: ﴿let him do righteous deeds﴾, meaning: whoever has obtained the hope of meeting God, let him occupy himself with righteous deeds. And since righteous deeds may be performed for God, and may be performed for showing off and reputation, two conditions are necessarily required in them: that they be performed for God, and that they be free from aspects of associating partners. So He said: ﴿and not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾.

It was said: this verse was revealed concerning Jundub ibn Zuhayr, who said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): ("I perform an action for God, exalted is He, but when someone looks at it, it pleases me." Then the Messenger of God, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "Indeed God does not accept what is associated with another in it.") It is also related that he said to him: ("You have two rewards: the reward of the secret and the reward of the public."). So the first narration is taken to apply when he intends by his action showing off and reputation, and the second narration is taken to apply when he intends that he be followed. The first station is the station of beginners, and the second station is the station of the perfected. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad, his family and all his companions.

The author, may God be pleased with him, said: The commentary on this surah was completed on Tuesday, the seventeenth of the month of Safar, in the year six hundred and two, in the town of Ghaznin. We ask God, the Most Generous of the generous and the Most Merciful of the merciful, to grant us forgiveness and bounty on the Day of Judgment, for He is the Lord of great bounty.
